lead: One path for Friday's hour with Pavlo. Start with the round and Coframe, then the languages, the live builds (each in Python and TypeScript, tested), and the platform design. Each topic: learn it, check yourself, explain the open question aloud, then compare and rate yourself. The squares show where you stand.

onepage.lead: What to have in your head walking into Friday's hour with Pavlo. Skim it; anything that doesn't click in one read, open its topic. Say only what you can explain one level down, and say plainly what you haven't built.

points.t: The round is a working session.
points.d: Most likely a live cousin of Pavlo's agent-engineer take-home: a small runnable harness, a hard limit (5 seconds), AI tools expected, then your decisions, edge cases and 'productionization'.

points.t: They judge how you drive the tool.
points.d: Plan first, hand the agent a small testable task, read the diff, run it yourself, catch the wrong assumption, say what you would never trust it with (auth, money, deletes, migrations).
For anything you build: where state lives, what fails first at 100x, timeouts and fallbacks, idempotency, observability, cost.

points.t: Coframe's delivery is a script on someone else's revenue page.
points.d: Synchronous head script, body hidden by an anti-flicker style, a 1-second timeout that fails open, escape hatches; the risks are LCP, CSP, SPA routes and hydration mismatch.
A Beta belief per variant, sample and pick the max, hourly updates; bandits cut regret but weaken naive inference, so holdouts, SRM checks and idempotent batch updates matter.

points.t: Python: the traps a co-founder tests.
points.d: Mutable defaults, late-binding closures, generators that run lazily, the GIL and when threads, processes or asyncio win, exception groups.
Types are for the checker; runtime data from a model or an API needs validation (pydantic), and dataclasses don't validate.
Structural typing, unknown over any, narrowing with discriminated unions and a never check; parse untrusted JSON with a schema (zod) and infer the type from it.

points.t: A coroutine is lazy, a promise is eager.
points.d: A coroutine does nothing until awaited or scheduled; a promise starts at once. gather does not cancel siblings on failure; TaskGroup does.
asyncio.timeout and CancelledError in Python, AbortController and AbortSignal.timeout in TypeScript; never swallow cancellation; clean up in finally.
Semaphores and queues for concurrency and backpressure; retries only on retryable errors, with exponential backoff and full jitter.
Persist each step so a run resumes after a crash; steps must be deterministic or wrapped as idempotent activities; in-flight tool calls are at-least-once.
Containers share a kernel; gVisor and Firecracker microVMs isolate more; no ambient credentials, egress allow-lists, limits, ephemeral filesystems.
An offline task set with checks (build passes, screenshot diff, a judge with position-bias control), plus online guardrails and auto-rollback after release.

You have built durable Postgres workers, a confirm flow with idempotency, ledger-based grounding guards and an eval harness; you have not built a sandbox fleet, remote browsers or a bandit in production.

modules.title: The round, and how to work in it
modules.blurb: Know what the hour with Pavlo probably looks like, and run it like a senior engineer driving an AI tool in front of a co-founder.

topics.title: What round 2 probably is
topics.brief: Pavlo wrote Coframe's three public take-homes himself, and the agent-engineer one is the closest public model of this hour: a Next.js TV storefront where a visitor's free-text q= must drive a generated page in under 5 seconds. Round 2 is probably a live, shorter cousin of it. The nuance: 5 seconds is shorter than a naive model call that writes a whole React page, so the design, not the prompt, is the answer.
points: The template: 35 real TVs behind GET /api/products, pages left static on purpose, a visitor arriving with q= and optional ids= from an upstream Coframe agent that has profiled them, and a hard limit of a full render in under 5 seconds.
Layout spec, not JSX: have the model return a small validated layout spec (structured output checked against a schema, zod in TypeScript) that fixed components render, instead of raw page code.
Budget and fallback: give the model 3 to 4 seconds, stream or render a fast shell first, and on a timeout or invalid output fall back to the default page, so something good always renders.
Untrusted inputs: q= is free text (prompt injection, and XSS if you ever render model HTML); ids= must be checked against the catalog so a hallucinated id cannot crash the page.
Cache: normalise the query and cache the spec, because many visitors ask the same thing in different words.
Format, not fact: the exact round is not public. The brief says coding plus technical conversation, Python and TypeScript, AI tools allowed, screen shared, real scripts run.
production: All three take-homes (agent-engineer, fde, applied-science) share a runnable harness, a hard limit or metric, a fixed time, AI expected, then a defence of decisions, edge cases and scale.
The fde take-home's mock API resets state on restart, so the test is reconciliation and idempotency, not event-only syncing: expect a similar trap.
The deliverables ask for the prompts, plans, agent outputs and iterations, and every AI tool used: they read the process, not only the result.

Likely live shapes from the research: a durable step runner with retries, a bounded-concurrency job runner, a bucketing function with an SRM check, a Thompson sampler, or an LLM call wrapper with timeout and fallback.

mcq.q: In the storefront task the page must render in under 5 seconds. Which design best protects that limit?
o: Ask the model to write the full React page and cache the compiled output per visitor id
Switch to the fastest model available and raise its temperature so it answers in fewer tokens
Generate the page in a background job and show a loading spinner until the model finishes
Ask the model for a small layout spec, validate it, render fixed components, fall back on timeout
Render the static page first and replace the entire body with model HTML when it arrives
mcq.why: A validated spec rendered by fixed components keeps output small and safe, and a timeout with a fallback guarantees a render. Raw page code is slow and unsafe; a spinner can still blow the limit.

mcq.q: The upstream agent passes ids=12,99,7 and id 99 is not in the catalog. What is the right handling?
o: Drop unknown ids after checking against the catalog and render with the valid ones
Pass all three ids to the model and let it explain that one product is unavailable
Return a 400 error so the upstream agent learns to send valid ids next time
Retry the upstream agent until it sends a list where every id is valid
Replace the unknown id with the closest numeric id that does exist in the catalog
mcq.why: ids= is untrusted input from another agent. Validate against the source of truth and degrade gracefully; the visitor should still get a page.

mcq.q: Why would a live round modelled on these take-homes end by asking how you would productionize it?
o: To check that you know the names of Coframe's cloud provider and queue
Because the live code is thrown away and only the design discussion is scored
Because all three READMEs end there: they want judgement about scale, failure and cost
To see whether you can estimate the hosting bill to the nearest hundred dollars
To test whether you add Kubernetes and Kafka to every design by default
mcq.why: Every take-home README ends with a productionization question. It tests whether you can see what breaks first and what you would build next, not vocabulary.

open.q: You have an hour and the storefront: a visitor arrives with q= and you must render a page for them in under 5 seconds. Walk me through what you would build first.
open.probe: Whether you design around the hard limit and the untrusted inputs before touching the tool.
a: Restate the limit and the inputs: q= is free text, ids= is a list from another agent, both untrusted.
Shape: the model returns a small layout spec validated by a schema; fixed components render it.
Budget: a 3 to 4 second timeout on the model call, a fast shell first, the default page as the fallback.
Validate ids against the catalog, never render model HTML, cache specs by normalised query.
Build order: fallback page and spec renderer first, then the model call, then the three example queries as tests.

say: The first thing I'd build is the fallback, because then the page always renders whatever the model does.
Then I'd have the model return a small layout spec, validate it, and render it with fixed components, with a timeout of three or four seconds. Raw JSX from a model is slow and I can't trust it.
And I'd treat q and ids as untrusted, check the ids against the catalog, and cache by normalised query. That's pretty much the whole skeleton.
avoid: Saying you know the exact format of the round: say 'the take-homes suggest', not 'the round is'.
Starting with the prompt instead of the limit and the fallback.

topics.title: What AI-allowed rounds judge
topics.brief: When AI tools are allowed, the thing being scored moves from producing code to judging it: you decide, the tool executes. The nuance people miss is that a flawless first generation scores less than a calm recovery from a bad one, because recovery shows control.
points: You decide, the tool executes: state the data model, the interfaces and the build order out loud, then delegate pieces. Letting the tool make architecture decisions is a named red flag.
Orientation first: strong candidates spend the first five to ten minutes reading, asking clarifying questions and forming a plan, with no prompt yet.
Decomposition: give the tool AI-sized chunks; pasting the whole problem in signals you outsourced the thinking.
Verification: prompt, review, run, confirm, move on. Silently accepting output, or not running it, costs the most.
Ownership and recovery: 'the AI wrote it' is never an answer to 'why does this do that'. Reverting, narrowing the prompt or hand-editing calmly is a positive signal.
production: Meta's AI-enabled round (from October 2025, per Hello Interview): 60 minutes in CoderPad, bug fixing, then 120 or more lines of implementation where AI is expected, then optimisation; scored on problem solving, code quality, verification, communication.

Shopify (Hello Interview): an empty repo, your own IDE and AI tools, screen shared; they watch decomposition, review of generated code, a testing strategy and narration. Closest to Coframe's open format.
Canva's engineering blog says candidates are expected to use Copilot, Cursor or Claude, and red flags are accepting output without scrutiny and not owning the code.
Anthropic's write-up on AI-resistant evaluations names the choice between a print statement and asking a model to build a debugger as a judgement signal.
Josh Payne says he wants to see how people work with you before you work fully with them, which is why this round is a working session, not a quiz.

mcq.q: Ten minutes in, the tool gave you working code on the first try. What will the interviewer most want to see next?
o: You moving straight to the next feature to use the time you saved
You asking the tool to add logging, config and docs before moving on
You regenerating once more to check the tool gives the same answer twice
You committing the change and telling the interviewer the tool is reliable today
You reading the diff aloud, saying what it does, and running it against an edge case
mcq.why: Working output still has to be reviewed and verified by you. The rhythm they score is prompt, review, run, confirm.

mcq.q: The tool's output is close but a test fails. Which response scores best?
o: Re-roll the same prompt until a version passes the test
Read the failure, find the defect yourself or with a targeted question, then fix
Delete the failing test, since the code matched the prompt you gave
Paste the whole file back and ask the tool to fix everything it can find
Switch to a different AI tool in case it handles this kind of problem better
mcq.why: Debugging by reading the failure and asking targeted questions shows control. Re-rolling or dumping the file hands the thinking back to the tool.

mcq.q: What is the most common way candidates lose the decomposition signal in an AI-allowed round?
o: Pasting the whole problem statement into the tool as the first prompt
Writing the interfaces by hand before asking for any implementation
Asking the tool for a test before asking it for the code under test
Keeping the plan in a file and editing it as requirements change
Spending the first five minutes reading the code without prompting
mcq.why: The full-problem dump signals outsourced thinking. The other options are the behaviours interviewers reward.

open.q: You used the agent a lot in the last twenty minutes. Why did you accept that last diff, and what would you not let it write?
open.probe: Whether your use of the tool is deliberate and owned.
a: Name what I checked: I read the diff, it matches the interface I wrote, and the test for the edge case passed when I ran it.
Name what I would change if I had more time, so it is clear I read it.
What I keep for myself: the core logic, concurrency, anything touching auth, money, migrations or deletes.
Why: those are where a plausible wrong answer is expensive and hard to see in a diff.

say: I think the way to use it here is that I make the decisions and it does the typing.
I accepted that diff because I read it, it matches the interface I wrote, and I ran the empty input and the duplicate case and both passed.
Where I'd take over is concurrency, auth and anything that writes data. A plausible wrong answer there is the expensive kind.
avoid: 'The AI wrote that part' as an answer to any why question.
Claiming you never need to check its output.

topics.title: Driving the tool on a shared screen
topics.brief: Drive the agent like a junior pair you guide and check: plan first, small testable asks, read every diff, run the real script, and say out loud what you would not trust it with. The nuance: with an agent like Claude Code the risk is it running ahead through many files, so you keep each step small enough to review in a glance.
points: Plan first: ask for a plan or write one, edit it yourself, reject parts out loud, keep it in a file.
Small testable asks: one function or one behaviour per prompt, with the file, the interface, the constraint and an example input and output.
Read the diff: say what it does and what you would change before accepting; do not let it touch files you did not ask about.
Run it: the real script after each change, plus the failure case on purpose (empty input, duplicate, crash after a side effect).
Thin slices and commits: smallest end-to-end thing first, commit after each green step, so a bad generation is one revert away.
Scope control: when it adds abstractions, config and logging nobody asked for, say 'that is more than I want' and cut it.
production: Pavlo's own take-home commits are co-authored by Claude Sonnet 4.6: he uses Claude Code himself and will recognise fluent versus careless use.

Use the tool where it is strong (scaffolding, tests, fixtures, regex, glue, API shapes) and write or spec the tricky part yourself (state machine, concurrency, the algorithm), because that is where he probes.
Interviewer quote from Hello Interview: they want to see you making decisions and using the AI to execute them.
Coframe's other posts name Claude Code, Cursor and Devin, and 'AI-driven software development workflows': fluency is assumed, judgement is what is scored.

mcq.q: You need a retrying job runner. Which first prompt is best on a shared screen?
o: Build a production-ready job runner with retries, metrics, config and a CLI
Here is the whole task description; implement it and tell me when the tests pass
Suggest five architectures for a job runner and pick the one you think is best
Write run_with_retry(fn, attempts, base_delay) in runner.py with a test for two failures then success
Write the job runner and also refactor any other files you think need cleaning up
mcq.why: Small, specific, testable: a named function, a file, a signature and an example behaviour. The others are dumps, delegation of decisions, or invitations to run ahead.

mcq.q: The agent edited three files when you asked for one function. What do you do?
o: Accept it, since more changes usually means the tool understood the bigger picture
Revert the unrequested edits, say why, and re-ask with the scope stated
Keep the edits but add a comment saying the tool made them
Ask the tool to explain the extra edits and accept them if the explanation sounds right
Run the tests and keep everything if they pass, whatever changed
mcq.why: Unreviewed scope creep is the agent-specific risk. Cutting it back out loud is the control signal; passing tests do not cover what you did not ask for.

mcq.q: Which part of a Coframe-style task should you keep for yourself rather than hand to the tool?
o: Test fixtures with three example queries
The regex that parses the comma-separated ids
TypeScript types for the products API response
Boilerplate for the Next.js route handler
The state transitions of a retry and resume loop
mcq.why: The state machine is where correctness lives and where he will probe. Fixtures, regex, types and boilerplate are what the tool is good at.

open.q: Show me how you'd use the agent to build this. Talk me through your first three prompts before you send them.
open.probe: Control of the tool: plan, granularity, verification.
a: Prompt one: propose a plan in a file; I edit it and say what I am cutting.
Prompt two: the smallest end-to-end slice, one function with its test, named file and signature.
Then I read the diff, run the test and the real script, and commit.
Prompt three: the next slice, or the failure case I want handled, with the expected behaviour stated.

say: The way I'd do it: first I ask for a plan and edit it myself, so the design is mine.
Then small asks, one function and its test at a time. I read every diff, run it, and commit when it's green, so a bad generation is one revert.
If it starts adding things I didn't ask for, I cut them. Smaller is easier to check.
avoid: Letting the agent run for minutes across many files while you watch silently.

topics.title: Setup, and narrating while it works
topics.brief: Everything that can fail before the problem starts should be tested the day before: logins, runtimes, a clean repo, screen sharing. While the agent works you hold two conversations, so decide in advance what you say in that gap: what you are about to verify. The nuance: if the tool is slow or down, carrying on by hand is a good signal, not a failure.
points: Ready to go: a working claude or codex login, a terminal, node and python both running, a clean git repo, a scratch folder, a one-line way to run the script and the tests.
Instructions file: a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md with your conventions (type hints, test style, no new dependencies unless asked); ask him if that setup is fine.
Screen: test sharing and a readable font size before the call.
Two conversations: narrate intent before each action and explain generated code as you accept it; silence while the agent types loses communication points.
Fill the wait: say what you will check ('the empty input, a duplicate id, a crash after the side effect'), or talk through the trade-off he is likely to ask about.
production: The research's own tactic: open by saying how you will use the tools (plan and interfaces yourself, agent for boilerplate and tests, every diff reviewed and run).

Language points worth having ready while the agent works: asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) and Semaphore for bounded concurrency, Promise.allSettled versus Promise.all, AbortController for timeouts, discriminated unions and satisfies.
Their take-homes use Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript run with tsx, Python 3 with uv: having both toolchains warm avoids a dead first five minutes.
Anthropic's progressive format (a secondary source, unverified) adds complexity every 15 to 20 minutes: keep the structure easy to change.

mcq.q: The agent is taking a minute to produce a change. What is the best use of that minute?
o: Stay quiet so the interviewer can watch the tool work uninterrupted
Open a second agent on the same task to see which one finishes first
Say what you will check when it finishes and why those cases matter
Apologise for the delay and explain that the tool is usually faster
Start writing a different feature by hand in the same file
mcq.why: Narrating the verification plan fills the gap with the judgement he is scoring. A parallel edit to the same file invites conflicts.

mcq.q: Ten minutes into the round the AI tool stops responding. What should you do?
o: Ask to reschedule, since the round is meant to test AI-assisted work
Wait for it to recover so the interviewer sees the intended workflow
Switch to a browser chatbot and paste the whole problem in
Say so, and keep going by hand on the smallest next slice
Spend the time debugging the tool's login until it works again
mcq.why: Carrying on by hand is a legitimate signal of skill and calm. Pasting the whole problem into another chat is the dump pattern again.

mcq.q: Why put a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md with your conventions in the repo before the round?
o: It encodes defaults like test style and no new dependencies, so each prompt can stay short
It lets the interviewer grade your prompts without watching the screen
It removes the need to read diffs, since the tool follows the rules
It is required for Claude Code and Codex to start in a new folder
It lets the tool decide the architecture without you stating it each time
mcq.why: An instructions file carries your standing conventions, so prompts stay small. It does not replace reviewing output or making the design decisions.

open.q: Before we start: how are you going to use the AI tools today?
open.probe: Whether you have a deliberate workflow you can state in thirty seconds.
a: I plan and write the interfaces myself.
The agent does boilerplate, fixtures and test scaffolding, in small asks.
I read every diff and run the script and tests before moving on, and commit when green.
I keep concurrency, data writes and the core algorithm for myself, and I will say when I override it.

say: I'll plan and write the interfaces myself, and use the agent for boilerplate and tests.
I'll read every diff and run it before I move on, and commit each green step so I can back out of a bad generation.
If it's slow, I'll keep going by hand and tell you what I'm checking.
avoid: Discovering a broken login or a missing runtime on the call.

topics.title: The standing productionization answer
topics.brief: Every Coframe take-home ends with 'how would you make this a scalable system?', so have one answer shape you can lay over anything you build in the hour. The shape: what breaks first, then the fixes in order of cost. The nuance: at Coframe's scale the first thing to break is usually model latency, rate limits or a bad generation reaching a customer, not compute.
points: First break: name it before listing fixes. For a generated UI it is model latency and cost per visitor; for an agent fleet it is provider rate limits, then human review capacity.
Cache and precompute: normalise inputs, cache outputs, generate ahead of traffic where you can, so the model is off the hot path.
Queue the slow work: anything long goes to a durable queue with workers, retries with backoff and idempotency keys, so a crash re-runs safely.
Gate quality: an eval set from real failures and validation on every output, failing closed before deploy; fail open on the customer's page.
See it: a trace per request or run, cost and latency per step, alerts on fallback rate and error rate.
Cost: budgets per run, cheaper models where evals say quality holds.
production: Coframe's own snippet fails open: a 1 second anti-flicker timeout and script.onerror both show the page. Deploy gates for generated changes should fail closed.
The research's sizing example (labelled an estimate): 1,000 concurrent agents at 20k tokens per minute each is 20M tokens per minute against provider limits, before any compute concern.
Ramp's write-up on its background coding agent says human review capacity became the bottleneck as agent parallelism grew.
For the storefront: specs cached by normalised query, a fallback page, model calls behind a timeout, and the fallback rate as the alarm.

mcq.q: Your storefront prototype calls the model on every visit. Traffic grows 100 times. What breaks first?
o: The Next.js server's CPU, because rendering fixed components is expensive
The products API, because 35 TVs is too many rows to serve quickly
Model latency, cost per visit and provider rate limits
The browser, because the layout spec is too large to parse
The cache, because normalised queries fill memory within minutes
mcq.why: Per-visit model calls scale cost and latency linearly and hit rate limits. Caching by normalised query and a fallback take the model off the hot path.

mcq.q: Which pairing of failure policies fits a system where agents generate changes for customers' live pages?
o: Fail closed on the page and fail open at the deploy gate
Fail open everywhere, so customers never see an error
Fail closed everywhere, so nothing unverified ever shows
Fail open at the deploy gate and retry on the page until it works
Fail open on the page and fail closed at the deploy gate
mcq.why: On the customer's page, showing the original beats a blank page. Before deploy, an unverified change should not ship. Coframe's snippet does the first.

mcq.q: In a fleet of thousands of coding agents, which limit does the research expect to bite after rate limits?
o: Disk space for repository clones
Human review capacity for the changes
Database connections from the control plane
DNS lookups from sandboxes
Git server bandwidth
mcq.why: Ramp reported review capacity as the bottleneck. The design answer is small changes, evidence in the PR and risk-tiered review.

open.q: That works for a demo. How would you make it a scalable system for hundreds of customers and hundreds of thousands of interfaces?
open.probe: Whether you see what breaks first and order fixes by cost.
a: Name the first break: model latency and cost per request, then rate limits.
Cache by normalised input and precompute where traffic is predictable; keep the fallback.
Move slow generation to a durable queue with idempotent retries.
Gate quality with validation and an eval set from real failures, fail closed before deploy, fail open on the page.
Trace each request, watch fallback rate and cost per request, set budgets.

say: I'd start with what breaks first, and here I think it's the model call on every visit: latency, cost and rate limits.
So cache by normalised query, keep the fallback, and push generation off the request path onto a queue.
Then gate quality before anything ships, and watch the fallback rate. If that climbs, something upstream is wrong.
avoid: Reaching for Kubernetes and Kafka before naming what actually breaks.
Claiming Temporal, Modal, E2B or Browserbase experience: name them as options, not as things you ran.

topics.title: What Pavlo likely values
topics.brief: Pavlo Razumovskyi is a co-founder and founding engineer at Coframe, before that a Staff ML Engineer at Pinterest and co-founder and CTO of INKHUNTER (YC S18). His public trail points to someone who reads quality as 'does it look right and measure right' and values ownership, speed and pragmatism. The nuance: his background is one search snippet deep, so use it to prepare, not to flatter him with it.
points: Taste in public: he wrote the three take-homes, tested Largest Contentful Paint in a repo of his own, and built a messy A/B dataset screen (duplicates, staging rows, uneven volume).
What that suggests: care for page performance, experiment hygiene, leakage and honest effect sizes.
Founder questions: expect 'what would you cut?' and 'what breaks first at 100x?'.
Title: public profiles say co-founder and founding engineer, not CTO.
Unverified: the Pinterest role appeared only in a search snippet; no talks or posts by him were found.
production: His GitHub (1um) shows a 2024 hackathon agent with actions for travel and LinkedIn, and 20 commits to Coframe's open-source Coffee project in late 2023.
INKHUNTER, an AR tattoo preview app, was reported at 20M+ users and sold: he has shipped to a large audience and will weight pragmatism over abstraction.
The applied-science take-home scores a policy walk-forward against hidden truth and must be leak-free and 'do no harm': a sign he probes for silent data mistakes.

mcq.q: Given his public repos, which kind of mistake is Pavlo most likely to notice in your work?
o: A page that renders correctly but slowly, or numbers built on dirty data
Missing docstrings on helper functions
Using TypeScript where he would have used JavaScript
Choosing pytest over plain asserts for tests
Not using the newest framework version
mcq.why: He tested LCP and built a messy A/B dataset screen: performance and data hygiene are what his trail shows he cares about.

mcq.q: How should you use the fact that he was at Pinterest and INKHUNTER?
o: Open by praising both companies to build rapport
Claim experience with AR so the conversation has common ground
Ask him to compare Pinterest's ML stack to Coframe's
Use it to expect pragmatic, measure-it questions, without leaning on it in the room
Avoid any example involving images or UI quality
mcq.why: The Pinterest detail is from a single snippet. Let it shape your preparation; leading with it risks being wrong and reads as flattery.

open.q: You have two hours and a client call. What do you cut, and what do you tell the client?
open.probe: Founder judgement: scope, honesty, what must work.
a: Keep the path the client will see working end to end, with the fallback.
Cut polish, extra cases and anything not on that path; write them down as next steps.
Tell the client what works, what does not yet, and when; no overclaiming.
Example: in the fde task, two-way sync with reconciliation over a flaky API beats a pretty one-way sync.

say: I'd keep the one path the client will actually use working end to end, including what happens when something fails.
Everything else I'd cut and write down as next steps.
And I'd tell the client plainly what works today and what doesn't yet. Overclaiming costs more later.
avoid: Calling him the CTO, or quoting his Pinterest title as settled fact.

modules.title: Coframe, as an engineer sees it
modules.blurb: Explain how Coframe's product works under the hood, where it can break a customer's page, and ask Pavlo questions only someone who read the code would ask.

topics.title: The pipeline, from idea to traffic
topics.brief: Coframe's agents analyse a customer's site, generate ideas and variants (copy, code, visuals), a human approves them in the app, then Coframe deploys, runs an optimiser, personalises by segment and tracks results. The nuance for a platform engineer: that loop is a long, multi-step agent run with side effects on someone else's revenue page, so it needs sandboxes, durable workflows, traces and a deploy gate underneath.
points: The loop: analyse, ideate, generate, approve, deploy, optimise, personalise, measure, learn. Winners and losers feed the next round of ideas.
Agents that check themselves: the Agent Engineer post asks agents to validate their own work and catch bugs, off-brand output and poor UX before launch, with online and offline evals.
Platform underneath: a sandbox to run generated code and tests, a durable workflow so a multi-hour run survives a crash, traces a human and an agent can read, an eval harness that gates deploy.
Scale words from the posts: 'hundreds of thousands of interfaces' and post-rollout regression monitoring.
Traffic floor: Josh Payne says they target sites with 200,000+ monthly visitors (lower for high-ticket), because bandits and tests need traffic.
production: Company facts: founded 2023, CEO Josh Payne, a $9.3M seed in October 2024 (from aggregator listings), SOC 2 Type II, content approval gates and automatic fallbacks before deployment.
Customers named in job posts: Dropbox, Replit, Intuit. The '$221.4M incremental revenue' and '120% QoQ' figures are the company's own claims.
Browserbase's case study describes Coframe using remote browsers to fetch pages and capture DOM and screenshots for the agents.
March 2026: acquired Haystacks to build an autonomous growth agent.

mcq.q: Which part of Coframe's loop most needs a durable workflow rather than a plain request handler?
o: Serving the variant to a visitor at page load
Reading the projectId from the inline snippet
Updating the Beta counts once an hour
The agent run that ideates, codes, renders and verifies a variant over many steps
Sending a conversion event to Google Analytics
mcq.why: A multi-step agent run with paid model calls and side effects must survive a crash without redoing everything. Serving and event forwarding are short requests.

mcq.q: An agent generated a variant that breaks the cart button on mobile Safari. Where should it be caught first?
o: By a pre-deploy gate that renders it in a real browser and checks the CTA works
By the bandit, which will send less traffic to it once conversions drop
By the customer, during in-app approval of the copy
By the anti-flicker timeout, which shows the original after one second
By Google Analytics alerts on the conversion rate the next morning
mcq.why: A rendered check before deploy fails closed. The bandit and analytics catch it only after customers have lost money; the timeout does not detect broken variants.

mcq.q: Why does Coframe target sites with a lot of traffic?
o: Because the edge script only works behind a large CDN
Because generating variants is free only above a traffic threshold
Because tests and bandits need enough conversions to tell variants apart
Because small sites cannot install a synchronous head script
Because SOC 2 requires a minimum visitor count
mcq.why: Learning which variant wins needs conversions, and conversions need visitors. Josh gives 200,000+ monthly as the target.

open.q: If you joined the platform team, what would the infrastructure under that idea-to-traffic loop need to be?
open.probe: Whether you can map the product loop to platform pieces.
a: A durable workflow per agent run, so a crash at step 30 resumes, not restarts.
Sandboxes and remote browsers to run generated code and render the variant.
A deploy gate: render, check the CTA and console errors, score brand, fail closed.
Traces per run that a person and the agent can read; regression monitoring after rollout.
Example: the broken cart button is caught at the gate, not by the bandit a day later.

say: The way I read it, the product is a long agent run that ends up changing someone's revenue page.
So underneath you need the run to be durable, the generated code to run somewhere isolated, and a gate before anything ships that actually renders it and checks the button works.
Then traces, so when something goes wrong a person or the agent can see why.
avoid: Quoting the revenue and growth figures as facts: they are the company's claims.

topics.title: The edge script, and failing open
topics.brief: The customer pastes one inline script in their head tag, synchronously, because it hides the page until variants are applied. It hides the body with a CSS variable, loads the SDK asynchronously, and shows the page after 1 second or on a load error whatever happens. The nuance: this is a third-party script mutating someone else's checkout, so every design choice is a trade between flicker, speed and the risk of breaking the page.
points: Synchronous by design: it must sit inline in head, not in a tag manager, because anti-flicker only works if it runs before first paint.
Hide, then show: it sets `body { opacity: var(--cf-show) !important }` with --cf-show at 0, then loads `cf.js` async from edge.cofra.me.
Fail open: `setTimeout(show, 1000)` and `script.onerror = show` mean a slow or failed SDK costs at most a second of hidden page, never a blank one.
Modes: Body hides the whole page; Include hides only marked elements; Exclude hides everything but marked elements. Narrower hiding means less delay.
Escape hatches: ?cf_disable in the URL, an emergency feature-flag shutdown, tracking-only, cookieless and cookie-consent modes, a CSP nonce option.
Check it is live: `Coframe.status.initialized` in the console, with userToken, sessionId and variantsAndElements.
production: The cost of hiding the body: Largest Contentful Paint can slip by up to the timeout, so the 1 second cap is a performance budget, not only a safety net.
CSP: a strict Content-Security-Policy blocks inline scripts unless they carry a nonce, hence the nonce option.
Consent: under GDPR the cookie-consent mode delays identity until the visitor agrees, which affects sticky assignment.
Integrations listed include Next.js, React, Nuxt, Webflow, Shopify, GTM and a server-side Conversion API.
The '2 minutes to install, about 30 ms' claim is from an old launch post: treat it as marketing.

mcq.q: Why must Coframe's snippet be installed inline and synchronously, not through a tag manager?
o: Tag managers cannot load scripts from a CDN domain
Synchronous scripts are cached longer by browsers than async ones
Tag managers strip the projectId from the configuration object
Synchronous loading makes the SDK itself download faster
Anti-flicker only works if the page is hidden before first paint, which an async tag manager cannot promise
mcq.why: The hide has to happen before the browser paints. The SDK itself still loads async; only the small hiding snippet is synchronous.

mcq.q: The SDK host is down for an hour. What does a visitor see with Coframe's snippet?
o: A blank page until the SDK host recovers
The original page after at most about one second, or sooner via onerror
The last variant they saw, served from the browser cache
An error banner asking them to reload
The control page, but only after the browser's network timeout of about 30 seconds
mcq.why: The timeout and the onerror handler both call show(). That is failing open: the customer's page wins over the experiment.

mcq.q: Which change would reduce the performance cost of anti-flicker most on a page where only the hero is tested?
o: Use Include mode so only the marked hero element is hidden
Raise the timeout to 3 seconds so the SDK always finishes
Move the snippet to the end of the body
Load the SDK synchronously as well
Switch to tracking-only mode permanently
mcq.why: Hiding only what changes lets the rest of the page paint. Moving the snippet down defeats anti-flicker; a longer timeout makes the cost worse.

open.q: Our script hides the body for up to a second. Is that acceptable? What are the alternatives and the costs?
open.probe: Whether you can weigh flicker against performance and safety on a customer's page.
a: It is a deliberate trade: no flash of the original, at the cost of up to a second of LCP on slow loads.
It fails open, which is right: the customer's page beats the experiment.
Cheaper: Include mode, hiding only changed elements.
Better where possible: decide at the edge or server so the variant is in the HTML, no hiding at all.
Watch: LCP on test pages versus control, and how often the timeout fires.

say: I think the one-second hide is a reasonable default, because it fails open. If anything goes wrong the customer's page shows.
The cost is LCP on slow connections, so I'd want to see how often the timeout actually fires, and use Include mode where only one section changes.
Where you control the server or the edge, I'd rather decide there and not hide anything.
avoid: Saying the snippet loads the whole SDK synchronously: only the small hiding snippet is synchronous.

topics.title: Flicker, hydration and the edge alternative
topics.brief: Flicker is the original rendering, then JavaScript swapping in the variant. Client-side swapping works on any site but fights frameworks: React and Next hydrate expecting the server's DOM, and single-page apps change routes without a page load. The nuance: deciding the variant at the edge removes flicker entirely, but then caching becomes the bug everyone hits.
points: Hydration mismatch: if the script mutates the DOM before React hydrates, React can warn, re-render over the change, or attach handlers to the wrong nodes.
SPA routes: a client-side route change loads no new page, so the script must listen for navigation and re-apply variants, or the change vanishes.
Edge decision: middleware assigns a variant, sets a cookie and rewrites to the variant route before any HTML is sent; no flicker, no layout shift, no third-party script.
HTML rewriting: for sites Coframe does not host, an edge HTMLRewriter-style patch is another option.
Cache trap: a CDN that caches one variant serves it to everyone. Key the cache on the variant (or separate variant paths) and never cache the assignment response.
Exposure: log the exposure when the visitor actually sees the changed element, or analysis is diluted by people who never reached it.
production: Vercel's A/B write-up stores the assignment in a cookie and rewrites the URL to the variant route in Edge Middleware.
Rewrite, not redirect: a rewrite serves the variant from the same URL with no extra round trip.
Set `Vary: cookie` (or variant-specific paths) so the CDN keys correctly.
Pavlo has an lcp-test repo of his own: page performance is something he has measured himself.

mcq.q: On a Next.js site the variant appears, then vanishes a moment later. What is the most likely cause?
o: The anti-flicker timeout fired before the SDK loaded
The CDN served a stale copy of the SDK
The visitor's cookie expired between requests
React hydration re-rendered over the DOM the script had already changed
The bandit reassigned the visitor to control
mcq.why: Hydration expects the server-rendered DOM; changes made before or during it can be overwritten. The timeout only affects visibility, not content.

mcq.q: On a single-page app, variants apply on the landing page but not after the visitor clicks to another route. Why?
o: Hydration overwrote the changes on the second page
A client-side route change loads no new page, so the script never re-runs unless it listens for navigation
The anti-flicker style was removed after the first page
Cookieless mode forgets the visitor between routes
The CDN cached the first route's variant for the whole site
mcq.why: SPAs swap content without a page load. The script has to hook navigation and re-apply; this is a different failure from hydration.

mcq.q: You move assignment to edge middleware and every visitor now sees variant B. What did you most likely miss?
o: The hash does not include the experiment id
The cookie is set with SameSite=Lax
The rewrite should have been a redirect
The middleware runs after the HTML is sent
The CDN caches the variant response without keying on the variant or cookie
mcq.why: The classic edge bug: the first variant served gets cached for everyone. Vary on the cookie or use per-variant paths.

open.q: Design how we would ship an AI-generated variant to a customer's page with no flicker. How do you cache it, and how do you keep assignment sticky?
open.probe: Edge versus client trade-offs, and the caching trap.
a: Where we sit in front of the site, decide at the edge: hash of experiment and visitor id, cookie, rewrite to the variant.
Cache per variant, never the assignment step; set Vary or use variant paths.
Sticky: persist the first assignment in a cookie so weight changes do not move existing visitors.
Where we cannot sit in front, the client script with narrow anti-flicker, SPA navigation hooks and care around hydration.
Log exposure when the element is seen.

say: If we can sit in front of the site, I'd decide at the edge: assign, set a cookie, rewrite to the variant. Then there's nothing to hide.
The thing I'd watch is the CDN caching one variant for everyone, so the cache has to key on the variant.
Where we can't, the client script is the fallback, and then hydration and SPA route changes are the two things that bite.
avoid: Claiming you know how Coframe's SDK handles hydration internally: you only know the public snippet.

topics.title: The Thompson-sampling optimiser
topics.brief: Each variant keeps a Beta(a, b) belief about its conversion rate; on every assignment Coframe samples one value from each and serves the highest. Conversions grow a, non-conversions grow b, updated hourly. The nuance: a bandit minimises lost conversions while learning, but the price is weaker inference about how big the effect really is.
points: Beta belief: a counts conversions, b counts non-conversions; with a uniform prior, Beta(1 + conversions, 1 + misses).
Sample, then argmax: `max(arms, key=lambda k: random.betavariate(a[k], b[k]))`. Uncertain arms sometimes sample high, which is the exploration.
Regret: traffic shifts toward winners as evidence grows, so fewer visitors see losers than in a fixed 50/50 test.
Arm replacement: AI generates new variants from performance data, consistent losers are replaced, and new arms get an incubation period so they are not killed early.
Priors and holdouts: priors can be uniform or industry-informed; experiment-level and global holdouts keep an unbiased baseline.
production: A two-arm simulation in the research with true rates 5% and 8% sent about 97% of 20,000 impressions to the better arm.
Coframe's '90% of the time' winner-finding rate against about 15% for classic A/B is a marketing figure; the applied-science take-home also uses a 0.15 win rate default.
Hourly batch updates rather than per-event: simpler, idempotent if replayed carefully, and tolerant of event lag.
Long-tail pages with little traffic each are where dynamic arms and bandits earn their keep (Coframe's long-tail post).

mcq.q: Variant A has 2 conversions from 10 visits and B has 200 from 1,000. Both have a 20% rate. What does Thompson sampling do differently with them?
o: Treats them identically, since their rates are equal
Always picks B, because it has more data
Samples A's value from a much wider Beta, so A sometimes wins the draw and gets explored
Drops A until it reaches 1,000 visits
Averages them into one arm until their rates diverge
mcq.why: Same mean, different certainty. The wide Beta for A produces high draws sometimes, which is how the bandit explores uncertain arms.

mcq.q: Why does Coframe give newly generated variants an incubation period?
o: To wait for the LLM to finish generating the variant code
So customers can approve the copy before it goes live
To let the CDN cache warm up for the new variant
So a new arm with few observations is not starved or replaced before its belief is informative
Because the Beta update only runs once a day
mcq.why: Against arms with long histories, a new arm can lose a few early draws and be cut on noise. Incubation protects it until there is evidence.

mcq.q: What does a bandit give up compared with a fixed-horizon A/B test?
o: An unbiased, easily interpreted estimate of the effect size
The ability to test more than two variants
Any protection against showing losing variants
The ability to use conversions as the metric
Randomisation of visitors to variants
mcq.why: Adaptive allocation biases naive estimates and p-values. It still randomises and can test many arms; it shows fewer visitors the losers.

open.q: Why would we use a bandit instead of a fixed 50/50 test, and when is the bandit the wrong tool?
open.probe: Regret versus inference, and knowing the limits.
a: Bandit: many variants, limited traffic, and the goal is conversions now, so fewer visitors see losers.
Thompson sampling: Beta per arm, sample and serve the highest, update hourly.
Wrong tool when you need a clean effect size for a decision, when conversions are long delayed, or when traffic is strongly non-stationary.
Keep a holdout either way, so there is an unbiased baseline.

say: I'd use the bandit when there are a lot of variants and not much traffic per page, because it stops wasting visitors on losers.
I'd run a fixed test when someone needs to know how big the effect is, because the bandit's numbers are biased by how it allocated.
And I'd keep a holdout either way. I haven't run a bandit in production, so that's from reading your post and simulating it, not from experience.
avoid: Implying you have run a bandit in production.
Deriving regret bounds or sequential test maths you cannot defend.

topics.title: Bandit trade-offs, and the engineering under them
topics.brief: The statistical trade-offs of a bandit (non-stationary traffic, delayed conversions, novelty) turn into engineering questions: where the counts live, whether replaying an event batch double counts, what happens when the sampler is down, and how weight changes interact with sticky assignment. The nuance most people miss: when bandit weights move, a pure hash reassigns existing visitors unless you persist their first assignment.
points: Sticky trap: a hash over changing weights moves visitors between variants. Persist the first assignment (cookie or server record) and apply new weights only to new visitors.
Idempotent updates: a counts per arm per segment must not double when an hourly batch is replayed; key updates by batch or event id.
Fail to control: if the sampler is unavailable, serve control rather than block the page.
Non-stationarity and delay: traffic mix changes by day and campaign, and recent visitors have not converted yet; discount old data and use a conversion window.
SRM: a 50/50 split showing 52/48 at large n means assignment, logging, redirects or bots are broken; check with a chi-square and alert at a strict threshold.
production: Assignment as a deterministic hash of experiment id, salt and visitor id mapped to [0, 1): stateless, stable, and independent across experiments because the experiment id is in the hash.
The research's SRM check: 5,200 against 4,800 gives p about 6e-05, investigate; a common alert threshold is p < 0.001.
A/A tests validate the bucketing before trusting any result.
Guardrails for an agent that edits live pages: Core Web Vitals, error rate, revenue per visitor, plus a synthetic browser that checks the page renders and the CTA works, with automatic rollback.

mcq.q: Bandit weights shift from 50/50 to 80/20 and returning visitors start seeing a different variant. Why?
o: The visitor ids changed when the weights changed
The CDN cache expired at the same time
The hash maps the same bucket to a different variant under new cumulative weights
Thompson sampling randomises returning visitors on purpose
The SRM check reassigned them to rebalance traffic
mcq.why: The bucket value is stable, but where it falls against new weights is not. Persist first assignments or edit a fixed bucket-to-variant map.

mcq.q: A 50/50 experiment shows 52,000 against 48,000 visitors. What should you conclude first?
o: Variant A is converting better, so the bandit sent it more traffic
The difference is noise at this sample size
Visitors prefer variant A's design
The hash function needs a longer salt
Something in assignment, logging, redirects or bot filtering is broken
mcq.why: That is a sample ratio mismatch with a tiny p-value. In a fixed split, traffic should not depend on the variant, so the pipeline is suspect before the result.

mcq.q: The event pipeline replays the last hour's batch after a crash. What protects the Beta counts?
o: Running the update less often, once a day
Recording which batch or event ids have been applied and skipping repeats
Resetting all arms to their prior after any crash
Sampling more draws per assignment to average out the error
Moving the counts into the visitor's cookie
mcq.why: At-least-once delivery means replays happen. Idempotent updates keyed by batch or event id stop double counting; resetting throws away the learning.

open.q: How do you handle the fact that bandit data biases effect estimates, conversions arrive late, and traffic is not stationary?
open.probe: Whether you can turn statistics caveats into concrete engineering.
a: Bias: keep a holdout or fixed control share for an unbiased baseline; report effects from it.
Delay: attribute within a conversion window and do not penalise impressions younger than it.
Non-stationarity: discount old observations or use a sliding window.
Engineering: idempotent hourly updates, persisted first assignment, fail to control, SRM and A/A checks.

say: For the effect size I'd trust the holdout, not the bandit's own numbers.
For late conversions I'd use a window, so the last hour's visitors don't look like losers yet.
And on the engineering side: make the update safe to replay, keep assignment sticky when weights move, and serve control if the sampler is down.
avoid: Quoting sequential-test formulas: say you would use an always-valid method and name the trade-off.

topics.title: Their eval culture: winner prediction and BrandBench
topics.brief: Coframe publishes unusually honest evals. Their winner-prediction post has a multimodal model compare screenshot pairs in both orders with majority voting: about 57% consistent accuracy on a public benchmark, dropping to 36 to 40% on their own production pairs. The nuance: they concluded it is for screening ideas before a test, not for deciding inside one, which is the judgement they will look for in you.
points: Position bias: each pair is shown in both orders (counterbalanced), because judges favour one slot.
Voting: a majority of about 9 samples; they compared a bigger model at 3 votes with a smaller one at 9 on cost per correct pair.
Held-out reality: 57.28% on WiserUI-Bench (300 pairs, 25% chance baseline) against 36 to 40% on 278 production pairs from 38 companies.
Use it where it holds: screen candidates before testing, never replace the live test.
BrandBench: an LLM-as-judge benchmark of 194 held-out sites scored 0 to 1 from logprobs, built for their fine-tuned UI model (+26% over base GPT-4o, reported October 2024).
production: The OpenAI work fine-tuned GPT-4o with vision on websites with a section masked out, asked to generate the missing section.
The research flagged 26%, 194 and 57.28% as worth a 30-second check on the source before quoting them to Pavlo.
For a variant gate: build passes, screenshot checks, console errors, accessibility and layout shift automatically; brand and taste by an LLM judge with bias controls; a human for edge cases.
The same discipline as a release gate: score against a baseline, block on regression.

mcq.q: Why does the winner-prediction study show each screenshot pair in both orders?
o: To cancel the judge's tendency to favour one position
To double the dataset size cheaply
Because the model cannot read two images at once
To check that the screenshots rendered correctly
To compute a confidence interval for each pair
mcq.why: LLM judges have position bias. Counterbalancing and requiring a consistent answer controls for it.

mcq.q: Accuracy was about 57% on a public benchmark but 36 to 40% on production pairs. What is the right conclusion?
o: The production data was labelled wrongly
Switch to the larger model and the gap will close
Stop running live tests, since 57% beats the 25% chance baseline
Use the predictor to screen ideas before a test, not to replace live tests
Raise the vote count until production matches the benchmark
mcq.why: Held-out production data shows the real performance. Coframe's own recommendation is screening, which keeps the live test as the decider.

mcq.q: For a gate on agent-generated UI, which check belongs with a human rather than automation?
o: The build compiles
Whether an unusual design is on brand for a new customer
No console errors on load
The CTA button is present and clickable
Cumulative layout shift stays under a threshold
mcq.why: Build, console, CTA and layout shift are deterministic checks. Brand fit for a new customer is subjective and where a judge model is least reliable.

open.q: How do you evaluate an agent that produces UI? Which parts are automatic and which need a human?
open.probe: Layered evals and honesty about judge limits.
a: Deterministic first: build, render in a browser, console errors, CTA works, accessibility, layout shift.
Model judge for brand and quality, with position-bias control and voting, checked against human labels.
Human for new customers, unusual designs and anything the judge is unsure about.
Score against a baseline and block on regression; real failures become new cases.
Your winner-prediction post is the example: it found the judge too weak to decide, so it screens.

say: I'd layer it. The deterministic checks first, because they're cheap and they don't lie: does it build, does it render, does the button work.
Then a model judge for brand and taste, with the order swapped to control for bias, and checked against what people actually picked.
I liked that your winner-prediction post said the accuracy dropped on production data. That's the number that matters.
avoid: Saying evals run on every change automatically in your own system: say a change is replayed on the bench before it ships.

topics.title: What the repos signal, and what to ask
topics.brief: Coframe's GitHub org forked browser and agent-runtime projects in the last two months: Kernel's browser images and neko, Vercel's agent-browser and Cloudflare's agents framework. Together they point at remote browsers and durable agent runtimes, which is this role. The nuance: forks can be bookmarks, so ask, don't assert.
points: kernel-images and neko (forked September 2026): browsers as a service, and a self-hosted virtual browser in Docker with WebRTC live view, so humans can watch an agent.
agent-browser (forked August 2026): a CLI and daemon driving Chrome over CDP for AI agents.
cloudflare-agents (forked August 2026): an agent framework built on Durable Objects.
Stack hints: older and adjacent posts list Python, TypeScript, Docker, Kubernetes, Kafka, Postgres, AWS. The platform post names no vendor; Temporal, Modal and E2B appear in no Coframe post.
Coffee (2023): their open-source React tag that sent a component and prompt to a model, with Docker isolating the agent's code; Pavlo has 20 commits on it.
production: Questions grounded in the trail: are browsers self-hosted or bought (the Kernel and neko forks)? Where do long-running agent runs live today?
How is a generated variant gated before it reaches a customer's site, and how do you evaluate 'on brand'?
What does the first 90 days on the agent platform look like?
The Browserbase case study suggests they have bought remote browsers before; the forks may mean a move to self-hosting. That is the question, not an assertion.

mcq.q: You noticed the Kernel and neko forks. Which way of raising it is best?
o: 'I see you've moved to self-hosted browsers on Kernel.'
'You should use Browserbase instead of self-hosting.'
'Kernel is the right choice; I would have picked it too.'
Avoid mentioning it, since forks are private decisions
'I saw the Kernel and neko forks. Are you self-hosting browsers or buying them?'
mcq.why: Forks are a weak signal. Asking shows you did the reading without claiming knowledge you do not have.

mcq.q: What does a fork of cloudflare/agents most plausibly suggest Coframe is evaluating?
o: A new CDN for the edge script
A replacement for their Thompson sampler
A durable, stateful runtime for agents built on Durable Objects
A browser automation library
A logging vendor for traces
mcq.why: Cloudflare's agents framework is built on Durable Objects, which give per-agent state and durability. It is not a CDN or browser tool.

open.q: What would you want to change about how we're doing this today?
open.probe: Respectful, specific engagement with their public material, without overclaiming.
a: Start with what I can see: the snippet fails open, the evals are honest, the forks point at browsers and durable runtimes.
Say what I cannot see: how runs are stored and gated today.
Offer a direction as a question: a fail-closed render gate per variant, traces an agent can read, durable runs that survive deploys.
Ask which of those already exists.

say: From the outside I can only see so much, so I'd rather ask than tell you.
I saw the Kernel and neko forks and the Cloudflare agents one. Are you self-hosting browsers now, and where do the long agent runs live?
If I had to guess where I'd add most, it's the gate before a variant ships and traces the agent can read. But I'd want to see what's there first.
avoid: Stating that Coframe uses Temporal, Modal, E2B or Kernel in production.
Criticising their stack without having seen it.

topics.title: Long-running and durable work
topics.brief: At alfred_ quick turns run in short serverless functions and long work goes onto a Postgres queue that lean Python workers claim with SKIP LOCKED; a job whose worker dies becomes claimable again, and a scheduled sweep catches anything missed. The nuance a platform engineer will press on: that is at-least-once queue durability, where a job re-runs from the top, not durable execution, where each step's result is checkpointed and a resume skips finished steps.
points: Classify first: what the run touches (only your system, a third party, or delivering outside) and whether it reads, researches or writes, and if it writes, whether doing it twice is harmless.

The class decides the retry: reads and research retry freely with backoff; a write carries an idempotency key so a retry returns the stored result; anything unsafe to repeat waits for the person to confirm.
SKIP LOCKED: `select ... for update skip locked` lets many workers claim the next job without two taking the same one or blocking each other.
Queue versus durable execution: a queue worker re-runs the job from the top after a crash; a workflow engine (Temporal, DBOS, Inngest, Restate) records each step and resumes after the last one.
At-least-once is the real guarantee either way: a step can act, the record can fail, and the step runs again, so side effects need idempotency keys like run_id:step_name.
production: DBOS checkpoints workflow input and each step's output to Postgres, one write per step, with no new infrastructure: the closest step up from a Postgres queue.
Temporal replays workflow code against its event history, so workflow code must be deterministic; it warns at 10,240 events and the escape is Continue-As-New.
Keep transcripts and screenshots out of workflow history: store the blob and pass a reference (claim check).
Anthropic used rainbow deployments so in-flight agents finish on old code while new runs start on new code.
The research's view: a Postgres queue with your own state machine is fine for a first version and short jobs; you rebuild a workflow engine badly as runs get longer.

mcq.q: A worker claims a job with SKIP LOCKED and dies halfway through. In a plain Postgres queue, what happens next?
o: The job resumes from the last step it finished, using saved results
The job is lost unless a person re-enqueues it
Postgres rolls back every external side effect the job made
The job becomes claimable again and a worker runs it from the top
The dead worker's lock blocks the job until the database restarts
mcq.why: The lock is released with the dead connection or lease, and the job re-runs from the start. Resuming from a step needs checkpoints, which is what a workflow engine adds.

mcq.q: What does a durable execution engine add over a queue worker with retries?
o: Step-level checkpoints, so a resumed run skips steps that already completed
Exactly-once side effects in external systems
Faster model calls, because results are cached across users
Freedom from idempotency keys, because steps never repeat
Automatic sandboxing of the code each step runs
mcq.why: Engines record step results and resume after the last one. A step can still run twice if it acts and then fails to record, so idempotency keys are still needed.

mcq.q: Which agent action should carry an idempotency key rather than retry freely?
o: Searching the web for a company's pricing page
Reading the user's last ten emails
Creating a calendar event for the user
Fetching a document's text to summarise it
Asking the model to draft a reply for review
mcq.why: Creating an event is a write that is harmful twice. Reads, research and drafts for review are safe to repeat.

open.q: A coding agent has been running for 40 minutes and the worker is killed mid tool call. What exactly happens next, and what would you guarantee the user?
open.probe: Whether you know the gap between queue durability and step-level recovery, and are honest about which you built.
a: In what I built, the job becomes claimable again and re-runs from the top; writes are safe because of idempotency keys, but paid work is repeated.
For a 40-minute agent I'd checkpoint at every tool call: messages and tool results persisted at step boundaries, keyed by run id.
On resume: replay skips recorded steps, the in-flight tool call is retried with its key or checked first.
Guarantee: no duplicate side effects, and at most one step redone. Honest caveat: a crash between acting and recording re-runs that one step.
Deploys: version workers so in-flight runs finish on the code they started with.

say: I start by classifying what the run touches, and that decides the retry. Reads retry freely, writes carry an idempotency key, and anything that can't safely repeat waits for the person.
Durability for us is the queue: jobs sit in Postgres, a worker claims one with SKIP LOCKED, a job that dies becomes claimable again, and a sweep catches anything missed.
That re-runs from the top, which is fine for our jobs. For a two-hour agent I'd want step checkpoints, something like DBOS on the same Postgres, so a crash costs one step, not the whole run.
avoid: Calling your queue 'durable execution' or implying you ran Temporal.
Promising exactly-once side effects.

topics.title: Evaluation and reliability
topics.brief: Three pieces: a scanner over real conversations that finds failures, a set of cases built from those failures, and a harness that runs the real agent against a frozen copy of the user's world so two versions can be compared fairly. It signed off the multi-turn rewrite. The nuance, and the failure that taught it: checking that an answer looks right is not checking that it is right; assert against ground truth you hold.
points: Cases from failures: a little over a hundred cases, each from a real production failure, each running the real agent against a frozen copy of that user's email and calendar.
Signed off a rewrite: you could see which cases got better and worse, and tool calls per task went from about 2.5 to 2.2.
Scanner: deterministic signals find candidates, an LLM classifies them, and real agent bugs above a confidence bar are promoted automatically.
Replay bench: real production turns replayed and graded by a person, for changes where a script cannot judge quality.
Ground truth: a ledger answer once left out two refunds and every shape check passed; now the case asserts every event the snapshot knows about appears.
Multi-turn trap: when the agent's reply changes, a recorded next user message stops making sense, so replay has to handle divergence.
production: Coframe's winner-prediction post is the same culture: counterbalanced pairs, majority voting, and an honest drop from about 57% on a benchmark to 36 to 40% on production pairs.
Evaluation as a deploy gate: an offline set of tasks with checks, plus online guardrails and regression alarms after rollout.
pass@k thinking: one good run of a stochastic agent is not evidence; run a case several times before trusting a pass.
Traces feed evals: a span per model and tool call with inputs, outputs, tokens, latency and cost is what lets a failure become a case.

mcq.q: An agent's ledger answer is well formatted and passes every schema check, but a user finds two refunds missing. What check was absent?
o: A stricter JSON schema for the ledger rows
An LLM judge rating the answer's helpfulness
A latency budget for the ledger tool call
A second model producing the same ledger to compare
An assertion against the events the frozen snapshot is known to contain
mcq.why: Shape checks and judges grade how it looks. Completeness needs ground truth you hold, which the snapshot provides.

mcq.q: Why run the real agent against a frozen copy of the user's email and calendar instead of the live account?
o: Frozen data makes the model's output deterministic
Two versions see the same world, so differences come from the agent, and nothing touches live systems
It is cheaper because frozen data needs fewer tokens
Live accounts cannot be read by the agent's tools
It removes the need for a person to grade any case
mcq.why: A fixed world makes comparisons fair and keeps writes away from real accounts. The model is still stochastic, so cases still vary run to run.

mcq.q: A new agent version passes a case once. What should you conclude?
o: Little on its own: a stochastic agent needs several runs before a pass means much
The case is fixed and can be removed from the set
The old version must have been broken by a dependency
The case's expected answer is probably wrong
The scanner can stop flagging that kind of failure
mcq.why: One good run is not evidence for a stochastic system. Repeated runs show whether it passes reliably.

open.q: How do you stop a prompt or model change from making the agent worse, and how do you know it got better?
open.probe: Whether your eval practice is real, grounded and honest about limits.
a: Cases come from real production failures, found by the scanner, not invented.
The real agent runs against a frozen copy of the user's world, so versions compare fairly with no live side effects.
Assert against ground truth the snapshot holds, not only the shape of the answer.
Compare per case, better and worse; the multi-turn rewrite went from about 2.5 to 2.2 tool calls per task.
Where a script cannot judge, replay real turns and have a person grade them.

say: At alfred_ I built a harness that replays real failures against a new version before it ships: a little over a hundred cases, each running the real agent against a frozen copy of that user's email and calendar.
That's how we signed off the multi-turn rewrite. We could see which cases got better and which got worse, and tool calls per task went from about 2.5 to 2.2.
The lesson I keep is 'does it look right' versus 'is it right'. We once passed a ledger that was missing two refunds, so now the case checks against what the snapshot knows is there.
avoid: Saying evals run on every commit automatically, or that an LLM verifies every reply.
Claiming hallucinations are gone.

topics.title: Isolation and safe actions
topics.brief: The rule at alfred_ is that safety lives in code, not in the prompt: side-effecting tools return a preview first, only an explicit confirm executes, and code floors hold whatever the model says. The hardest production fix followed the same idea: the model kept inventing email threads, so it now sees only opaque handles and code reattaches the real ids. The nuance: you have isolated the agent's world and its credentials, but you have not built sandboxed code execution, and should say so.
points: Confirm flow: a side-effecting tool first returns a preview; only an explicit confirm executes; idempotency keys make retries safe.
Code floors: limits no prompt can override, so a send or irreversible delete always needs the person.
Grounding guard: a reply that claims an action is checked in code against the turn's tool-execution ledger.
Strict-ID working memory: the model picks from opaque handles and writes the sentence; code attaches the real ids, so it cannot point at a thread that does not exist. Tests enforce it.
Scoped credentials: the voice worker gets a short-lived scoped token that can never send.
Isolated world: the harness runs the real agent against its own copy of the user's data with no path to live systems.
production: Isolated execution in the research: container, microVM (Firecracker) or gVisor, or a V8 isolate; the threat model is untrusted generated code and prompt injection.
Controls: no ambient credentials, an egress allow-list, CPU, memory and wall-clock limits, an ephemeral filesystem, short-lived scoped tokens.
Credentials outside the sandbox: a git proxy holds a scoped GitHub App token, validates the operation and attaches the credential, the pattern Anthropic describes for Claude Code on the web.
Prompt injection from page content or a q= parameter is treated as untrusted input: the agent's tools, not its prompt, decide what it can do.

mcq.q: The model keeps attaching the wrong email thread to a task. Which fix removes the class of error rather than making it rarer?
o: Add examples of correct thread ids to the prompt
Lower the temperature so the model guesses less
Ask a second model to check every id before saving
Give the model opaque handles from a real list and have code attach the real ids
Retry the call whenever the id format looks invalid
mcq.why: If the model never handles real ids, it cannot invent one. Prompting, temperature and checkers reduce the rate but leave the failure possible.

mcq.q: Where should the rule 'an email is never sent without the person confirming' live?
o: In the system prompt, stated firmly
In code around the send tool, which only executes after an explicit confirm
In the model's fine-tuning data
In a nightly audit of sent emails
In the user's settings page as a default toggle
mcq.why: A code floor holds whatever the model generates. Prompts and training shift probabilities; audits find the problem after it happened.

mcq.q: An agent runs code an LLM wrote. Which control matters most against a prompt injection that tries to leak secrets?
o: A longer system prompt warning about injections
Running the sandbox on a faster machine
Logging every command the agent runs
Using a larger model that follows instructions better
No ambient credentials in the sandbox and an egress allow-list
mcq.why: If the sandbox holds no secrets and can reach only allowed hosts, an injection has nothing to steal and nowhere to send it. Logging only tells you afterwards.

open.q: How do you isolate code an LLM wrote? What is your threat model, and what do you give it access to?
open.probe: Threat model first, honest about what you have built.
a: Threat model: untrusted generated code and prompt injection from content it reads.
Isolation level by risk: container for low risk, microVM or gVisor for untrusted code.
Access: no ambient credentials, egress allow-list, resource and time limits, ephemeral filesystem, credentials attached by a proxy outside.
What I built is the same instinct one level up: scoped tokens that can never send, previews and confirms, code floors, an isolated copy of the user's world for evals.
Gap: I haven't built sandboxed code execution; that's what I'd learn here.

say: My rule is that safety lives in code, not in the prompt. A tool that does something returns a preview first, and only an explicit confirm executes it.
The hardest fix I made was the model inventing email threads. Prompting harder didn't hold, so now it only sees opaque handles and code puts the real ids back.
I haven't built sandboxed code execution yet. But the instinct is the same: give it nothing it could misuse, and decide what it can do outside the model.
avoid: Saying hallucination is impossible, or that you built a multi-tenant sandbox fleet.
Describing a scoring or verdict system you did not build.
