topics.title: Latency and cost
topics.brief: Spend where the thinking happens and make the repeat cheap: start with the strongest model everywhere to get it right, then step down stage by stage where the evals say quality holds. Latency is the same shape: keep the critical path small and streamed, and push slow work off it. The nuance: without an eval set, 'step down' is a guess; the evals are what make cost cutting safe.
points: Where the thinking is: in your workflows, creating one is expensive and gets the strongest model; running it is cheap because the steps are known and mostly deterministic.
Step down with evidence: replace a stage with a cheaper model only where the eval cases still pass.
Fast first pass: a fast model answers simple turns or escalates to a heavier agent; code guards turn a reply that promises an action or claims completion into an escalation.
Parallel on voice: a lean agent answers on the call while the main agent works the same request in parallel, so the caller is never left in silence.
Critical path: stream what the user sees, move slow work to the queue.
production: Anthropic's multi-agent research write-up reports multi-agent runs using about 15 times the tokens of chat: token budgets are a first-class platform concern.
At fleet scale the research expects provider rate limits (tokens per minute) to bite before compute: 1,000 agents at 20k tokens a minute is 20M tokens a minute, an estimate.
LLM gateways (LiteLLM's router, for example) give retries, fallback across providers and per-tenant limits in one place.
Coframe's own winner-prediction post compared a bigger model at 3 votes with a smaller one at 9 on cost per correct pair: cost per correct answer, not per call.

mcq.q: You want to cut model cost in a multi-stage workflow. What should decide which stage moves to a cheaper model?
o: The stage with the longest prompt
The stage that runs most often, whatever its quality impact
The stage where eval cases still pass with the cheaper model
The stage the newest model release benchmarks best on
The stage users interact with least
mcq.why: Frequency tells you where savings are; evals tell you where they are safe. Without the eval, a step down is a guess.

mcq.q: On a voice call, the main agent needs several seconds for a tool-heavy request. Which design keeps the caller engaged without lying to them?
o: Play hold music until the main agent finishes
Have the fast model answer the full request itself
Cut the main agent's tools so it answers faster
A lean agent talks to the caller while the main agent works the same request in parallel
Ask the caller to call back in a minute
mcq.why: Parallel lean and heavy agents keep the conversation live while the real work happens. A fast model answering alone risks claiming things it has not done.

mcq.q: What does the first-pass guard do when the fast model's reply says 'I've rescheduled your meeting'?
o: Turns it into an escalation to the heavier agent, because the fast pass cannot claim an action
Sends the reply, since the fast model is usually right on simple turns
Rewrites the reply to sound less certain
Retries the fast model with a stricter prompt
Logs the reply and asks the user to confirm it later
mcq.why: A reply that promises or claims an action is caught in code and escalated; the fast pass only answers turns that need no action.

open.q: How do you think about latency and cost when you design an agent system?
open.probe: A method, not a list of tricks, and evidence behind cost cuts.
a: Find where the thinking is and spend there; make the repeated part cheap and deterministic.
Start with the best model, harden, then step down stage by stage where evals say quality holds.
Latency: small streamed critical path, slow work on the queue.
Example: a fast first pass that escalates, and on voice a lean agent answering while the heavy one works in parallel.
At fleet scale, token budgets and rate limits before compute.

say: I start from where the thinking actually happens. Creating a workflow is the expensive part, so it gets the strongest model. Running it is cheap, because the steps are known.
So I start with the best model everywhere, harden it, then step down stage by stage where the evals say quality holds.
Latency works the same way: keep the critical path small and stream it. On voice, a lean agent answers on the call while the heavy one works in parallel.
avoid: Quoting per-user cost numbers or traffic figures for alfred_.

topics.title: How you use AI tools
topics.brief: Heavily, with scaffolding: Claude Code with project instructions and skills for repeated jobs, a review pass, and a check that runs the real thing rather than trusting that it compiled. The nuance: you do not trust an agent's own report of what it did, which is the same instinct as the product guard that checks action claims against the tool ledger.
points: Scaffolding: project instructions and skills carry conventions, so prompts stay short and output stays consistent.
Drive or take over: let it drive on well-tested, boring parts; take over on permissions, concurrency and database changes.
Verify by running: a check that runs the real thing, not a claim that it passed.
No self-reports: an agent saying 'done' is a claim to check, from a model or from yourself.
Same rule in the product: action claims are checked in code against what tools actually ran.
production: Pavlo's take-home commits are co-authored by Claude Sonnet 4.6, and other Coframe posts name Claude Code, Cursor and Devin: fluency is expected.
Anthropic sandboxes Claude Code's filesystem and network access, so an agent can act with fewer prompts without broad access.
Interview rubrics in the research score the same habits: decompose, prompt specifically, read the diff, run it, own every line.

mcq.q: Claude Code reports 'all tests pass' after a change. What do you do before moving on?
o: Accept it, since the tool ran the tests itself
Ask it to confirm again in different words
Run the tests and the real script yourself and look at the output
Check the diff size and move on if it is small
Commit, and let CI catch anything it missed
mcq.why: An agent's report is a claim. Running it yourself is the check, the same principle as verifying action claims against a tool ledger.

mcq.q: Which task would you be least willing to let the agent drive unreviewed?
o: Writing fixtures for a parser's tests
Renaming a variable across one module
Formatting a file to the project style
Drafting a docstring for a helper
A migration that changes a table's row-level permissions
mcq.why: Permissions and schema changes are where a plausible wrong answer is costly and hard to undo. The others are cheap to check and revert.

open.q: Walk me through how you actually use AI tools day to day. Where do you not trust them?
open.probe: A real, deliberate workflow, and calibrated trust.
a: Claude Code every day, with project instructions and skills for jobs I repeat.
It drives on well-tested, boring parts; I take over on permissions, concurrency and database changes.
A review pass, then a check that runs the real thing.
I never take its report of what it did as proof, the same reason our product checks action claims against the tool ledger.

say: Heavily, but with scaffolding. Claude Code with project instructions and skills for the jobs I repeat, a review pass, and a check that actually runs the thing.
I let it drive on the well-tested, boring parts and take over on permissions, concurrency and database changes.
And I don't trust an agent's own report of what it did. It's the same instinct as our guard against the agent claiming actions it never took.
avoid: Implying the tool writes code you then ship without reading.

topics.title: What you have not built, and how you'd learn it
topics.brief: Most of the posting maps to work you have done for one production agent: long-running work, tracing and evaluation, safe actions, cost. The gaps are real and you name them first: remote browsers, sandboxed code execution, a multi-tenant sandbox fleet, Kubernetes at scale, a bandit in production, and a platform shared by several teams. The nuance: naming the gap with a concrete plan to close it reads as senior; hedging reads as hiding.
points: Done, for one product: durable workers on a Postgres queue, the eval harness and scanner, safe actions in code, scoped credentials, cost by evidence.
Not done: sandboxed code execution, remote browsers, a multi-tenant sandbox fleet, Kubernetes at scale, a bandit in production, Temporal, Modal, E2B or Browserbase in production.
What carries over: isolation (the harness has no path to live systems), claiming from a queue, scoped short-lived tokens, tracing each run.
How you'd learn: buy first, read how the vendor isolates, build a small version (one sandbox per run, one browser session with a live view), then decide what to own.
Remote browser basics: headless Chrome over CDP, screenshot and DOM back to the model; wait on a condition, never a sleep.
production: The research's build-versus-buy view for sandboxes: buy first (E2B or Modal), since Modal reports scaling its scheduler to very large sandbox counts, engineering a small team should not repeat early.
Isolation options by cost and strength: container with a hardened profile, gVisor, Firecracker microVM with snapshots for fast start.
Fast start: prebuilt images per repo refreshed on a schedule (Ramp every 30 minutes), warm pools, restore from snapshot.
Coframe's recent forks of Kernel's browser images and neko suggest they are weighing self-hosted browsers: the gap is in the exact area you would grow into.

mcq.q: Pavlo asks about sandboxed code execution, which you have not built. Which answer lands best?
o: Describe the eval harness as a sandbox so the answer stays positive
Say you haven't built it, name what transfers, and say how you'd build a first version
Say you have used E2B on side projects, which is close enough
Say it is a solved problem and any vendor would do
Change the subject to the voice agent, where you are strongest
mcq.why: A plain gap plus what transfers plus a concrete plan reads as senior. Stretching the harness or implying vendor experience invites a probe you cannot follow.

mcq.q: Which of these can you honestly claim as shipped?
o: Workers that claim jobs from a Postgres queue with SKIP LOCKED
A multi-tenant sandbox fleet on Kubernetes
Remote browsers that agents drive over CDP
A Thompson-sampling bandit serving live traffic
Durable workflows on Temporal
mcq.why: The Postgres queue with SKIP LOCKED is yours. The rest are gaps to name plainly.

mcq.q: A remote-browser test is flaky: it passes locally and fails in the pool. What is the most likely culprit to check first?
o: The model's temperature
The DNS resolver in the pool
The screenshot format
A fixed sleep instead of waiting on a condition such as an element appearing
The CDP protocol version
mcq.why: Timing differs across machines and load; waiting on a condition removes the race. It is the standard browser automation fix.

open.q: The role asks for sandboxes and remote browsers. You haven't built either. How would you get productive on them here?
open.probe: Honesty, transferable instincts, and a concrete learning plan.
a: Say it plainly: not built yet.
What transfers: isolation of the eval world, scoped tokens that cannot send, queue claiming, tracing every run.
First weeks: read how the current setup works, run a vendor sandbox and a browser session end to end.
Build a small version: one sandbox per run with no ambient credentials, one browser with live view, both traced.
Then make the build-or-buy call with numbers: start time, cost per run, failure rate.

say: I haven't built sandboxed code execution or remote browsers yet, and I'd rather say that plainly.
What carries over is the instinct: our eval harness runs the real agent in an isolated copy of the user's world, and our voice worker gets a scoped token that can never send.
I'd start by running what you have end to end, then build a small version myself, so the build-or-buy call is made with numbers.
avoid: Implying Kubernetes at scale, Temporal, Modal, E2B or Browserbase in production.

topics.title: Working in a small team
topics.brief: alfred_ is four engineers, so ownership is real: the eval harness and failure scanner, working memory, the voice agent end to end, and much of the worker infrastructure are yours, decided, built and run by you. On a small team nobody hands you a backlog: you look at what is breaking and what is being asked, and decide. The nuance: argue once with evidence, then commit, because a small team cannot afford relitigating.
points: Ownership: name the things that are yours plainly, and say the team is four.
No backlog: decide from what is breaking and what users ask for.
Disagree once: make the case with evidence, ideally a real example or a quick prototype, then commit to the decision.
Speed with a net: small changes, a check that runs the real thing, evals before a risky change ships.
Coframe's values: Agency, Velocity, Truth-seeking, Growth; your habits map to the first three.
production: Josh Payne says early hires came from hackathon winners and that he wants to see how people work with you before working fully together: the round itself is a sample of working with you.
Each Coframe take-home is a fixed-time task ending in a defence of decisions: ownership under time pressure is what they select for.
The research expects 'what would you cut?' from Pavlo: a small-team answer keeps the path users see working and writes the rest down.

mcq.q: You disagree with the co-founder's choice of approach on a small team. What is the best move?
o: Go along silently to keep things moving
Make the case once with a real example or a quick prototype, then commit to the decision
Keep raising it in each planning meeting until it changes
Build your approach in parallel and ship whichever finishes first
Escalate to the CEO for a ruling

modules.title: Python in depth
modules.blurb: Explain what the Python in front of you actually does, spot the traps in AI-written code, and defend each choice of concurrency, typing and validation.

topics.title: The data model and mutability traps
topics.brief: Names are references to objects, and assignment never copies. Default arguments are evaluated once, when def runs, and closures capture variables rather than values, so one object gets shared where you expected a fresh one. In an agent platform that shows up as history leaking between runs, which is a cross-tenant data bug, not a logic bug.
points: Mutable default: `def f(x, acc=[])` builds the list once, when `def` runs, and stores it on the function; write `acc=None`, then `acc = [] if acc is None else acc` (ruff B006 flags it)
Late binding: `[lambda: i for i in range(3)]` all return 2, because each lambda reads `i` when it is called; bind now with `lambda i=i: i` or `functools.partial` (ruff B023)
Identity vs equality: `==` calls `__eq__`, `is` compares identity; use `is` only for `None` and sentinels like `_MISSING = object()`, never rely on small-int or string interning (a CPython detail)
Aliasing: `[[0]] * 2` holds the same inner list twice, and `t = ([1], 2); t[0] += [3]` raises TypeError after the list has already become `[1, 3]`

Copying: `copy.copy` is shallow (new outer container, same inner objects); `copy.deepcopy` recurses and handles cycles but is slow and tries to copy locks, sockets and clients; 3.13 adds `copy.replace(obj, **changes)` (dataclasses, namedtuples, any class with `__replace__`), the clean way to modify a frozen dataclass
production: Conversation history or a tool-call list held in a default argument or a module-level list leaks between runs: treat it as a cross-tenant data bug.
dataclasses refuse a bare `[]` default and make you write `field(default_factory=list)`, for the same reason.
Ruff B006 (mutable default) and B023 (closure over a loop variable) catch both traps in review.
Agent state for stop and resume is snapshotted as plain JSON-able data, not by deep-copying live objects that hold clients and locks.
A callback made in a loop, `loop.call_later(1, lambda: handle(job))`, sees the last `job`; pass arguments with `partial` or to a coroutine call, which evaluates them immediately.

mcq.q:
def add(x, acc=[]):
    acc.append(x)
    return acc

add(1)
print(add(2))

What prints?
o: TypeError: a list default is not allowed
mcq.why: The default list is built once, when def runs, and lives in add.__defaults__. Every call that does not pass acc appends to that one list.

mcq.q:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])

What prints?
o: NameError: name 'i' is not defined
mcq.why: Each lambda closes over the variable i, not its value. They run after the loop has finished, when i is 2. The closure cell keeps i alive after the loop, so there is no NameError.

mcq.q:
t = ([1], 2)
t[0] += [3]

What happens?
o: TypeError, and t[0] is now [1, 3]
TypeError, and t[0] is still [1]
No error, and t[0] is [1, 3]
No error, and t is rebound to a new tuple ([1, 3], 2)
AttributeError: tuple has no __iadd__
mcq.why: += calls list.__iadd__, which extends the list in place and returns it. Python then tries t[0] = result, which the tuple refuses. The mutation has already happened.

open.q: Here's a function from an agent runner: `def run(task, history=[])`. Tests pass, but in staging two users see each other's messages. Walk me through it.
open.probe: Whether you know when defaults are evaluated, and treat shared state as a tenancy problem.
a: The default list is created once, when def runs, and stored on the function object.
Every call that does not pass history appends to that one list, across users and runs.
Fix: default to None and create the list inside, or give the run object its own history.
Stop it coming back: ruff B006 in CI, and a test that runs two tasks and asserts histories are separate.
Then look for its relatives: module-level lists, class attributes holding mutables, late-bound closures in loops.

say: That's the mutable default. The list gets built once when def runs and lives on the function, so every call that doesn't pass history appends to the same list.
The fix is a None default and a fresh list inside, and I'd turn on ruff B006 so it doesn't come back.
But I'd call it what it is, a cross-tenant leak, so I'd also check what else holds state at module level. Per-run state lives on the run, never on the function.
avoid: Saying `is` works for small numbers because they are cached: that is a CPython detail, never something to rely on.

topics.title: Iteration and generators
topics.brief: An iterator is single-pass: once consumed it yields nothing, and it does so silently. Generators give lazy, constant-memory pipelines, and closing one raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield so its finally runs. The trap: hand a generator to a function that iterates twice and the second pass does nothing.
points: Iterable vs iterator: an iterable has `__iter__`; an iterator also has `__next__` and returns itself from `__iter__`, so `list(it)` twice gives the items, then `[]`
Pipeline: `read_lines -> nonblank -> parse -> batch`, each stage a generator; nothing is materialised until the consumer pulls
yield from: delegates to a sub-generator, passes `send()` values through, and evaluates to the sub-generator's `return` value
close(): raises `GeneratorExit` at the paused `yield`, so `finally` runs; that is how a stream releases its resource when the consumer stops early

itertools: `batched(it, n)` (3.12; `strict=` in 3.13), `pairwise` (3.10), `chain.from_iterable`, `islice` (no negative indices); `groupby` groups only consecutive equal keys, like Unix `uniq`, so sort first
tee: can need unbounded auxiliary storage and is not thread-safe; if one copy will consume most of the data first, `list()` is faster
production: Model tokens and log lines stream through generator transforms without buffering the whole transcript; the async version is an async generator.
`itertools.batched` for bulk inserts and for batching tool calls.
A 10 GB log grouped by session id: stream the lines into a dict of small per-session aggregates, or sort externally and use `groupby`; never `readlines()`.

mcq.q:
g = (x * x for x in range(3))
print(sum(g), sum(g))

What prints?
o: TypeError on the second sum
mcq.why: 0 + 1 + 4 is 5. The first sum exhausts the generator, and an exhausted iterator yields nothing, so the second sum is 0 with no error.

mcq.q:
import itertools
print([k for k, _ in itertools.groupby("aabaa")])

What prints?
mcq.why: groupby starts a new group whenever the key changes, like Unix uniq. To group all equal keys together you sort first.

mcq.q: A generator is paused inside `try: yield row` with `finally: conn.release()`. The consumer stops early and calls `g.close()`. What happens?
o: finally never runs, and the connection leaks until garbage collection
close() raises StopIteration in the caller
The generator resumes and yields the next row before closing
close() is ignored unless the generator catches GeneratorExit
GeneratorExit is raised at the paused yield, so finally runs and releases
mcq.why: close() throws GeneratorExit in at the yield where the generator is paused, so finally and with blocks run. If the generator yields again instead of exiting, close() raises RuntimeError.

open.q: You have a 10 GB log of agent runs and need tool errors counted per session. Sketch the code and tell me its memory profile.
open.probe: Whether you stream by default and know where memory actually goes.
a: Iterate the file object line by line through a generator, never readlines().
Filter and parse lazily in further generator stages.
Aggregate into a dict keyed by session id holding small counts, so memory grows with sessions, not lines.
If sessions themselves do not fit, sort externally by session id and use groupby, which needs consecutive keys.
Batch any writes with itertools.batched so the sink is not called per line.

say: I'd stream it. Read the file line by line through a generator, filter and parse lazily, and keep a dict of counts per session.
So memory is roughly the number of sessions times a small counter, not the size of the file.
If even the sessions don't fit, I'd sort by session id outside Python and use groupby, because groupby only groups neighbours.
Pretty much, nothing gets materialised unless I need it.
avoid: Calling a generator thread-safe or rewindable: it is neither, and tee is not thread-safe either.

topics.title: The GIL and choosing threads, processes or asyncio
topics.brief: The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time per interpreter, but it is released around blocking I/O and inside many C extensions, so threads still help for I/O. It does not make your code thread-safe: `counter += 1` is a read, an add and a store. An agent platform is I/O-bound, so asyncio does the waiting, and processes or containers take CPU work and isolation.
points: GIL: one thread executes bytecode at a time in an interpreter; the running thread is asked to yield every switch interval (default 5 ms, `sys.getswitchinterval()`)
Not thread safety: `counter += 1` can be interrupted between the read and the store; use a `threading.Lock`, a `queue.Queue`, or no shared mutable state
Measured in R2 (3.12, Windows, 4 tasks of a pure-Python loop): serial 0.98 s, 4 threads 0.94 s, 4 processes 0.62 s including spawn cost; threads do not speed up CPU-bound Python, processes do

Free-threading: 3.13 (PEP 703) is an experimental separate build (`python3.13t`); 3.14 (PEP 779) makes it officially supported but optional, not the default; the single-thread penalty is quoted as 5 to 10 percent (What's new) and 1 to 8 percent (HOWTO), so measure
Free-threading caveat: importing a C extension that does not declare support re-enables the GIL automatically, with a warning; ecosystem readiness is the practical limit

Choosing: many network calls, asyncio; a blocking SDK with no async API, threads via `asyncio.to_thread`; CPU-bound pure Python, `ProcessPoolExecutor`; untrusted code, processes at minimum and containers or microVMs for real isolation; numpy, hashing and zlib release the GIL, so threads work there
production: An agent loop of LLM call, test run, LLM call: asyncio for the network calls, and the test suite in a subprocess with a timeout, so it has its own interpreter and can be killed.
asyncio gives concurrency, not parallelism: one blocking call (a sync SDK, `time.sleep`) stalls every task on the loop, so push it to `asyncio.to_thread`.
Processes cost memory and pickle every argument and result; threads give the least isolation and need locks for shared state.
3.14 adds `concurrent.interpreters` (PEP 734) and `InterpreterPoolExecutor`: isolated interpreters in one process, with slow start, extra memory and almost no sharing of objects.
PEP 779 caps Phase II overhead at 15 percent and targets about 20 percent more memory; making free-threading the default (Phase III) is deferred.

mcq.q: On standard CPython 3.12, four threads each run `counter += 1` 100,000 times on a shared int with no lock. Is the final count guaranteed to be 400,000?
o: Yes, the GIL makes each statement atomic
No, it is a read, an add and a store, and a switch can land between them
Yes, but only for ints below 256 because they are cached
No, but only on the free-threaded build
Yes, as long as the threads are daemon threads
mcq.why: The GIL serialises bytecode, not statements. The thread can be asked to yield between loading the value and storing the sum, and an update is lost.

mcq.q: A pure-Python CPU-bound function runs four times, first serially, then in four threads, on standard CPython 3.12. Roughly what happens to wall time with threads?
o: About 4 times faster
About 2 times faster, from hyperthreading
4 times slower, from lock contention on every line
Faster on Linux, unchanged on Windows
About the same, because only one thread runs bytecode at a time
mcq.why: R2 measured serial 0.98 s against 0.94 s for four threads. Processes, each with its own interpreter and GIL, got 0.62 s including spawn cost.

mcq.q: An agent calls an LLM, then runs the repo's test suite (CPU-heavy, can hang), then calls the LLM again, for thousands of agents at once. Which shape fits?
o: asyncio for the LLM calls, and the test suite as a subprocess with a timeout
Threads for everything, since the GIL is released during network calls
One process per LLM call, so each call gets its own GIL
asyncio for everything, with the tests run on the event loop thread
The free-threaded build, so the tests run in parallel threads
mcq.why: The LLM calls are waiting, which asyncio does cheaply and cancellably. The tests need their own interpreter for CPU and isolation, and a subprocess can be killed when it hangs.

mcq.q: On the 3.14 free-threaded build, you import a C extension that does not declare free-threading support. What happens?
o: ImportError: the module refuses to load
It loads and runs without the GIL, at your own risk
The interpreter crashes on the first call into it
The GIL is re-enabled automatically, with a warning
Only that extension's calls take the GIL
mcq.why: The interpreter turns the GIL back on for the whole process and warns. That is why dependency readiness, not the interpreter, decides whether free-threading pays off.

open.q: We run thousands of agents that call an LLM, run the user's tests, and call the LLM again. How do you structure the concurrency in Python, and would you use free-threading?
open.probe: Whether you match the tool to the workload and are honest about free-threading's status.
a: Name the workload: mostly waiting on the network, with bursts of untrusted CPU work.
asyncio for the LLM and HTTP calls, with timeouts and a concurrency limit.
Tests in a subprocess or container with a timeout and a kill, never in the loop thread; sync SDKs via to_thread.
Scale out with more processes or workers, not more threads in one process.
Free-threading: officially supported in 3.14 but optional, extensions can re-enable the GIL, so not for this; maybe later for in-process CPU work like parsing, after measuring.

say: I'd start from the workload. It's mostly waiting on the LLM, so asyncio with timeouts and a semaphore does that well.
The test run is CPU work and untrusted, so it goes in a subprocess with a timeout I can kill, not in the event loop.
In my own system the Python workers are lean and claim jobs from Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, so scaling is more workers, not more threads.
Free-threading I wouldn't reach for here. It's supported in 3.14 but optional, and one extension can turn the GIL back on.
avoid: Saying the GIL makes code thread-safe.
Quoting one free-threading overhead number as settled: the sources differ, so say single digits to low teens and that you would measure.

topics.title: Errors and exception groups
topics.brief: Since 3.11 several failures can travel together in an ExceptionGroup, and any TaskGroup can raise one, so `except ValueError` around a TaskGroup does not match. `except*` splits a group by type and re-raises whatever nobody handled. The other classic: a `return` in `finally` overrides the original return, and swallows an exception in flight.
points: ExceptionGroup: `ExceptionGroup(msg, [excs])`; each `except*` clause takes its matching subset, and the unmatched rest is re-raised in a new group; `eg.split(T)` and `eg.subgroup(T)` do it in code
except* rules: no mixing `except` and `except*` in one `try`; no `return`, `break` or `continue` inside `except*`; a bare exception reaching `except*` is wrapped into a group
Chaining: `raise New from exc` sets `__cause__`; raising inside `except` sets `__context__` automatically; `from None` suppresses the context
Notes: `e.add_note("run=r1 step=3")` (3.11) attaches context that prints in the traceback, without wrapping the exception
finally trap: `try: return "try"` with `finally: return "finally"` returns "finally"; a `return` or `raise` in `finally` overrides the original result or exception
Context managers: `with` guarantees `__exit__` on every path; `contextlib.contextmanager` keeps begin, commit, rollback and release in one place
production: Retry transient transport errors and 429 or 5xx responses at the call boundary, with a budget.
Validation errors go back to the model as tool-result text, so it can correct itself.
Cancellation is control flow, not an error to log: never `except Exception: pass` in an agent loop, log with the traceback, and let `CancelledError` through.
Callers of a TaskGroup handle `except*`; a plain `except ValueError` wrapped around one is a frequent bug.

o: It returns "caught"
An ExceptionGroup holding the ValueError propagates past the except
The TaskGroup logs the ValueError and swallows it
It returns None, and the other tasks keep running
RuntimeError: TaskGroup does not allow failures
mcq.why: A TaskGroup cancels the other children and raises an ExceptionGroup, even for one failure. except ValueError does not match a group; except* ValueError does.

mcq.q:
def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        return "finally"

print(f())

What prints?
o: try
None
SyntaxError: return is not allowed in finally
finally
('try', 'finally')
mcq.why: The finally block runs after the try's return is set up, and its own return replaces it. The same override would discard an exception raised in try.

o: An ExceptionGroup containing only the ValueError
The whole group, because one member did not match
Nothing: both are considered handled
A bare ValueError, unwrapped
Nothing: unmatched members are dropped
mcq.why: except* removes the subset it handled. What is left is re-raised as a new ExceptionGroup, still wrapped, for an outer handler.

open.q: Your agent fans out five tool calls in a TaskGroup. Two fail: one with a validation error, one with a timeout. How should the caller handle that, and what do you retry?
open.probe: Whether you know TaskGroups raise groups, and can separate retryable from model-correctable from fatal.
a: The TaskGroup cancels the remaining calls and raises an ExceptionGroup with both failures.
Handle it with except*: one clause for validation errors, one for timeouts and transport errors.
Timeouts and 429 or 5xx: retry at the call boundary with backoff and a budget.
Validation errors: return the message to the model as tool-result text for a bounded retry.
Never catch-all and continue; let CancelledError through, and add a note with the run id and step before re-raising.

say: First thing, a TaskGroup raises an ExceptionGroup, so a plain except ValueError won't match. I'd use except*.
The timeout I'd retry at the call boundary with backoff and a budget. The validation error goes back to the model as text so it can fix the call.
And I'd add a note with the run id and step, so the trace says where it happened. Cancellation I let through, always.
avoid: Saying you catch Exception and carry on in the agent loop: it hides bugs and can eat cancellation.

topics.title: Typing: what the checker sees and what runs
topics.brief: The runtime does not enforce annotations: `x: int = 'a'` runs, and a TypedDict is a plain dict. Static checkers (mypy, pyright) enforce them before merge, and libraries like pydantic read them at runtime to validate. Know which of the three you are relying on for each piece of data.
points: Protocol (PEP 544): structural typing, a class matches if it has the members, no inheritance; `@runtime_checkable` allows `isinstance`, but it only checks that the attributes exist, not their signatures, and it is slow
TypedDict: dict-shaped data with known keys; `total=False`, `Required` and `NotRequired` (3.11), `ReadOnly` (3.13); good for typing JSON you do not own, pydantic when you need validation
Generics: `T = TypeVar("T")`, or the 3.12 syntax `def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T` and `class Box[T]`, with bounds `[S: str]`; `type Vec = list[float]` (3.12); TypeVar defaults in 3.13 (PEP 696)
ParamSpec (3.10) and Concatenate: type a decorator so the wrapper keeps the wrapped function's parameters, as in `def deco[**P, R](fn: Callable[P, R]) -> Callable[P, Result[R]]`

More: `Literal` for closed sets and discriminators; `@overload` (only the implementation exists at runtime); `Self` (3.11), `@override` (3.12); `TypeIs` (3.13) narrows both branches, unlike `TypeGuard` (3.10)

3.14 (PEP 649): annotations are evaluated lazily rather than at def time, except under `from __future__ import annotations`; libraries that read them at runtime (pydantic, dataclasses) are the ones affected
production: Tools as a Protocol: anything with a `name` and an `async __call__` is a Tool, so outside tools plug in without inheriting your base class.
Protocol vs ABC: a Protocol is structural and suits a consumer's interface; an ABC is nominal and suits shared behaviour you own.

One checker in strict mode on new code and gradually on old; what matters is that the gate exists. R2 marks the mypy vs pyright comparison as general knowledge: pyright faster and stricter on narrowing, mypy the older reference with plugins.
`Any` switches off checking and propagates through everything it touches.

mcq.q:
x: int = "a"
print(x)

What happens?
o: TypeError at the assignment
TypeError when x is next used
None prints, the assignment is skipped
A RuntimeWarning, then a
a prints, with no error
mcq.why: Annotations are stored, never enforced by the interpreter. A static checker would flag this line; the runtime does not care.

o: False, because __call__ is not async
False, because the signature differs
True, because it only checks that the members exist
TypeError: Protocols cannot be used with isinstance
True, but only if Impostor inherits from Tool
mcq.why: runtime_checkable checks attribute presence only. Signatures and async-ness are the static checker's job.

mcq.q: You write a decorator whose wrapper takes exactly the wrapped function's parameters but returns Result[R] instead of R. How do you type it so callers keep checked arguments?
o: A TypeVar F bound to Callable[..., Any], returning F
ParamSpec P and TypeVar R: Callable[P, R] in, Callable[P, Result[R]] out
Callable[..., Any] in and out
An @overload for each function it will wrap
A Protocol whose __call__ takes *args: Any and **kwargs: Any
mcq.why: ParamSpec carries the parameter list across while letting the return type change. A bound TypeVar would claim the return type is unchanged; Callable[..., Any] throws the parameters away.

o: Nothing: it is a plain dict and nothing checks it
ValidationError on construction
TypeError: 'banana' is not a valid Literal
It becomes a Msg instance with a frozen schema
KeyError for a missing key

open.q: The model returns JSON for a tool call and a teammate has typed it as a TypedDict. They say that's enough. What do you say?
open.probe: Whether you separate static guarantees from runtime validation at an untrusted boundary.
a: A TypedDict is a plain dict at runtime; the annotation checks our code, not the model's output.
Model output is untrusted input, so it needs runtime validation at the boundary: pydantic, or a hand validator.
Keep the TypedDict or Protocol types inside, after validation, where the checker gives real value.
One source of truth: the validating model also emits the JSON Schema given to the model as the tool definition.

say: I'd say the TypedDict helps us, not at runtime. It's a plain dict, so if the model sends role banana, nothing stops it.
The model's output is untrusted input, so I validate it at the boundary with pydantic, and keep the static types for everything after that.
The checker is there to catch our mistakes. Validation is there to catch the model's.
avoid: Saying type hints are checked at runtime, or that runtime_checkable verifies signatures.

topics.title: Dataclasses, attrs, pydantic: validate at the boundary
topics.brief: dataclasses write the boilerplate but validate nothing: `Step(name=3)` is accepted. pydantic v2 parses and validates, but by default it coerces in lax mode (`'10'` becomes `10`) and ignores unknown keys. Validate once at the trust boundary (HTTP input, model output, tool arguments), then use plain types inside.
points: dataclasses (stdlib): generated `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`; `frozen=True` for immutability and hashing, `slots=True` (3.10); no validation, so use them for trusted internal data
attrs (third party; R2 marks this as general knowledge): the older, richer relative, with validators and converters; validation without pydantic's schema machinery

pydantic v2: Rust core (`pydantic-core`); lax by default, `strict=True` turns coercion off; `extra` defaults to ignore, `extra="forbid"` rejects unknown keys; `model_validate_json` validates straight from JSON text

pydantic tools: `field_validator` for one field, `model_validator` for cross-field rules, `TypeAdapter` for any type without a model, `model_json_schema()` for the tool schema; `frozen=True` blocks assignment but nested mutables stay mutable
Discriminated union: `Annotated[Union[Click, Type_], Field(discriminator="kind")]` gives one precise error (kind must be click or type) instead of a wall of union failures
production: LLM output is untrusted input: parse tool arguments through a model, turn a ValidationError into a short message back to the model, retry a bounded number of times, never repair silently.
One source of truth: the same pydantic model validates the arguments and generates the JSON Schema handed to the model as the tool definition.
Strict mode for internal contracts and wherever silent coercion would hide a bug.
R2's check: `Field(30, ge=1, le=300)` shows up as `maximum: 300` in `model_json_schema()`, so the bound the model sees is the bound the code enforces.

o: TypeError: name must be str
Step(name='3'), coerced to a string
A DeprecationWarning, then Step(name=3)
Step(name=3), accepted without complaint
ValueError raised by the generated __post_init__
mcq.why: dataclasses generate __init__ from the annotations but never check types. That is why they suit trusted internal data, not model output.

mcq.q: A pydantic v2 model with default config has `timeout_s: int`. You call `Args.model_validate_json('{"url": "x", "timeout_s": "10"}')`. Result?
o: ValidationError: '10' is not an int
timeout_s == 10, coerced in lax mode
timeout_s == '10', kept as a string
timeout_s falls back to its default
ValidationError only if the model is frozen
mcq.why: Lax mode is the default and coerces a numeric string to int. Pass strict=True, or set strict in the config, and the same input raises.

mcq.q: A pydantic v2 model with default config receives a key it never declared, `"force": true`. What happens?
o: ValidationError: extra fields not permitted
The key is kept as an attribute on the model
A warning is logged and the key is kept
TypeError inside model_validate
The key is ignored and dropped
mcq.why: extra defaults to ignore. For tool arguments you usually want extra="forbid", so a hallucinated parameter fails loudly instead of vanishing.

mcq.q: The model's tool call fails validation: one field is missing. What is the best default?
o: Repair the JSON with a regex and run the tool
Retry the same prompt until it parses
Return the validation error to the model as text, with a bounded number of retries
Switch to lax mode so the call goes through
Fail the whole run and page someone
mcq.why: The error message is the cheapest, most precise feedback the model can get. Silent repair hides a broken contract, and an unbounded retry burns tokens.

open.q: Our tools take arguments from the model. Dataclass, attrs or pydantic? And what happens when the model sends `timeout_s: "10"` or a field the tool doesn't have?
open.probe: Whether you know pydantic's defaults and design the boundary deliberately.
a: pydantic at the boundary, because model output is untrusted and pydantic validates and emits the JSON Schema; dataclasses inside.
Default lax mode turns "10" into 10; strict mode rejects it. Choose per contract and say why.
Default extra is ignore, so an unknown field silently disappears; for tools set extra="forbid".
On failure, return the error to the model and retry a bounded number of times; never repair silently.
Validation is one layer: anything with side effects still needs a confirm step and idempotency.

say: Pydantic at the edge, plain dataclasses inside. The model is an untrusted client, so its arguments get validated once, at the boundary.
Out of the box pydantic would turn "10" into 10 and drop the unknown field. For tools I'd forbid extras, and decide on strict per tool.
When it fails, the error goes back to the model and it gets a couple of tries.
And validation isn't the safety. In my system side-effecting tools return a preview first, only an explicit confirm executes, and idempotency keys make retries safe.
avoid: Saying you fix malformed model JSON silently: validate and return the error instead.

topics.title: Descriptors, slots, decorators and contextvars
topics.brief: Descriptors are the mechanism under properties, methods and ORM fields, and a data descriptor (one with `__set__`) beats the instance `__dict__`. A decorator that wraps an `async def` in a sync wrapper times or retries nothing, because it returns an un-awaited coroutine. contextvars give each asyncio task its own copy of request-scoped values, where a global or `threading.local` would leak across tasks.
points: Descriptor: an object with `__get__`, `__set__` or `__delete__` placed as a class attribute; functions are non-data descriptors (that is how methods bind), and `__set_name__` tells it its attribute name

__slots__: fixed attributes, no per-instance `__dict__`, so less memory, faster access, and a typo raises AttributeError; costs: no dynamic attributes, awkward multiple inheritance, no weakrefs unless `__weakref__` is listed; `@dataclass(slots=True)` writes it for you

Decorators: always `functools.wraps` (keeps `__name__`, `__doc__` and the signature for tracing); branch on `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` and give async functions an `async def` wrapper that awaits; type it with ParamSpec
contextvars: create `ContextVar`s at module level; each asyncio task gets a copy of its creator's context, so a child's `set()` never leaks up; `set()` returns a Token for `reset()`

Propagation: `asyncio.to_thread` copies the context, `loop.run_in_executor` does not (wrap the call in `contextvars.copy_context().run`); a plain `threading.Thread` starts empty in the default build but inherits under the free-threaded build
production: Tracing, retry, timeout and rate-limit decorators are the core of an agent SDK; the sync or async branch and `wraps` are what interviewers check.

Run id, tenant id, trace and span id, and the current sandbox handle live in contextvars, so every log line carries them without passing arguments through every call (OpenTelemetry builds on this; R2 marks that as general knowledge).
Millions of small objects such as trace spans and events: `@dataclass(slots=True, frozen=True)` drops the per-instance dict.
Thread-locals leak across asyncio tasks, because many tasks share one thread.

o: About 1 s, the full call
Near zero: it timed creating the coroutine, not running it
An error: decorators cannot wrap async functions
About 2 s, because the coroutine runs twice
Nothing: the wrapper never calls the function
mcq.why: Calling an async function only creates a coroutine. The sync wrapper returns it, the finally fires, and the real work happens later when the caller awaits.

mcq.q: Inside a task where `run_id` (a ContextVar with default "-") is set to "parent", what do `await asyncio.to_thread(run_id.get)` and `await loop.run_in_executor(None, run_id.get)` return?
o: "parent" and "parent"
"parent" and "-"
"-" and "parent"
"parent" and a LookupError
mcq.why: to_thread copies the current context into the worker thread; run_in_executor does not, so the thread sees the default. Wrap with copy_context().run to fix it.

mcq.q: class Positive defines __get__ and __set__; `Cfg.retries = Positive()`. After `c = Cfg(3)`, you run `c.__dict__["retries"] = 99`. What is `c.retries`?
o: 3: a data descriptor takes precedence over the instance dict
99: the instance dict always wins
AttributeError: the descriptor blocks __dict__ writes
99, but only until the next assignment
ValueError from __set__
mcq.why: Lookup checks data descriptors on the type before the instance __dict__. Only non-data descriptors, like plain functions, are shadowed by an instance attribute.

o: A new attribute nmae is created silently
name is set, by fuzzy matching
FrozenInstanceError, slots implies frozen
It works, with a warning
AttributeError
mcq.why: With __slots__ there is no instance __dict__, so only declared attributes can be set. slots does not imply frozen; assigning s.name still works.

open.q: How would you make every log line carry the run id, across asyncio tasks and the threads you push blocking work into?
open.probe: Whether you know contextvars semantics, and where propagation silently breaks.
a: A module-level ContextVar for run id, set once at the start of the run.
A logging filter or tracing decorator reads it, so no function takes run_id as an argument.
Each asyncio task gets a copy of its creator's context, so concurrent runs cannot clobber each other the way a global or thread-local would.
asyncio.to_thread carries it into threads; run_in_executor and bare threads do not, so wrap them with copy_context().run.
Test it: two concurrent runs, assert each log line has its own id.

say: I'd put the run id in a module-level ContextVar and have the log filter read it, so nothing passes run_id around by hand.
Each task copies its parent's context, so two runs on the same loop can't mix ids, which a thread-local would get wrong.
The trap is threads. to_thread carries the context, run_in_executor doesn't, so I'd wrap that with copy_context().run, and write a test with two runs at once.
avoid: Saying threading.local is safe for request data in asyncio: many tasks share one thread.

topics.title: Tooling, tests and profiling
topics.brief: The working kit: uv for environments and locks, ruff for lint and format, pytest with fakes at the boundary, and measurement before tuning: cProfile locally, py-spy on a live process, tracemalloc for growth. In an AI-allowed round the judgement shows in how you read what the tool wrote, not in typing speed.
points: uv (Astral): one Rust tool in place of pip, pip-tools, virtualenv, pipx and Python installs: `uv init`, `uv add`, `uv lock` (cross-platform `uv.lock`), `uv sync --frozen`, `uv run`, `uvx`; PEP 723 inline metadata lets one script declare its own dependencies (the docs claim 10 to 100 times faster than pip)

ruff (R2 marks the rule codes as general knowledge): linter and formatter in one; rules for this domain: B006 mutable default, B023 loop closure, ASYNC for blocking calls in async code, RUF006 for a dangling `create_task`

pytest: fixtures with scopes (`function` default, `module`, `session`), and a `yield` fixture tears down after the test; `parametrize` gives each case its own test id; `monkeypatch` undoes everything after the test; async tests need a plugin
Patch where it is used: if the module did `from os import getcwd`, patch `mymodule.getcwd`, not `os.getcwd`

Profiling: `python -m cProfile -o out.prof` is deterministic and function-level, with overhead; py-spy samples a running process by PID with no restart (`record`, `top`, `dump`; `--native`, `--gil`, `--idle`) and needs ptrace, so `SYS_PTRACE` in Docker or Kubernetes

Memory: `tracemalloc` snapshots allocations by line and diffs two snapshots; `sys.getsizeof` is shallow; leaks in long-running agents are usually unbounded caches or queues, task sets that never discard, or `lru_cache` on a method keeping `self` alive
production: Reproducible builds: commit `uv.lock`, install with `uv sync --frozen` in CI and in images.
Make the model client injectable and fake it at the boundary (or `httpx.MockTransport` for HTTP), so tests never touch the network or spend tokens.
Why is the worker slow in production: `py-spy dump` or `top` against the live PID, no redeploy.
p99 spikes every few seconds in an async service: usually one CPU-heavy call blocking the loop; asyncio debug mode reports slow callbacks.

Live coding with AI: state the constraints before prompting, read the diff aloud, and look for swallowed `CancelledError`, `except Exception: pass`, missing HTTP timeouts, mutable defaults, blocking calls in async code and unbounded concurrency.

mcq.q: mymodule.py does `from os import getcwd` and calls `getcwd()`. In a test you want it to return "/fake". What do you patch?
o: os.getcwd, because that is where it is defined
builtins.getcwd
Both, or neither patch takes effect
mymodule.getcwd, the name the module bound at import
Nothing works: from-imports cannot be patched
mcq.why: The from-import copied a reference into mymodule's namespace. Patching os.getcwd rebinds the os attribute, which mymodule no longer looks at.

mcq.q: A Python worker in Kubernetes has gone slow and you cannot restart it without losing the evidence. First move?
o: Add cProfile to the entry point and redeploy
py-spy dump or top against its PID, with SYS_PTRACE granted
Take tracemalloc snapshots and compare them
Raise the log level to DEBUG and wait
Call sys.setprofile from a REPL attached to the pod
mcq.why: py-spy samples from outside the process, with no code change or restart, and dump shows every thread's current stack. It needs the ptrace capability in a container.

mcq.q: An agent worker's memory climbs steadily over several hours. Which tool finds the line that is allocating?
o: sys.getsizeof on the main objects
py-spy record with --gil
tracemalloc snapshots taken apart in time, compared by line
gc.collect() on a timer
cProfile sorted by cumulative time
mcq.why: tracemalloc diffs show which source lines grew. getsizeof is shallow, py-spy and cProfile measure time, and gc only helps with cycles.

open.q: One worker's memory grows over hours, and another async service has p99 spikes every few seconds. How do you diagnose each, in production?
open.probe: Whether you measure before guessing, and know the usual causes in long-running agent code.
a: Memory: tracemalloc snapshots some time apart, diffed by line, to find what grows.
Usual suspects: unbounded caches or queues, a set of tasks never discarded, history in a global list, lru_cache on a method.
Latency: py-spy top or dump on the live process, no restart, to see what holds the loop.
Usual cause: one CPU-heavy or blocking call on the event loop; move it to a thread or process; asyncio debug mode flags slow callbacks.
Then a test or a bound (maxsize, bounded queue) so it cannot come back.

say: I'd measure before touching anything. For the memory one, tracemalloc snapshots an hour apart and diff them by line. It's almost always something unbounded, a cache, a queue, a set of tasks.
For the latency spikes I'd attach py-spy to the live process, no redeploy, and look for one blocking or CPU-heavy call sitting on the event loop.
Fix it, then put a bound or a test in so it stays fixed.
avoid: Claiming py-spy or uv experience at depth you have not used; describe what each does and how you would apply it.

modules.blurb: Defend TypeScript choices in the room: what the type system checks, where it is unsound, and how untrusted model output becomes a type you can trust.

topics.title: Structural typing and its surprises
topics.brief: TypeScript checks compatibility by shape, not by declared name: anything with at least the right properties fits. The nuance is that the excess property check, which catches extra keys, only fires on a fresh object literal, so a typed parameter can still carry extra keys (a secret, junk from a model) at runtime.
points: Structural: with `class Usd { cents = 0 }` and `class Eur { cents = 0 }`, `const e: Eur = new Usd()` compiles; the names never enter into it
Excess property check: `const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }` errors, but assign the same object to a variable first and `const p: Point = p3` compiles
Weak types: a type whose properties are all optional rejects a value with no property in common, so `{ retry: 3 }` does not fit `{ retries?: number }` even through a variable
Object.keys: returns `string[]` on purpose, because the runtime object may hold more keys than its type lists; cast once in a helper, only for objects you build yourself
Nominal exceptions: a `private` or `protected` member makes a class match only itself; for strings and ids you use a brand (see the satisfies topic)
production: Tool args and request bodies: a value typed by its shape can carry extra keys, so copy the declared fields (or let zod's `z.object` strip unknown keys) before logging, storing or prompting with it
`Object.entries` gives `[string, T][]`; iterate with it rather than forcing `keyof` onto a value you did not create
Spread loses the prototype: `{ ...instance }` keeps the fields and none of the methods at runtime

mcq.q: `interface Point { x: number; y: number }` and `const p3 = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }`. Which line fails to compile?
o: `const a: Point = p3;`
`f(p3)` where `function f(p: Point) {}`
`const c: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };`
`const d = p3 as Point;`
`const e: { x: number } = p3;`
mcq.why: Only a fresh object literal gets the excess property check. Every other line passes a value that has at least the required fields, which is all structural typing asks.

mcq.q: Why does `Object.keys(user)` return `string[]` and not `(keyof User)[]`?
o: A value typed User may hold more keys at runtime than User lists
keyof is erased before Object.keys runs, so the compiler cannot see it
The lib typings for Object predate keyof and were never updated
Numeric keys would make keyof User unsound for arrays
Strict mode widens every key union to string for safety
mcq.why: Structural typing lets a value with extra properties stand in for User, so promising only User's keys would be a lie. The honest type is string[].

mcq.q: `class Usd { cents = 0 }` and `class Eur { cents = 0 }`. What does `const e: Eur = new Usd()` do?
o: Fails to compile, because class types are nominal
Compiles only when written with `as Eur`
Compiles, then throws because the prototypes differ
Compiles; a private member in each class would stop it
Fails unless both classes implement one shared interface
mcq.why: Classes are compared by their members like any other type. Private and protected members are the exception: they match only when they come from the same declaration.

open.q: A teammate says the tool args are typed, so the handler can log the whole args object safely. You disagree. Why, and what do you change?
open.probe: Whether he knows a type is a claim about shape, not a guarantee of exact keys at runtime
a: TypeScript is structural: a value with at least the declared fields fits the type, extra keys included.
The excess property check only catches a fresh literal written in the code, never data from a model or a request.
So the logged object holds whatever the model sent, including keys it should not have or sensitive values.
Parse at the boundary into a new object with only the declared fields (zod's z.object strips unknown keys by default), then log that.
If an extra key should make the model correct itself, use a strict schema that rejects unknown keys instead of stripping them.

say: I think the thing people miss is that TypeScript checks shape, not exact shape.
A value with extra keys still fits the type, and the excess property check only fires on a literal I wrote myself.
So anything from a model or a request, I parse into a fresh object with only the fields I declared. Then the type and the runtime value agree.
avoid: Saying TypeScript removes extra properties: types are erased and change nothing at runtime

topics.title: any, unknown and never
topics.brief: `any` turns the checker off and spreads to everything read from it; `unknown` is the safe top type, usable only after you narrow it; `never` is the empty type, returned by a function that always throws and left over when every case is handled. The nuance: `JSON.parse` and `res.json()` hand you `any` silently, so the leak starts in the standard library, not in your code.
points: any: contagious; with `const a: any = JSON.parse(s)`, the line `const n: number = a.count` compiles even when count is missing, and `n + 1` is NaN
unknown: every value is assignable to it and nothing can be done with it until narrowed; use it for `JSON.parse`, `fetch().json()`, tool input and catch variables
never: assignable to every type, nothing is assignable to it; `function fail(m: string): never { throw new Error(m) }` fits in `const x: string = ok ? v : fail("no")`

Catch variables: `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (part of `strict`) makes `catch (e)` unknown, rightly, because `throw "a string"` is legal; normalise with `e instanceof Error ? e : new Error(String(e))`
Rule of thumb: unknown at every boundary, never for exhaustiveness, any only in a commented escape hatch
production: Wrap `JSON.parse` in a helper typed to return unknown, so the next line has to parse what came back
Every catch block that reads `.message` normalises first with a `toError(e)` helper, because a library can throw a string or a plain object
TypeScript 7 turns `strict` on by default, so unknown catch variables are the default on new projects; old code upgraded to it starts failing exactly there

mcq.q: `const a: any = JSON.parse("{}"); const n: number = a.count;` What does `n + 1` give?
o: A compile error: any is not assignable to number
NaN at runtime, with no error anywhere
A TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined
1, because undefined converts to 0
A compile error under strict for an implicit any
mcq.why: any is assignable to number, so it compiles. a.count is undefined and undefined + 1 is NaN, which nobody notices until much later.

mcq.q: Inside `catch (e)` with `strict` on, which line compiles?
o: `console.log(e.message)`
`const err: Error = e`
`throw e.cause`
`if (e.message) retry()`
`const msg = e instanceof Error ? e.message : String(e)`
mcq.why: With useUnknownInCatchVariables the catch variable is unknown, so it must be narrowed first. instanceof Error narrows it, and String(e) covers a thrown string or object.

mcq.q: `function fail(msg: string) { throw new Error(msg) }` is used as `const x: string = ok ? v : fail("no")`. Which annotated return type makes that compile?
o: void
undefined
never
unknown
Error
mcq.why: never is assignable to every type, so a call to fail fits where a string is expected. void and undefined are not assignable to string, and unknown is assignable to nothing but unknown and any.

open.q: The model's tool arguments arrive and your codebase types them as any. Walk me through what can go wrong, and what you would change.
open.probe: Whether he treats model output as untrusted input and knows how any spreads
a: any switches the checker off for that value and for everything read from it, so a wrong or missing field compiles.
The failure then shows up far away: a NaN in a budget, an undefined id in a database call.
Change the type to unknown, so code cannot touch the args until they are parsed.
Parse with a schema at that one point (zod's safeParse), which turns unknown into a real type and gives a readable error.
Send that error back to the model as an is_error tool result instead of crashing the loop.

say: The way I think about it, any is the checker giving up, and it spreads.
Model output is the least trustworthy data I have, so it comes in as unknown and nothing touches it until a schema parses it.
never I use the other way round, for the case that should not exist, so the compiler tells me when it does.
avoid: Calling unknown 'any but stricter' without saying it must be narrowed before any use

topics.title: Narrowing, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness
topics.brief: Narrowing is the checker following your control flow: after `typeof v === "string"` it knows v is a string. A discriminated union (every member has a literal tag) plus a switch with a `never` default turns 'I added an event type' into a compile error everywhere it must be handled. The nuance: a hand-written type guard is a promise the compiler believes without checking.
points: Built-in narrowing: `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, equality, truthiness and assignment; the handbook calls it control flow analysis
Discriminated union: `{ type: "text"; delta: string } | { type: "done"; reason: "stop" | "length" }`; checking `e.type` narrows e to one member

Exhaustiveness: `default: return assertNever(e)` with `assertNever(v: never): never`; an unhandled new member makes that line a compile error, and at runtime it throws on an event the build does not know
Type predicate: `function isX(v: unknown): v is X` is unchecked; if the body only checks the tag, tsc still trusts the whole shape
Assertion function: `function assertString(v: unknown): asserts v is string` narrows the caller's variable after it returns, or throws
TS 5.5: `[1, undefined, 2].filter((x) => x !== undefined)` is inferred as `number[]` without a hand-written predicate
production: Agent stream events (`text | tool_call | done`) and run states (`idle | running | paused | failed`) as discriminated unions, every switch ending in a never default
For anything structured, a schema such as `z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])` beats a hand-written guard: the same narrowing, backed by a runtime check
Keep the never branch throwing (or logging and skipping) at runtime: an older client can receive an event type a newer server added

mcq.q: `type Ev = { type: "text"; delta: string } | { type: "done" }`. A teammate adds `{ type: "tool_call"; name: string }`. Where does the compiler complain?
o: Nowhere: adding a union member is always backward compatible
Only where an object of the new member is created
At every place that reads e.delta without a check
At each switch on e.type whose default calls assertNever(e)
At the type declaration, until every switch has a case
mcq.why: In those switches the default branch now receives the new member instead of never, so the assertNever call stops compiling. Switches without that default compile silently, which is why the pattern matters.

mcq.q: `function isText(v: unknown): v is { type: "text"; delta: string } { return typeof v === "object" && v !== null && "type" in v && v.type === "text"; }` is called on `{ type: "text" }`. What happens?
o: It returns true, and v.delta is typed string but is undefined
A compile error: the body does not prove that delta exists
It returns false, because the delta property is missing
It returns true, and tsc marks delta as optional on v
A TypeError inside the guard when it reads the delta
mcq.why: A type predicate is trusted, not verified. The body checked only the tag, so the caller gets a string-typed field that is undefined at runtime.

mcq.q: Which is the strongest reason to parse model output with `z.discriminatedUnion` instead of a hand-written type guard?
o: It narrows more precisely than a switch on the tag does
It checks every field at runtime, so the narrowed type is earned
It closes the union, so no new members can be added later
It removes the need for a never default in each switch
It runs at compile time, so bad output never reaches production
mcq.why: Both give the same static narrowing. The schema also verifies each field when the data arrives, which a predicate only promises.

open.q: Your agent streams events to the UI: text deltas, tool calls, done. Next month someone adds a thinking event. How do you make sure nothing drops it silently?
open.probe: Discriminated unions and exhaustiveness as a design tool, plus the runtime side of it
a: Model the events as a discriminated union on a literal type field.
End every switch over it with a default that passes the value to assertNever, typed never.
Adding thinking then makes each unhandled switch a compile error: a to-do list from the compiler.
Decide what that default does at runtime (throw, or log and skip), because an old client can receive the new event from a newer server.
Parse incoming events with a schema, so the union is backed by a check rather than a cast.

say: I'd make the events a discriminated union and end every switch with a never default.
Then adding an event type is a compile error everywhere it isn't handled, which is pretty much a to-do list for free.
The one thing I'd add is a runtime decision in that default, because an older client can still get the new event over the wire.
avoid: Claiming exhaustiveness checks protect you at runtime by themselves: they only hold if the data was parsed into the union

topics.title: Generics, conditional, mapped and template literal types
topics.brief: A generic is a type parameter the caller fills in, and constraints such as `K extends keyof T` tie one parameter to another. Conditional types with `infer` take types apart, mapped types build object types key by key, and template literal types match strings. The nuances: a conditional type distributes over a union only when the checked type is a naked type parameter, and indexing a map with a union key (the correlated union) needs a generic function to typecheck.
points: Constraints: `function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(o: T, k: K): T[K]` rejects a key the object lacks; a type parameter that appears once in a signature is usually a lie, so use the concrete type
infer: `type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer U> ? Unwrap<U> : T` gives number for `Promise<Promise<number>>`; `ReturnType` of an overloaded function uses the last overload
Distribution: `T extends unknown ? T[] : never` on `string | number` gives `string[] | number[]`; written `[T] extends [unknown]` it gives `(string | number)[]`
Mapped types: `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` builds a type key by key; an `as` clause renames keys (getName from name, with a template literal) and remapping a key to never drops it
Newer tools: `const` type parameters (TS 5.0) keep `["a", 1]` as `readonly ["a", 1]`; `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) stops a default argument from widening T
Correlated unions: `handlers[call.name](call.args)` fails because TS cannot tie name to args across the union; a generic `dispatch<K extends keyof Tools>` with one cast at the parse seam fixes it
production: A tool registry: `type Handlers = { [K in keyof Tools]: (args: ArgMap[K]) => Promise<string> }` makes a missing or mistyped handler a compile error
Template literal types for string formats: a route type can pull "id" | "jobId" out of "/users/:id/jobs/:jobId" (ParseRoute in the code file)
Type-level tests: `Expect<Equal<A, B>>` aliases fail the build when a derived type drifts, so clever types are tested like code
Restraint: if a type needs a page of conditional types to be right, the API is probably wrong; the next reader matters more than the last cast

mcq.q: `type ToArr<T> = T extends unknown ? T[] : never`. What is `ToArr<string | number>`?
o: `(string | number)[]`
`never`
`unknown[]`
`string[] & number[]`
`string[] | number[]`
mcq.why: A conditional on a naked type parameter distributes: it runs once per union member and joins the results. Wrap both sides in a tuple, [T] extends [unknown], to get (string | number)[].

mcq.q: `Handlers` maps each tool name to a handler for that tool's args, and `ToolCall` is the union of `{ name, args }` pairs. Why does `handlers[call.name](call.args)` fail inside `function run(call: ToolCall)`?
o: call.name widens to string, so the index is not a known key
Mapped types cannot be indexed with a key of union type
name and args are unrelated to TS, so the call needs every args type
The handlers object needs `as const` for its keys to stay literal
An async handler cannot be called from a function that is not async
mcq.why: Indexing with a union gives a union of functions, callable only with the intersection of their parameters. A generic dispatch over K lets TS relate handlers[K] to ArgMap[K].

mcq.q: `function pick<T extends string>(opts: T[], def?: NoInfer<T>)`. What does `pick(["a", "b"], "c")` do?
o: A compile error: "c" is not "a" | "b"
Compiles, with T inferred as "a" | "b" | "c"
Compiles, with T widened to string
A compile error: NoInfer needs an explicit type argument
Compiles, and returns undefined at runtime
mcq.why: NoInfer stops def from being a source for inferring T, so T comes from opts alone. Without it T would grow to include "c" and the check would catch nothing.

open.q: Type a tool registry so that adding a tool without a handler, or with a handler that takes the wrong arguments, fails to compile.
open.probe: Mapped types over keyof, the correlated union limitation, and where the one cast goes
a: Keep one object of tool schemas (zod in real code) and derive everything else from typeof it.
A mapped type over its keys gives the args type per tool; a second mapped type gives Handlers, so every key needs a correctly typed handler.
Indexing a mapped type with [keyof Tools] turns it into the ToolCall union for the model's calls.
Dispatch is generic over K extends keyof Tools; the parse result is cast to ArgMap[K] once, because TS cannot relate name and args across a union.
Put satisfies on the registry so the keys stay literal while the shape is checked.

say: I'd keep one object of schemas and derive the rest with mapped types, so a tool without a handler won't compile.
The rough edge is the correlated union: TypeScript can't tie the tool name to its args across a union.
So I make dispatch generic and put a single cast at the seam, right after the parse, and I'd call that out in review.
avoid: Writing a page of conditional types to remove that last cast: one documented cast at the parse seam is the readable answer

topics.title: satisfies, as const, readonly and branded ids
topics.brief: An annotation checks a value and widens it to the declared type; `satisfies` checks it and keeps the narrow inferred type; `as` checks almost nothing and lies silently. `as const`, `readonly` and brands live only in the type system. The nuance: none of them does anything at runtime, so `as const` does not freeze, `readonly` does not stop another alias, and a brand is only as good as the constructor that checks it.
points: Annotation: `const c: Colors = {...}` widens each value to the declared type, so `c.red.toUpperCase()` fails when red is `string | number[]`
satisfies (TS 4.9): `{...} satisfies Colors` checks the shape and keeps red as string; on a `Record<string, T>` registry it keeps the literal keys, so a typo in a key is caught
as: an assertion, not a conversion; `JSON.parse('{"retries":"3"}') as { retries: number }` then `+ 1` gives "31"; `as unknown as T` is a review red flag
as const: `["search", "fetch"] as const` with `(typeof X)[number]` gives a runtime list and the union "search" | "fetch", the modern replacement for an enum; `Object.isFrozen` is still false
readonly: shallow, compile-time and one-way; a `number[]` assigns to `readonly number[]` and the original alias can still push
Brand: `type RunId = string & { readonly __brand: "RunId" }`, made only by a constructor that validates; a plain string or a TenantId no longer fits
production: Model and config registries: `satisfies Record<string, ModelSpec>` keeps the keys literal, so `keyof typeof MODELS` is a real union
Branded run, tenant, trace and sandbox ids, created only at the boundary; zod's `z.string().brand<"RunId">()` produces one by parsing
`as const` objects instead of enums: enums are not erasable syntax, so they fail Node's type stripping and `erasableSyntaxOnly`
When a runtime guarantee is needed, `Object.freeze` or a copy; readonly only documents intent

mcq.q: `type Colors = Record<"red" | "green", string | number[]>`. Which declaration checks the object against Colors and still lets `c.red.toUpperCase()` compile?
o: `const c: Colors = { red: "#f00", green: [0, 255, 0] }`
`const c = { red: "#f00", green: [0, 255, 0] } satisfies Colors`
`const c = { red: "#f00", green: [0, 255, 0] } as Colors`
`const c = { red: "#f00", green: [0, 255, 0] } as const`
`const c: Readonly<Colors> = { red: "#f00", green: [0, 255, 0] }`
mcq.why: satisfies checks against Colors but keeps red inferred as string. The annotation and the as cast both make red string | number[]; as const keeps the literal but checks nothing.

mcq.q: `const cfg = JSON.parse('{"retries":"3"}') as { retries: number }`. What is `cfg.retries + 1`?
o: A compile error, because the JSON does not match the type
A TypeError thrown by the as check at runtime
NaN
mcq.why: as only changes what the compiler believes. retries is still the string "3", so + 1 concatenates.

mcq.q: `type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: "UserId" }`. Which statement is true?
o: It stops a malformed id from existing at runtime
It makes `typeof id` return "UserId" at runtime
It needs a runtime library to attach the brand
Every UserId value carries a hidden __brand property
A plain string no longer fits, but only the constructor checks anything
mcq.why: The brand exists only in the type system; the values are plain strings. Put the validation in the one function allowed to cast.

open.q: Run ids, tenant ids and trace ids are all strings on your platform, and someone passed a tenant id where a run id was expected. How do you stop that class of bug?
open.probe: Branded types, where the one cast lives, and what brands do not protect
a: Brand each id: a string intersected with a readonly tag type, so the types stop being interchangeable.
Make branded values only at the boundary, in a constructor or schema that validates the format; that is the one place a cast is allowed.
Functions take RunId, so a TenantId or a raw string is a compile error.
State the limit: brands are erased, so ids from the database or the model must pass through the constructor or the protection is fiction.
The same idea, taken further for a model: it sees only opaque handles and code reattaches the real ids.

say: I'd brand them. A RunId is a string with a type-only tag, and the only way to make one is a function that checks the format.
After that, passing a tenant id where a run id goes doesn't compile.
At alfred_ we went further for the model: it only sees opaque handles and code reattaches the real ids, so it can't swap them at all.
avoid: Saying brands validate anything at runtime: they are erased, and the constructor does the checking
