topics.title: Strict flags and variance
topics.brief: `strict` turns on the checks that make types mean something, and two flags outside it, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, close the most common runtime holes. The nuance: with all of them on, TypeScript is still deliberately unsound in places (method parameters are bivariant, arrays are covariant, narrowing survives a call that mutates), and a senior engineer can name them.
points: strict: bundles noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, useUnknownInCatchVariables, alwaysStrict and strictBuiltinIteratorReturn; on by default in TypeScript 7
noUncheckedIndexedAccess: `arr[0]` and `record[key]` become `T | undefined`, so `counts["x"].toFixed()` stops compiling
exactOptionalPropertyTypes: `title?: string` may be absent but not `undefined`; it matters because JSON drops an undefined key but keeps null, and `"title" in obj` is true for an explicit undefined

Variance: under strictFunctionTypes a function-typed property checks parameters contravariantly, but method syntax `handle(x: T): string` stays bivariant, so a Dog handler can pose as an Animal handler and crash
Other holes: `Dog[]` assigns to `Animal[]` and then accepts any Animal; narrowing of `box.v` survives a call that sets it to null; `const f: () => void = () => 42` compiles
Explicit variance: `interface Producer<out T>` and `interface Consumer<in T>` (TS 4.7) state it instead of leaving it to inference
production: Turn on strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes and accept the friction; the last can break libraries that pass undefined for optional props, so check dependencies first
Declare callbacks as function-typed properties (`on: (e: E) => void`) to get the strict check; use method syntax only where bivariance is needed
PATCH bodies: exactOptionalPropertyTypes is what keeps 'leave this field alone' (absent) apart from 'clear it' (null)

mcq.q: `interface H<T> { handle(x: T): string }`. An `H<Dog>` that calls `d.bark()` is assigned to an `H<Animal>` variable, which is then called with a plain Animal. What happens?
o: It compiles, then throws a TypeError at runtime
A compile error under strictFunctionTypes
A compile error only with noImplicitAny on
It compiles and quietly returns undefined
A compile error unless T is marked `out`
mcq.why: Parameters declared with method syntax stay bivariant even under strict, an intentional hole. Written as handle: (x: T) => string, the assignment would fail to compile.

mcq.q: With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` on and `interface Patch { title?: string }`, which line fails to compile?
o: `const p: Patch = {}`
`const p: Patch = { title: "x" }`
`const p: Patch = { title: undefined }`
`const p: Partial<Patch> = {}`
`const p: Patch = JSON.parse("{}")`
mcq.why: The flag separates absent from explicitly undefined. The difference is real at runtime: "title" in p is true for an explicit undefined, and JSON.stringify drops the key.

mcq.q: Which flag makes `const n = counts[key]` typed `number | undefined` for `counts: Record<string, number>`?
o: strictNullChecks
exactOptionalPropertyTypes
noImplicitAny
noUncheckedIndexedAccess
strictPropertyInitialization
mcq.why: noUncheckedIndexedAccess is not part of strict. Without it, indexing a record or an array claims the value is always there.

open.q: Is TypeScript's type system sound? Give me concrete examples where it isn't, and what you do about them.
open.probe: Whether he knows the deliberate holes and the flags or habits that close some of them
a: No, by design: it trades soundness for usability, and the handbook calls method bivariance unsound but pragmatic.
Method parameters stay bivariant under strict; arrays are covariant, so a Dog[] seen as Animal[] accepts a Cat.
Narrowing on a property survives a function call that changes it; any and as switch checking off entirely.
Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, indexing claims the value exists; without exactOptionalPropertyTypes, absent and undefined blur.
So: those two flags on top of strict, callbacks as function-typed properties, readonly inputs, and runtime parsing at boundaries, since types are erased anyway.

say: No, and that's on purpose.
My go-to examples are method parameter bivariance, array covariance, and narrowing that survives a call that changed the value.
I turn on noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes on top of strict and accept the friction. And because types are erased, I still parse at every boundary.
avoid: Calling TypeScript sound once strict is on: this question exists to see whether you can name the holes

topics.title: Validation at the boundary and Result types
topics.brief: Types are erased, so every place data enters (HTTP bodies, env vars, database JSON, model output, tool arguments) needs a runtime check that produces the type. With zod the schema is the check and `z.infer` derives the type from it, so the shape is written once. The nuance: a failed tool validation is not a crash but the next message to the model, which is why expected failures fit a Result type better than an exception.
points: z.infer: `type SearchArgs = z.infer<typeof SearchArgs>` is the output type; with `.default()`, `.transform()` or coercion the input differs, so `z.input` and `z.output` are not the same type
safeParse vs parse: `safeParse` returns a success flag with data or error and never throws; `parse` throws ZodError; in a tool path use safeParse and send `z.prettifyError(...)` back to the model
Unknown keys: `z.object` strips them by default, `z.strictObject` rejects them; strip is forgiving, strict makes the model correct itself
Coercion trap: `z.coerce.boolean().parse("false")` is true, because it is `Boolean("false")`; parse env flags explicitly, while `z.coerce.number()` is fine for a port
Tool schemas: `z.toJSONSchema(schema, { io: "input" })` gives the model-facing schema; without `io: "input"`, a field with a default is listed as required
Result: `{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` for expected failures (validation, not found, quota), exceptions for bugs; a tool failure becomes a `tool_result` with `is_error: true`
production: Anthropic tools: the model returns `tool_use` blocks with id, name and input; the next user message starts with `tool_result` blocks, `is_error: true` on failure, and the docs say the model usually retries 2 to 3 times with corrections after invalid input
OpenAI strict function calling: every property in `required` and `additionalProperties: false`, optional modelled as a union with null, so `.optional()` becomes `.nullable()` there

SDK helpers: Anthropic's TypeScript SDK has `betaZodTool()` and a tool runner that returns a thrown error as an is_error tool result; the Vercel AI SDK has `tool({ description, inputSchema, execute })`
Tool output (web pages, emails) is untrusted too: it stays in tool_result blocks, never in the system prompt
Error classes: subclass Error, set name, keep cause, and tag retryable so the retry layer does not have to guess

mcq.q: A tool schema has `limit: z.number().default(10)`. You emit its input_schema with `z.toJSONSchema(schema)` and no options. What goes wrong?
o: Nothing: defaults are left out of JSON Schema output
Emitting fails, because a default is not valid JSON Schema
limit is listed as required, so the model thinks it must send it
limit is emitted as nullable, so the model may send null
The default is applied twice, by the model and by zod
mcq.why: The default view describes parsed output, where limit always exists. The model produces input, so emit with { io: "input" } and limit becomes optional.

mcq.q: A search tool receives `{ query: "" }` from the model and validation fails. What is the best response?
o: Throw, so the loop's top-level handler logs it and ends the run
Fill in a default query and run the tool anyway
Drop the call silently and let the model carry on
Retry the same model call at a higher temperature
Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a readable message
mcq.why: Invalid arguments are an expected failure, so they are data for the model, not a crash. A clear message lets it correct the call on the next turn.

mcq.q: Where does a Result type earn its place over an exception?
o: Everywhere, so that no function in the codebase ever throws
Expected domain failures callers must handle, like validation or quota
Programming bugs, so that they appear in the function signature
Synchronous code only, because await cannot return a Result
The HTTP layer only, where status codes already exist
mcq.why: A Result puts the failure in the type, so the compiler makes callers handle it. Bugs should still throw, and libraries throw anyway, so keep Result at module boundaries.

open.q: The model returns tool arguments. Take me from that raw value to a typed call you trust, and tell me what happens when it is wrong.
open.probe: The boundary mindset, z.infer, input against output schemas, and failure as data for the model
a: Tool arguments are untrusted input, exactly like a request body: unknown until parsed.
One zod schema per tool: z.infer types the handler and z.toJSONSchema with io input gives the model-facing schema, so the two cannot drift.
safeParse at the seam; on failure return a tool_result with is_error true and the prettified error, and the model usually corrects itself.
On success the handler gets typed args; still authorise and bound them (limits, ids the user owns), because a valid shape is not a permitted action.
Tool failures come back as a Result, not an exception, so the loop turns them into tool results instead of crashing.

say: I treat tool arguments like a request body.
One schema per tool: the type comes from z.infer and the model's schema from the same object, so they can't drift.
If parsing fails, the error goes back as a tool result with is_error, and the model usually fixes it.
At alfred_ the side-effecting tools return a preview first and only an explicit confirm executes, so even valid arguments don't act on their own.
avoid: Saying the schema makes the model's output correct: it makes it well formed, and the meaning still needs checking

topics.title: Modules, runtimes, tsconfig and testing
topics.brief: Modern TypeScript is checked by `tsc --noEmit` and run by something that strips the types: Node, Deno, Bun or a bundler. The module format decides how imports resolve: under `nodenext`, ESM relative imports need the file extension and a `.ts` file follows the nearest package.json `type`. The nuance: type stripping only erases syntax, so enums, namespaces and constructor parameter properties fail, and tsconfig is not read at runtime.
points: Type stripping: Node runs `.ts` by erasing types (on by default from 22.18 and 23.6); it rejects `enum`, runtime namespaces and `constructor(private x: number)`, needs real `.ts` extensions in imports and `import type` for types; `erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8) makes tsc flag the same constructs

ESM vs CJS: a `.ts` file with no `"type": "module"` in package.json is treated as CommonJS; ESM relative imports need the extension; ESM has no `__dirname`, so use `import.meta.dirname` or `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)`
require(esm): unflagged from Node 22.12 and 20.19; fails with ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE if the graph has top-level await; dynamic `import()` always works from CJS

A tsconfig worth defending: strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, exactOptionalPropertyTypes, verbatimModuleSyntax, isolatedModules, nodenext for a Node service (preserve and bundler for a bundled app), noEmit
TypeScript 7: the native compiler written in Go, roughly 8 to 12 times faster; `strict` on and `types: []` by default, so `@types/node` globals vanish unless listed
Testing: vitest transpiles with esbuild and does not type-check, so `tsc --noEmit` is its own step; with fake timers and promise code use `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync`
production: Node, Deno, Bun: Node and Deno run on V8, Bun on JavaScriptCore; Deno is default-deny, Node's opt-in `--permission` is described by its docs as a seat belt, Bun has no permission model, and none of them replaces container or microVM isolation for untrusted agent code
Deno, as in Supabase edge functions: `npm:` and `jsr:` specifiers or an import map in deno.json, `node:` prefixes for built-ins, no `Buffer` or `__dirname` globals
An ESM-only dependency (p-limit 7, many AI SDK pieces) in a CJS build: move the package to `"type": "module"` with nodenext; `await import()` or require(esm) are stopgaps
Dual-package hazard: a package shipping both ESM and CJS can load twice, which breaks instanceof checks and singletons
LLM code in tests: a fake model client that returns a scripted tool_use turn, then end_turn; fast deterministic tests stay apart from slower evals

mcq.q: You run `node app.ts` on Node 22.18. Which line in app.ts makes it fail before anything runs?
o: `import type { Cfg } from "./cfg.ts"`
`const x = y satisfies Cfg`
`type Id = string & { __brand: "Id" }`
`enum Level { Low, High }`
`function f<T>(x: T): T { return x }`
mcq.why: Type stripping only erases syntax. An enum emits a runtime object, so strip-only mode rejects it; every other line erases to plain JavaScript.

mcq.q: A Node ESM file has `import { helper } from "./util"` and util.ts exists, under `moduleResolution: nodenext`. What happens?
o: tsc errors, and Node throws ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND
It works: Node tries .ts and then .js
tsc accepts it, and only Node fails
It works only when tsconfig sets baseUrl
tsc rewrites it to ./util.js on emit
mcq.why: Node's ESM resolver does not guess extensions, and nodenext mirrors that. TS does not rewrite import paths unless rewriteRelativeImportExtensions (TS 5.7) is on.

mcq.q: Your vitest suite is green but `tsc --noEmit` fails on the same files. Why?
o: vitest bundles a newer TypeScript than the tsc you ran
vitest only runs the test files that changed
tsc checks test files against a stricter lib by default
vitest ignores type errors in test files but not in sources
vitest transpiles with esbuild and never type-checks
mcq.why: Transpiling strips types file by file without checking them. That is why tsc --noEmit runs as its own step.

open.q: Node, Deno or Bun for the agent worker runtime, and what tsconfig would you start from?
open.probe: Operational judgement over benchmarks, what permission models do not cover, and a tsconfig he can defend flag by flag
a: Node LTS for long-running platform services: its ecosystem, APM agents, profilers and native modules are the most mature.

modules.blurb: Say exactly what runs when, who gets cancelled on failure, and how you bound, retry, stream and stop concurrent work in both languages.

topics.title: The event loop in each language
topics.brief: Both runtimes run your code on one thread with a loop that picks the next ready piece of work. The nuance is the queues: JS drains every microtask (promise reactions) before the next macrotask (timers, I/O), while asyncio has one FIFO ready queue and a new task waits its turn. Ordering you can see in a log is not always ordering you can rely on.
points: One thread: an event loop gives concurrency, not parallelism. While one callback or coroutine step runs, nothing else on that loop does.

JS microtasks: promise reactions and `queueMicrotask` drain completely after each macrotask, so a resolved `.then` always beats `setTimeout(fn, 0)`. Recursive microtasks or `process.nextTick` starve the loop and I/O never runs.

Node phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check (`setImmediate`), close. `setTimeout(0)` against `setImmediate` from the main module is not deterministic; inside an I/O callback `setImmediate` wins.
nextTick is not portable: in Node ESM promise reactions run before `process.nextTick`, in CommonJS nextTick runs first, and Deno and Bun differ again. Never write code that depends on it.

asyncio ready queue: `loop.call_soon` and task steps run FIFO. `create_task` schedules the task for a later iteration; awaiting a coroutine directly runs it inline in the current task, with no loop trip.

Eager tasks (3.12): with `asyncio.eager_task_factory`, `create_task` runs the body at once up to its first real suspension. Faster for cache hits, and it changes ordering assumptions in existing code.
production: Debug mode: `asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)` or `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1` logs any callback that holds the loop for more than 100 ms.
Python 3.14 adds `python -m asyncio ps PID` and `pstree PID` to list a live process's tasks and await tree: the first thing to reach for on a hung worker.
The measured ordering table in the research: Node 22 ESM prints sync, queueMicrotask, promise.then, nextTick, immediate, timeout; Node 22 CommonJS prints nextTick before promise.then.
A hung Node service with 100% CPU and no I/O served is often a tight async loop that never yields to a macrotask.

mcq.q: In a Node ESM module you register, in this order: `setTimeout(() => log('timeout'), 0)`, `Promise.resolve().then(() => log('then'))`, `queueMicrotask(() => log('micro'))`, then `log('sync')`. What is printed?
o: timeout, then, micro, sync
sync, timeout, then, micro
sync, then, micro, timeout
sync, micro, then, timeout
then, micro, sync, timeout
mcq.why: Synchronous code finishes first, then the microtask queue drains in FIFO order (the then was queued before the queueMicrotask), and only then does the loop reach the timer macrotask.

mcq.q: In Python: `t = asyncio.create_task(work())`, then `print('sync')`, then `await asyncio.sleep(0)`. With the default task factory, when does the first line of `work` run?
o: Inside create_task, before 'sync' is printed
After 'sync', once the current task yields at its await
Only when some code later does `await t`
On a worker thread, in parallel with 'sync'
After every pending timer on the loop has fired
mcq.why: create_task only schedules the task. It starts at the next loop iteration, which happens when the running task reaches a suspension point. With eager_task_factory it would run inside create_task instead.

mcq.q: A Node worker sits at 100% CPU and stops answering health checks. The code has a function that, when it finishes, calls `queueMicrotask` on itself to process the next item. What is the most likely cause?
o: The microtask queue never empties, so the loop never reaches I/O
The default thread pool has run out of free threads
V8 garbage collection is pausing the loop for long periods
setImmediate callbacks are starving the timers phase
Promise reactions are being run on a second thread
mcq.why: The loop drains all microtasks before moving to the next phase. A microtask that always queues another one means the poll phase, and so every socket, never gets a turn.

open.q: Walk me through what happens, in order, when this script runs: a setTimeout of 0, a resolved promise's then, a process.nextTick and a console.log. Then tell me how asyncio would order the same idea.
open.probe: Whether he knows microtasks against macrotasks, and is honest that nextTick ordering is not portable.
a: Sync code first: the log prints.
Then microtasks drain: the promise reaction; nextTick runs before or after it depending on ESM or CommonJS (and Deno and Bun differ), so I would never rely on it.
Then the loop moves to macrotasks: the timer fires in the timers phase, no earlier than 1 ms.
asyncio has one FIFO ready queue: create_task and call_soon wait their turn, and awaiting a coroutine runs it inline with no trip round the loop.
Eager tasks in 3.12 run a new task at once up to its first await, which changes that order.
The practical rule in both: design for 'later', never for an exact interleaving.

say: I think of both as one thread with a queue. In JS the twist is microtasks: every promise reaction drains before the next timer or I/O callback, which is also how you starve a Node process.
In asyncio a new task waits its turn on a FIFO queue, and awaiting a coroutine directly runs it inline.
I wouldn't write code that depends on nextTick against promise order. It changes between ESM and CommonJS, and between runtimes.
avoid: Saying asyncio or Node runs your code in parallel: it is one thread; parallelism needs threads, processes or workers.
Quoting one fixed nextTick order as a fact of JavaScript.

code.title: What runs when: a coroutine call, call_soon, create_task, await, and the eager task factory
code.src:
# Exercise: what runs when on one asyncio loop (a coroutine call, call_soon, create_task, await, eager tasks).
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-event-loop_test.py
import asyncio


async def order(eager: bool = False) -> list[str]:
    log: list[str] = []
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    if eager:
        loop.set_task_factory(asyncio.eager_task_factory)  # 3.12: run a new task until its first suspension

    async def child(name: str) -> None:
        log.append(f"{name} start")
        await asyncio.sleep(0)  # one trip round the loop
        log.append(f"{name} resumed")

    coro = child("never")  # a coroutine object: its body has not run
    coro.close()  # close it, or Python warns "coroutine was never awaited"
    loop.call_soon(log.append, "call_soon")
    t = asyncio.create_task(child("task"))  # scheduled for the next iteration, not started (unless eager)
    log.append("sync")
    await child("awaited")  # awaiting a coroutine runs it inline, in this task, with no loop trip
    await t
    loop.set_task_factory(None)
    return log

topics.title: Coroutines, tasks and promises
topics.brief: A Python coroutine is lazy: calling an async def builds an object and runs nothing until it is awaited or wrapped in a task. A JS promise is eager: calling an async function runs its body up to the first await and the work has started whether you await it or not. Most async bugs in both languages come from forgetting which one you are holding.
points: Coroutine: `fetch_user(1)` without await creates an object and runs nothing; Python warns 'coroutine was never awaited' when it is collected.

Task: `asyncio.create_task(coro)` schedules it on the loop so it runs concurrently; it can be awaited, cancelled and named. The loop holds only a weak reference, so keep a strong one (a set plus `add_done_callback(set.discard)`) or use a TaskGroup.
Promise: an async function's body runs synchronously up to its first `await`, so the request is already sent when the call returns. A promise has no cancel method.

Floating promise: an async call with no await or catch loses its errors; Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` then exits the process with code 1. Lint with `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` and mark intentional ones with `void`.
Sequential against concurrent: two 50 ms awaits in a row take 100 ms; `TaskGroup` or `Promise.all` takes about 50 ms. `array.forEach(async ...)` returns at once and nobody waits for the callbacks.
return await: inside `try` in an async function, `return promise` skips the catch; `return await promise` is caught.
production: The research measured three 20 ms awaits in a for...of at about 91 ms against about 31 ms through `Promise.all(map)`.
Unbounded `Promise.all(items.map(call))` over 10,000 items fires 10,000 requests at once; bound it with a limiter (see the backpressure topic).
In a long-running worker, let unhandled rejections crash loudly after logging the trace id, and let the supervisor restart it, rather than running with `--unhandled-rejections=none`.
Python 3.12 `eager_task_factory` skips the loop trip for tasks that finish without suspending, such as cache hits; `Task.get_coro()` returns None for those.

mcq.q: Inside an async Python function someone writes `save_trace(run)` without await, where `save_trace` is an `async def`. What happens?
o: It runs in the background, like an unawaited promise
It runs synchronously up to its first await, then pauses
It is scheduled as a task on the next loop iteration
Nothing runs; a warning appears when the object is collected
It raises a TypeError at the call site straight away
mcq.why: Calling an async def only builds a coroutine object. Without await or create_task nothing executes, and Python warns 'coroutine was never awaited'.

mcq.q: In TypeScript someone writes `saveTrace(run)` without await, where `saveTrace` is async and later rejects. On Node 22 with default flags, what happens?
o: Nothing runs until something awaits the returned promise
The body starts at once; the rejection is unhandled and the process exits with code 1
The body starts at once; the rejection is logged as a warning and ignored
The body is queued as a macrotask and its error is dropped
The call throws synchronously because the promise was not awaited
mcq.why: Promises are eager: the body runs up to its first await at the call. Node's default unhandled-rejection mode is throw, which raises an uncaught exception and exits with code 1.

mcq.q: `ids.forEach(async (id) => { await save(id); }); log('all saved');` What is wrong?
o: forEach runs the callbacks one after another, so it is slow
The saves run in parallel with no limit, which is the only problem
TypeScript rejects async callbacks passed to forEach
Each save runs twice because forEach retries rejected promises
'all saved' is logged before any save finishes, and their errors float
mcq.why: forEach ignores the promises the callbacks return. Nothing waits, so the log is a lie and any rejection is unhandled. Use for...of with await, or Promise.all over map.

open.q: You see `asyncio.create_task(flush_traces())` with the result thrown away, and in the TypeScript service `flushTraces()` with no await. Are these the same bug?
open.probe: Lazy coroutine against eager promise, and lost tasks against lost errors.
a: Not quite. The Python one does start running, because create_task schedules it, but the loop holds only a weak reference, so it can be collected mid-run, and any exception is never seen.
Fix in Python: put it in a TaskGroup, or keep a strong reference in a set with a done callback that discards it.
The TypeScript one has already started at the call. The risk is the error: an unhandled rejection exits Node with code 1 by default.
Fix in TS: await it, or attach a catch that logs, and mark deliberate fire-and-forget with void so the lint rule passes.
In both, I'd ask whether it should be fire-and-forget at all: trace flushing usually belongs to the run's scope, so it finishes or is cancelled with the run.

say: The thing I keep straight is that a Python coroutine is lazy and a JS promise is eager. Calling an async def does nothing; calling an async function in TypeScript has already started the work.
So in Python the bug is work that never ran or got collected, and in TypeScript it's an error nobody caught.
I lint for floating promises and I default to TaskGroup, so nothing is fire-and-forget by accident.
avoid: Saying an async def call 'starts a coroutine in the background'.

code.title: A lazy coroutine, sequential against TaskGroup timing, a safe fire-and-forget
code.src:
# Exercise: a coroutine is lazy (nothing runs until it is awaited or made a task); sequential awaits add up, a TaskGroup overlaps.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-coroutines-promises_test.py
import asyncio
import time


async def call(name: str, log: list[str], delay: float = 0.05) -> str:
    log.append(f"start {name}")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return name


def lazy() -> list[str]:
    log: list[str] = []
    c = call("x", log)  # creates a coroutine object; the body has not started
    seen = list(log)
    c.close()
    return seen


async def sequential(log: list[str]) -> tuple[list[str], float]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = [await call("a", log), await call("b", log)]  # b starts only after a finishes
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t0


async def concurrent(log: list[str]) -> tuple[list[str], float]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        ta = tg.create_task(call("a", log))
        tb = tg.create_task(call("b", log))
    return [ta.result(), tb.result()], time.perf_counter() - t0


_background: set[asyncio.Task] = set()


def fire_and_forget(coro) -> asyncio.Task:
    # The loop keeps only a weak reference to a task: hold a strong one until it is done.
    t = asyncio.create_task(coro)
    _background.add(t)
    t.add_done_callback(_background.discard)
    return t

topics.title: Fan-out: who cancels what on failure
topics.brief: Running several calls at once is easy; the question is what happens to the others when one fails. In Python, `gather` raises the first error and leaves the siblings running, while `TaskGroup` cancels them and raises an `ExceptionGroup`. In JS no combinator cancels anything: `Promise.all` rejects early and the rest keep running and spending tokens.
points: gather: the first exception reaches the caller and the other awaitables keep running. With `return_exceptions=True` errors come back as results. If gather itself is cancelled, its children are cancelled.
TaskGroup (3.11): when a child fails, the siblings are cancelled, the block waits for them, and the errors arrive as an `ExceptionGroup` you handle with `except*`.
wait: `asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` returns `(done, pending)`; it never cancels pending tasks and never raises on timeout. You own the cleanup.
Promise.all and allSettled: all rejects on the first rejection with nothing cancelled; allSettled never rejects and gives `{status, value | reason}` per input.

Promise.race and any: race settles with the first to settle, rejection included; any takes the first to fulfil and rejects with an `AggregateError` only if all reject (an empty input rejects at once).
Stopping the losers in JS: share one `AbortController`, pass its signal to every call, and abort it on the first failure or the first winner.
production: The research's verified test: a TaskGroup with one failing child and one 5 s child records the 5 s child as cancelled; the same pair under gather leaves it running until it finishes.
A bare gather in an agent runtime leaks work: orphaned tool calls keep spending tokens after the step has already failed.
Fan out five tool calls where one failure should not sink the others: `Promise.allSettled`, then turn each rejection into a `tool_result` error for the model.
Hedged requests: `Promise.any` over two providers with a shared signal, aborting the loser once one answers.

mcq.q: `await asyncio.gather(a(), b())`: a raises ValueError after 10 ms, b takes 5 s. Right after your `except ValueError`, what is b doing?
o: It was cancelled when a failed
It finished early because gather waits for all
It is still running, and nobody will cancel it
It was paused and resumes if you await gather again
It raised CancelledError into your except block
mcq.why: gather propagates the first exception but does not cancel the other awaitables. b keeps running in the background unless you cancel it yourself.

mcq.q: The same a and b inside `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg`. What happens when a fails?
o: b keeps running and the ValueError is raised at once
b is cancelled, the block waits for it, then an ExceptionGroup is raised
b is cancelled and the plain ValueError is raised without waiting
The block waits for b to finish, then raises the ValueError
a's error is stored on its task and nothing is raised
mcq.why: TaskGroup cancels the siblings, waits for them to finish cancelling, and raises the collected errors as an ExceptionGroup, so nothing leaks out of the block.

mcq.q: You run `await Promise.race([callModel(), timeout(5000)])` and the timeout wins. What happens to callModel?
o: race aborts it, so the request is closed
It is garbage collected once nobody holds the promise
Node rejects it with an AbortError automatically
It finishes only if another await is attached to it
It keeps running and spending tokens until it settles
mcq.why: Promises have no cancel. race only stops waiting. To stop the call, pass an AbortSignal (AbortSignal.timeout) to the request itself.

open.q: An agent step calls five tools in parallel. One throws. Walk me through what happens to the other four in Python and in TypeScript, and what you would want to happen.
open.probe: Whether he knows gather and Promise.all leave orphans, and has a deliberate policy.
a: First decide the policy: if the step is all-or-nothing, cancel the rest; if each tool result stands alone, collect every outcome.
Python all-or-nothing: TaskGroup, which cancels the siblings and raises an ExceptionGroup; a bare gather would leave four calls running and spending.
Python collect-all: gather with return_exceptions=True, then map each exception to an error tool result.
TypeScript collect-all: Promise.allSettled. All-or-nothing: one AbortController shared by the five calls, aborted on the first failure, and still wait for all of them before leaving.
For an agent I'd usually collect all and hand failures back to the model as error results, because a failed search should not throw away four good ones.

say: My default in Python is TaskGroup, because when one child fails the others are cancelled and nothing outlives the block.
gather on its own leaves orphans, and in an agent an orphan is a tool call still spending tokens.
In TypeScript nothing cancels for you, so I pass one AbortSignal to every call and abort it. For tool fan-out I usually want allSettled and the errors handed back to the model.
avoid: Saying Promise.all or Promise.race cancels the other promises.
Calling gather and TaskGroup interchangeable.

code.title: gather leaves the sibling running, TaskGroup cancels it, wait leaves cleanup to you
code.src:
# Exercise: who gets cancelled when one child fails: gather (nobody), TaskGroup (the siblings), wait (nobody, you clean up).
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-fan-out_test.py
import asyncio


async def child(n: float, log: list[str], fail: bool = False) -> float:
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(n)
        if fail:
            raise ValueError(f"boom {n}")
        log.append(f"done {n}")
        return n
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        log.append(f"cancelled {n}")
        raise


async def with_gather() -> tuple[str, list[str], bool]:
    log: list[str] = []
    slow = asyncio.ensure_future(child(0.1, log))
    try:
        await asyncio.gather(child(0.01, log, fail=True), slow)
    except ValueError as e:
        err = str(e)
    still_running = not slow.done()  # gather raised, but did not cancel its sibling
    await slow
    return err, log, still_running


async def with_gather_settled() -> list[object]:
    log: list[str] = []
    return await asyncio.gather(child(0.01, log, fail=True), child(0.02, log), return_exceptions=True)


async def with_taskgroup() -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    log: list[str] = []
    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
            tg.create_task(child(0.01, log, fail=True))
            tg.create_task(child(5, log))
    except* ValueError as eg:
        errs = [str(e) for e in eg.exceptions]
    return errs, log


async def with_wait() -> tuple[float, int, list[str]]:
    log: list[str] = []
    ts = [asyncio.create_task(child(d, log)) for d in (0.01, 5)]
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(ts, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
    n_pending = len(pending)
    for p in pending:
        p.cancel()  # wait() never cancels for you
    await asyncio.gather(*pending, return_exceptions=True)
    return done.pop().result(), n_pending, log

topics.title: Cancellation and timeouts
topics.brief: Cancellation is cooperative in both languages. In Python `task.cancel()` raises `CancelledError` at the task's current await, and `asyncio.timeout` turns that into `TimeoutError`; in JS you pass an `AbortSignal` down and only code that checks it stops. The trap in Python is swallowing `CancelledError`, which silently breaks timeouts, TaskGroups and shutdown.
points: CancelledError: derives from `BaseException` since 3.8, so `except Exception` does not catch it but a bare `except:` or `except BaseException` does. Catch it only to clean up, then re-raise.
asyncio.timeout (3.11): cancels the task on expiry and raises `TimeoutError` at the edge of the block; `.reschedule()` moves the deadline. Prefer it over `wait_for` because it nests and composes.
shield: `await asyncio.shield(task)` lets the inner task finish when the awaiting caller is cancelled; the caller still gets `CancelledError`. Keep a reference to the inner task and await it later.
AbortController: `signal.reason` carries why. `abort()` with no argument gives a DOMException named AbortError; `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` gives one named TimeoutError.
AbortSignal.any: combines the user's signal with a deadline; its `reason` is the reason of whichever source fired, so you can tell a timeout from a Stop.

Cooperative: a signal only stops code that accepts it (`fetch`, streams, child processes) or calls `signal.throwIfAborted()` at loop boundaries. Remove abort listeners in `finally` or they leak on long-lived signals.
production: Stop-and-resume agents are cancellation systems: Stop cancels the run's task tree, the `finally` writes a checkpoint and releases the sandbox or browser lease.
Layer the deadlines: one `asyncio.timeout` for the whole agent step, plus per-call timeouts on the HTTP client.

Error names differ by API: fetch with a timed-out signal rejects with TimeoutError, while Node's `timers/promises` rejects with an AbortError whose `cause` is the TimeoutError. Check `signal.reason`, not only `e.name`.
Voice barge-in: when the caller starts talking again, everything downstream of the old turn is cancelled, which only works if every stage takes the same signal.
A task that ignores cancel is usually swallowing CancelledError, blocked in a thread, or stuck in sync code that never reaches an await.

mcq.q: Inside `async with asyncio.timeout(2):` a tool wrapper does `try: return await tool() except BaseException: return None`. The tool hangs. What happens?
o: TimeoutError is raised after 2 s as usual
The process exits because CancelledError escaped
The wrapper returns None and the block carries on past the deadline
The tool keeps hanging, because timeout cannot interrupt an await
TimeoutError is raised inside the wrapper and logged
mcq.why: The timeout works by cancelling the task. The wrapper swallows the CancelledError, so the timeout sees no cancellation at its edge and raises nothing; the code runs on as if no deadline existed.

mcq.q: `const s = AbortSignal.any([user.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(30000)])`. After 2 s the user calls `user.abort(new Error('stop'))`. What is `s.reason`?
o: The user's Error('stop')
A DOMException named AbortError
A DOMException named TimeoutError
An AggregateError holding both reasons
undefined, because any() does not keep reasons
mcq.why: The combined signal takes the reason of the source that aborted. That is how you tell a user Stop from a deadline in one catch.

mcq.q: A caller does `await asyncio.shield(commit_task)` and the caller is cancelled. What happens?
o: Both the caller and commit_task are cancelled
The caller gets CancelledError; commit_task keeps running
The caller is not cancelled until commit_task finishes
commit_task is cancelled and the caller continues normally
The cancel is ignored and recorded as a pending request
mcq.why: shield protects the inner task from the outer cancellation only. The outer await still raises CancelledError; cancelling commit_task directly would still cancel it.

open.q: A user hits Stop on a long agent run. Walk me through what should happen, from the HTTP request down to the model call, in Python or TypeScript.
open.probe: Cancellation as a first-class path: propagation, cleanup that must finish, and not swallowing the signal.
a: One cancellation source per run: in Python cancel the run's task; in TypeScript abort the run's AbortController.
It must reach every layer: the agent loop, each tool call, the fetch to the model. In TS that means the same signal passed down; in Python the TaskGroup cancels the children.
Cleanup in finally: write a checkpoint and release the sandbox or browser lease; in Python shield the part that must finish.
Never swallow it: catch CancelledError only to clean up, then re-raise, or the timeouts and the group break.
Make the in-flight step safe to run again, because resume will repeat it.

say: I treat Stop as a normal path, not an error. In Python I cancel the run's task and let the TaskGroup cancel the children; in TypeScript one AbortSignal goes through every layer down to the fetch.
The finally writes the checkpoint and releases whatever we were holding, and I shield that bit so it finishes.
The bug I look for in generated code is a broad except that swallows CancelledError. Then the timeout quietly stops working.
avoid: Saying a Promise.race against a timer is a timeout: it gives up waiting, it does not stop the work.

code.src:
# Exercise: cooperative cancellation: clean up and re-raise, what swallowing CancelledError breaks, timeout(), shield().
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-cancellation_test.py
import asyncio


async def cancel_cleanly() -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    log: list[str] = []

    async def worker():
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(10)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            log.append("save checkpoint")
            raise  # always re-raise
        finally:
            log.append("release lease")

    t = asyncio.create_task(worker())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # let it reach its await
    t.cancel()
    try:
        await t
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    return t.cancelled(), log


async def timeout_fires() -> str:
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.02):
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
    except TimeoutError:  # the CancelledError became TimeoutError at the edge of the block
        return "TimeoutError"
    return "no timeout"


async def swallow_breaks_timeout() -> str:
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(0.02):
            try:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                pass  # the bug: the deadline is eaten
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # carries on past the deadline
    except TimeoutError:
        return "TimeoutError"
    return "no timeout"


async def shield_commit() -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    log: list[str] = []

    async def commit():
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02)
        log.append("committed")

    inner = asyncio.create_task(commit())  # keep a reference to the inner task

    async def caller():
        await asyncio.shield(inner)

    c = asyncio.create_task(caller())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    c.cancel()  # the caller is cancelled, the commit carries on
    try:
        await c
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        pass
    await inner  # someone must still await it
    return c.cancelled(), log

topics.title: Blocking the loop, threads and CPU work
topics.brief: One synchronous call inside async code freezes every task on that loop. In Python you move blocking I/O to `asyncio.to_thread` and CPU-bound pure Python to a process pool; in Node you move CPU work to `worker_threads` or another process. The nuance: `to_thread` copies contextvars and `run_in_executor` does not, and a thread you started cannot be cancelled.
points: Blocking: `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, a big JSON parse or a CPU loop inside an async function stalls every other task for its whole duration.
to_thread (3.9): runs the function in the default thread pool and copies the current contextvars context. It helps only when the work releases the GIL (I/O, many C extensions).
run_in_executor: does not copy the context, so a ContextVar like `run_id` reads its default there; wrap with `contextvars.copy_context().run`. Pure-Python CPU work needs `ProcessPoolExecutor`.
Cancel limits: cancelling an await on `to_thread` cancels the await; the thread runs to completion and keeps its resources.
contextvars: each task gets a copy of its creator's context, so `run_id.set()` in a child never leaks to the parent or a sibling, unlike a module global or `threading.local`.
Node: CPU work on the main thread delays every timer and request; offload to `worker_threads`, a child process or a separate service.
production: The research's measurement: four pure-Python CPU tasks took 0.98 s serial, 0.94 s on four threads and 0.62 s on four processes (Windows, 3.12): threads do not speed up CPU-bound Python.
Free-threaded Python is supported but optional in 3.14 with a single-digit to low-teens single-thread cost; for an I/O-bound agent platform asyncio plus processes or containers is the shape.
Run id, tenant id and trace id live in ContextVars so every log line carries them without threading arguments through each call.
An agent platform that parses large traces or diffs big files in the same Node process that serves SSE should push that work to a worker.

mcq.q: An async FastAPI-style handler calls the sync `requests.get()` that takes 2 s. Fifty other requests are in flight on the same loop. What happens?
o: Only this request waits; the GIL is released during I/O
The other tasks slow a little while the threads share the GIL
requests detects the running loop and switches to async I/O
The handler raises because sync I/O is not allowed in async def
Every task on that loop is frozen for the full 2 s
mcq.why: The GIL is released, but the loop's only thread is the one blocked in requests.get, so no other coroutine step can run. Use `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, url)` or an async client.

mcq.q: Logs from a function run via `loop.run_in_executor(None, fn)` show `run_id='-'` while the same function via `asyncio.to_thread(fn)` shows the real id. Why?
o: to_thread copies the current context; run_in_executor does not
run_in_executor uses processes, which cannot share memory
ContextVars are reset whenever a thread pool is reused
to_thread runs the function on the event loop thread itself
run_in_executor needs the ContextVar declared as global
mcq.why: to_thread runs the function inside a copy of the caller's context. run_in_executor does not, so wrap with `contextvars.copy_context().run` if you must use it.

mcq.q: An async Python worker parses a 200 MB trace in pure Python for 3 s per file. Which fix keeps the loop responsive and uses more cores?
o: `await asyncio.to_thread(parse, path)`
Add `await asyncio.sleep(0)` before the parse
`loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), parse, path)`
Wrap the parse in `asyncio.timeout(3)`
Turn parse into an async def and await it
mcq.why: Pure-Python CPU work holds the GIL, so a thread barely helps and still competes with the loop. A process has its own interpreter and GIL; the cost is pickling arguments and results.

open.q: An agent calls an LLM, then runs the test suite, then calls the LLM again, and a teammate reports p99 spikes for every other run on the same worker. How do you find and fix it, in Python and in Node?
open.probe: Spotting a blocked loop, choosing threads against processes against workers, and keeping context across them.
a: Suspect something blocking the loop: a sync call or CPU work inside async code. Turn on asyncio debug mode, which logs callbacks over 100 ms; on 3.14 `python -m asyncio pstree` on the live process.
Blocking I/O with no async API goes to `asyncio.to_thread`, which also carries the run id across.
The test suite is a subprocess, so use `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec` and await it; CPU-heavy pure-Python parsing goes to a process pool.
In Node the same thing: CPU work to worker_threads or a child process, so SSE and health checks keep flowing.
Remember a cancelled to_thread keeps running, so give the blocking call its own timeout.

say: One sync call in async code freezes everything on that loop, so that's the first thing I look for when p99 spikes.
Blocking I/O goes to to_thread, which also keeps the run id in context. Pure-Python CPU work goes to a process pool, because a thread still fights over the GIL.
In Node it's worker threads or a child process. I'd measure before reaching for free-threaded Python; for an I/O-bound platform I don't need it.
avoid: Saying the GIL is released so threads fix CPU-bound Python.

code.title: A frozen ticker under time.sleep, a free one under to_thread, contextvars across threads and tasks
code.src:
# Exercise: one blocking call stalls every task; to_thread keeps the loop free and copies contextvars, run_in_executor does not.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-blocking_test.py
import asyncio
import contextvars
import time

run_id: contextvars.ContextVar[str] = contextvars.ContextVar("run_id", default="-")


async def ticks_during(blocking: bool) -> int:
    ticks = 0

    async def ticker():
        nonlocal ticks
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)
            ticks += 1

    t = asyncio.create_task(ticker())
    await asyncio.sleep(0)
    if blocking:
        time.sleep(0.1)  # a sync call inside async code: the loop is frozen
    else:
        await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.1)  # a pool thread waits, the loop keeps running
    t.cancel()
    return ticks


async def context_in_threads() -> tuple[str, str, str]:
    run_id.set("run-42")
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    a = await asyncio.to_thread(run_id.get)  # context copied
    b = await loop.run_in_executor(None, run_id.get)  # context NOT copied
    c = await loop.run_in_executor(None, contextvars.copy_context().run, run_id.get)  # the fix
    return a, b, c


async def child_sets_do_not_leak() -> tuple[tuple[str, str], str]:
    run_id.set("parent")

    async def child(v):
        run_id.set(v)  # visible only inside this task's copy
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return run_id.get()

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        a = tg.create_task(child("A"))
        b = tg.create_task(child("B"))
    return (a.result(), b.result()), run_id.get()

topics.title: Bounded concurrency, queues and backpressure
topics.brief: Unbounded fan-out opens thousands of sockets and trips rate limits; unbounded queues turn a slow consumer into an out-of-memory kill. Bound concurrency with a semaphore or a limiter, and let a full buffer make the producer wait. The nuance: a semaphore limits how many at once, not how many per second.
points: Semaphore: `asyncio.Semaphore(n)` with `async with sem:` keeps at most n inside; in JS, p-limit or a ten-line limiter does the same. Neither is a rate limit: 10 concurrent 100 ms calls is about 100 per second.
Token bucket: bounds rate with a burst; charge it by estimated tokens for a tokens-per-minute limit. Use it with the semaphore, and match the HTTP pool size (`httpx.Limits(max_connections=...)`).
Bounded queue: `asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N)` makes `await put()` wait when full, pushing slowness upstream. 3.13 adds `Queue.shutdown()` so you no longer need a None sentinel.
Pull-based: an async generator only runs when the consumer asks for the next value, so it never runs ahead; an EventEmitter pushes and buffers without bound.

Web Streams: `pull()` is called only while `desiredSize` (highWaterMark minus what is queued) is above zero; `pipeTo` and `pipeThrough` carry backpressure for you. In Node streams `write()` returns false and you wait for 'drain'.
Limiter queues are unbounded too: at the edge, reject with 429 when the waiting count passes a threshold instead of queueing forever.
production: Crawl 5,000 pages against an upstream that allows 50 requests per second: a semaphore for sockets, a token bucket for rate, one shared HTTP client.
Agent event streams (tool started, token chunk, trace span) to a slow sink need a bounded buffer and an explicit policy: block, drop oldest, or spill to disk.
Use `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises` over `.pipe()`: it propagates errors, destroys every stream on failure and accepts an AbortSignal.
Across a fleet an in-process limiter is not enough: limits are per provider key, per tenant or per sandbox host, enforced by a shared queue or a bucket in Redis or Postgres.
In alfred_ durable work sits in Postgres and lean workers claim one job at a time with SKIP LOCKED, so the worker count is the concurrency bound.

mcq.q: You wrap every model call in `asyncio.Semaphore(10)`. Calls take about 100 ms and the provider allows 50 requests per second. What happens?
o: You stay under the limit, because only 10 run at once
You run at about 100 per second and get rate limited
The semaphore spaces the calls out to 10 per second
Python's loop caps outgoing requests at the pool size
The calls queue until the provider sends Retry-After
mcq.why: A semaphore limits how many are in flight, not how often they start. Ten slots turning over every 100 ms is about 100 per second; add a token bucket for rate.

mcq.q: A producer emits trace events faster than the database consumer can write them, through `asyncio.Queue()` with no maxsize. What is the failure mode?
o: put() starts raising QueueFull once memory is tight
The loop slows the producer down automatically
Events are dropped silently when the queue is long
Memory grows until the process is killed
The consumer is given more loop time to catch up
mcq.why: An unbounded queue accepts everything, so the backlog lives in memory until an out-of-memory kill. With maxsize, `await put()` waits and the producer slows to the consumer's pace.

mcq.q: A `ReadableStream` with `highWaterMark: 2` has a `pull()` that enqueues one item each call. Nobody has read from it yet. How many times has `pull()` been called?
o: Zero, pull runs only on read
Once, to prime the stream
Two times, then it waits
Until the source is exhausted
Three times: the mark plus one
mcq.why: The stream pulls while desiredSize, the highWaterMark minus what is queued, is above zero. It fills to 2 and stops; each read makes room for one more pull.

open.q: You have 5,000 pages to fetch for an agent and the upstream allows 50 requests per second. Design the concurrency control, and tell me what changes when it runs on twenty workers.
open.probe: Concurrency against rate, backpressure, and what breaks across processes.
a: Separate the two limits: a semaphore (or p-limit) bounds sockets in flight, a token bucket bounds requests per second with a small burst.
One shared HTTP client whose pool size matches the semaphore, with per-call timeouts.
Results flow through a bounded queue to the slow stage, so a slow sink slows the fetchers instead of filling memory.
On twenty workers the in-process limits multiply by twenty: the bucket has to be shared (Redis or Postgres), or each worker gets a fifth of the budget.
Honour 429 and Retry-After, and keep retries at one layer so the limit is not blown by retry storms.

say: I separate how many at once from how many per second. A semaphore does the first and a token bucket does the second.
Between stages I use bounded queues, so a slow sink slows the producer down instead of eating memory.
In alfred_ the durable work sits in Postgres and each lean worker claims one job with SKIP LOCKED, so the number of workers is the bound. Across a fleet the limit has to live somewhere shared.
avoid: Calling a semaphore a rate limiter.

code.title: A semaphore holding peak concurrency at 3, a bounded queue making the producer wait
code.src:
# Exercise: bound concurrency with a Semaphore, and push slowness upstream with a bounded asyncio.Queue.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-backpressure_test.py
import asyncio


async def bounded_map(items, fn, limit: int) -> tuple[list, int]:
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)
    in_flight = peak = 0

    async def one(x):
        nonlocal in_flight, peak
        async with sem:  # at most `limit` inside at once; the rest wait here
            in_flight += 1
            peak = max(peak, in_flight)
            try:
                return await fn(x)
            finally:
                in_flight -= 1

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tasks = [tg.create_task(one(x)) for x in items]
    return [t.result() for t in tasks], peak


async def pipeline(n: int, maxsize: int) -> tuple[list[int], int, list[str]]:
    q: asyncio.Queue[int | None] = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=maxsize)
    got: list[int] = []
    events: list[str] = []
    peak = 0

    async def producer():
        nonlocal peak
        for i in range(n):
            await q.put(i)  # waits while the queue is full: the producer slows to the consumer's pace
            events.append(f"put {i}")
            peak = max(peak, q.qsize())
        await q.put(None)  # sentinel; 3.13 adds q.shutdown()

    async def consumer():
        while (item := await q.get()) is not None:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.005)  # a slow sink: a database, a websocket
            got.append(item)
            events.append(f"got {item}")

    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
        tg.create_task(producer())
        tg.create_task(consumer())
    return got, peak, events

topics.title: Retries with jitter, and streaming LLM responses
topics.brief: Retry only what can succeed next time and is safe to repeat, with capped exponential backoff and full jitter so a fleet does not retry in lockstep. Stream model output with an async iterator under one total deadline, and make sure leaving the loop early closes the upstream connection. The nuance: a per-chunk read timeout never fires on a stream that trickles.
points: What to retry: connection errors, timeouts, 408, 429 and 5xx; never a 4xx validation error; a non-idempotent POST only with an idempotency key. Honour `Retry-After`.
Full jitter: wait a random time in `[0, min(cap, base * 2**n)]`. Plain doubling makes every worker that failed together retry together; jitter spreads them out.
Bounds: cap attempts and total elapsed time, make the sleep abortable, and retry at one layer only: SDK, gateway and agent loop at 3 each is 27 calls.
Streaming deadline: httpx's read timeout is per chunk, which catches a stalled stream but not a slow one; wrap the whole read in `asyncio.timeout()`.

Closing: `break` out of `for await` calls the iterator's `return()`, so its `finally` runs and the body is cancelled. In Python wrap async generators in `contextlib.aclosing`, and note closing a parser generator does not close the source it was reading.
SSE framing: a frame ends at a blank line, several `data:` lines join with a newline, lines starting with ':' are heartbeats, and many APIs end with `data: [DONE]`.
production: tenacity and backoff do retries declaratively in Python; be ready to write the loop by hand in the room.
Retrying a whole agent step that already sent an email or opened a PR is a correctness bug: side-effecting tools need idempotency keys or a recorded result per step.
In alfred_ side-effecting tools first return a preview, only an explicit confirm executes, and idempotency keys make retries of that execute safe.
Server side SSE: stop generating when the client disconnects (`res.on('close')` aborting the run), respect `write()` returning false, and send `: ping` so proxies keep the connection open.
For long runs the stream is a view over durable, replayable events, so a reconnect with Last-Event-ID resumes instead of restarting.

mcq.q: Why use full jitter, a random wait in [0, min(cap, base * 2**n)], instead of a plain doubling delay?
o: It makes the average wait shorter than doubling does
It guarantees the provider's Retry-After is respected
It keeps the total number of attempts lower
It lets you retry 4xx errors without harm
Clients that failed together stop retrying together
mcq.why: After an outage every client failed at the same moment. With a fixed schedule they all come back at the same moment too, exactly when the service has least capacity; randomness spreads the load.

mcq.q: The SDK retries 3 times, the gateway retries 3 times and the agent loop retries 3 times. The provider is hard down. How many calls reach it for one step?
o: It depends only on the backoff cap
mcq.why: Each layer multiplies the one below: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Keep retries at one layer and make the others fail fast.

mcq.q: An httpx stream has `Timeout(30)`. The model sends one token every 10 s for 20 minutes. What happens?
o: It never times out: each chunk resets the read timeout
It times out after 30 s of total streaming
It times out on the first gap longer than 5 s
The pool timeout fires once the stream passes 30 s
httpx buffers the stream and fails at the end
mcq.why: The read timeout measures the gap between chunks, not the whole response. A total deadline needs `asyncio.timeout()` around the read.

mcq.q: Your code reads model output with `for await (const d of sseData(res.body))` and breaks after the answer is complete. What happens to the HTTP body?
o: It stays open until the server finishes sending
break calls return(), which cancels the body and closes it
It is closed only when the response object is collected
It throws an AbortError into the loop
It keeps buffering in memory until you read it again
mcq.why: Leaving a for await loop calls the iterator's return(); the generator's iteration over the body ends and the stream is cancelled, so you stop paying for tokens nobody reads.

open.q: Design the retry policy for LLM and tool calls in an agent runtime. What do you retry, what don't you, and how do you avoid doing a side effect twice?
open.probe: Error classification, jitter and budgets, one layer, and idempotency for side effects.
a: Classify: retry connection errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx; never 4xx validation errors, which become an error tool result for the model instead.
Capped exponential backoff with full jitter, Retry-After honoured, a cap on attempts and on total time, and an abortable sleep so Stop works mid-wait.
One layer only: if the SDK retries, the agent loop does not, or attempts multiply.
Side effects: a tool that sends or writes carries an idempotency key, or the step's result is recorded so a retry reads it back instead of running again.
For example the confirm flow I built: a preview first, an explicit confirm executes, and the idempotency key makes a retried confirm a no-op.

say: I retry what can actually succeed next time: timeouts, 429, 5xx. A 400 goes back to the model as an error result.
Backoff is capped and jittered, Retry-After wins, and only one layer retries, or three layers of three turn into twenty-seven calls.
Anything with a side effect carries an idempotency key. That's how our confirm flow works: preview first, confirm executes, and a retry can't do it twice.
avoid: Promising exactly-once delivery: idempotency keys give effectively-once effects, not exactly-once calls.

code.title: Backoff with full jitter and Retry-After over a fake client; an SSE reader under one total deadline
code.src:
# Exercise: retries with capped exponential backoff, full jitter and Retry-After; an SSE stream read under one total deadline.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-retries-streaming_test.py
import asyncio
import random
from contextlib import aclosing
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

RETRYABLE = {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}


@dataclass
class Resp:  # stands in for an httpx.Response
    status: int
    headers: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


def full_jitter(n: int, base: float, cap: float, rng: random.Random) -> float:
    return rng.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2**n))  # spread retries out so workers do not stampede together


async def with_retries(send, *, attempts=4, base=0.5, cap=20.0, rng=None, sleep=asyncio.sleep):
    rng = rng or random.Random()
    for n in range(attempts):
        try:
            r = await send()
        except ConnectionError:  # httpx.TransportError in real code: timeouts and resets
            if n == attempts - 1:
                raise
            await sleep(full_jitter(n, base, cap, rng))
            continue
        if r.status not in RETRYABLE or n == attempts - 1:
            return r  # success, a 4xx that will never succeed, or out of attempts
        ra = r.headers.get("retry-after", "")
        await sleep(float(ra) if ra.isdigit() else full_jitter(n, base, cap, rng))


async def sse_data(lines):
    """Yield each event's data until [DONE]. A frame ends at a blank line; several data lines join with a newline."""
    buf: list[str] = []
    async for line in lines:
        if line == "":
            if buf:
                d = "\n".join(buf)
                buf = []
                if d == "[DONE]":
                    return
                yield d
        elif line.startswith("data:"):
            buf.append(line[5:].removeprefix(" "))
        # lines starting with ":" are comments (heartbeats); other fields ignored here


async def read_stream(lines, total: float) -> list[str]:
    out: list[str] = []
    async with asyncio.timeout(total):  # the read timeout is per chunk; this caps the whole stream
        # aclosing closes both generators on any exit (done, break, timeout); with httpx, `async with client.stream(...)` plays the outer part
        async with aclosing(lines), aclosing(sse_data(lines)) as events:
            async for d in events:
                out.append(d)
    return out

topics.title: Structured concurrency, the senior opinion
topics.brief: Structured concurrency means a child task never outlives the scope that started it, a child's error reaches the scope, and cancelling the scope cancels every child. Python has it in the standard library as `TaskGroup` plus `timeout()`; JavaScript does not, so you build it from one `AbortController` per scope and waiting for every child. For an agent run it is the difference between Stop meaning stop and a run that leaks tool calls.
points: The rule: no orphan tasks. Every task has an owner scope that waits for it, sees its error and can cancel it.
Python: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup()` is the scope; nest groups for sub-steps and add `asyncio.timeout()` for a deadline. Trio and anyio are where the idea came from, with richer cancel scopes.
JS by hand: one `AbortController` per scope, every child gets its signal, the first failure aborts the rest, and the scope awaits `Promise.allSettled` of all children before it returns.
The agent run: one scope per run; children are the tool calls, a heartbeat that renews the run's lease and the trace flusher. Stop cancels the scope and the `finally` releases the sandbox.
Checkpoint on the way out: save it in `finally`, shielded in Python, so a second cancel cannot cut the write short.
Resume repeats the step that was in flight, so steps must be idempotent or carry idempotency keys.
production: The design sentence: a run is a task tree under one TaskGroup; state lives outside the process (an append-only event log plus a checkpoint per step), so a crash resumes from the last checkpoint.
Heartbeats and a lease timeout let another worker take over a dead run; in alfred_ a job whose worker dies becomes claimable again and a scheduled sweep catches anything missed.
In the voice agent he owns, a lean agent answers on the call while the main agent works the same request in parallel: two children of one call, which is exactly where an owning scope matters.
Durable execution engines such as Temporal record step results so replays skip completed work; he has not run Temporal in production and says so.

mcq.q: Which of these breaks structured concurrency in an agent run?
o: Tool calls created inside the run's TaskGroup
A nested TaskGroup for the tools of one step
A `finally` that saves a checkpoint under shield
A trace flusher started with a bare create_task that outlives the run
An asyncio.timeout around the whole step
mcq.why: A task with no owning scope can outlive the run, hide its errors and ignore Stop. Give the flusher to the run's TaskGroup, or flush in the run's finally.

mcq.q: JavaScript has no TaskGroup. Which pattern gives you the same guarantees for a set of tool calls?
o: `Promise.all` over the calls, since it rejects on the first failure
`Promise.race` with a timer, so nothing runs past the deadline
One AbortController per scope, abort on first failure, then await allSettled of every child
`Promise.any`, so one success is enough and the rest are dropped
Fire each call without await and catch errors in a global handler
mcq.why: You need all three properties: the error reaches the scope, the siblings are actually stopped (the signal), and nothing outlives the scope (waiting for every child). The combinators alone give only the first.

mcq.q: A run is stopped mid-step and later resumed from its last checkpoint. The step that was in flight runs again. What makes that safe?
o: The TaskGroup cancelled it, so it had no effects
Each side effect carries an idempotency key or a recorded result
The checkpoint was saved under shield
The heartbeat stopped, so the lease was released
asyncio guarantees each await executes exactly once
mcq.why: Cancellation can land after a side effect happened but before the checkpoint recorded it. Only idempotent steps or recorded results make the repeat harmless.

open.q: If you were building our agent runtime's concurrency model from scratch, what is your opinion, and what would you refuse to let into the codebase?
open.probe: A clear senior position with reasons, an honest view of the limits, and concrete rules.
a: Structured concurrency: one scope per run, every task owned by a scope, Stop cancels the scope, and the finally releases the sandbox and saves a checkpoint.
Python: TaskGroup plus timeout. TypeScript: an AbortSignal through every async function that does I/O, and a small scope helper that aborts on the first failure and waits for all children.
State outside the process: an event log and a checkpoint per step, with idempotency keys on side effects so resume is safe.
What I'd refuse: bare create_task with no owner, gather without return_exceptions, swallowed CancelledError, Promise.race as a timeout, and anything unbounded (queues, retries, steps, tokens).
The honest limit: a scope does not survive a crash, which is why the durable state matters; an engine like Temporal does that for you, and I have not run one in production.

say: My opinion is structured concurrency everywhere: no task without an owner. In Python that's TaskGroup plus timeout; in TypeScript it's a signal through every async function and a small scope helper.
For an agent run that means one scope per run. Stop cancels it, the finally saves a checkpoint and releases the sandbox, and side effects carry idempotency keys so resume is safe.
A scope doesn't survive a crash, though. That's why the state lives in Postgres, like our jobs that any worker can pick up again.
avoid: Implying he has run Temporal or another durable engine in production.
Quoting anyio or Trio API details, which the research did not verify.

code.title: One run as one TaskGroup: Stop cancels tools and heartbeat, a shielded checkpoint, no leaked tasks
code.src:
# Exercise: one agent run as one TaskGroup: stopping the run cancels every child, and the finally saves a checkpoint that a second cancel cannot interrupt.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/async-structured_test.py
import asyncio


async def run_agent(store: dict, tools: list[float], log: list[str]) -> None:
    async def tool(n: float):
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(n)
            log.append(f"tool {n} done")
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            log.append(f"tool {n} cancelled")
            raise

    async def heartbeat():
        while True:  # renews the run's lease so no other worker takes it over
            store["beats"] = store.get("beats", 0) + 1
            await asyncio.sleep(0.01)

    async def save_checkpoint():
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # a database write
        store["checkpoint"] = list(log)

    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:  # no child outlives this block
            hb = tg.create_task(heartbeat())
            async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tools_tg:
                for n in tools:
                    tools_tg.create_task(tool(n))
            hb.cancel()  # the work is done, stop the heartbeat
    finally:
        await asyncio.shield(asyncio.ensure_future(save_checkpoint()))  # must finish even while we are being cancelled
