topics.title: Running generated code in a child process
topics.brief: Run code an agent wrote and get back a clean result: exit code, capped stdout and stderr, and whether it timed out, with no secrets in its environment and its scratch directory gone afterwards. The nuance: this is process management, not isolation. The child still has your user, your files, your network and your kernel, and you should say so before he asks.
points: Clarify first: which language, how long a run may take, how much output matters, whether it needs the network or files, and whether this is a dev tool or the real multi-tenant path (that answer decides subprocess or microVM).

Wall clock, then kill the tree: `subprocess.run(timeout=)` kills only the direct child. Start the child in its own session (`start_new_session=True`, `detached: true` in Node) and kill the group (`os.killpg`, `process.kill(-pid)`). A CPU limit misses a process that sleeps; a wall clock catches both. On Windows a tree needs a Job Object or `taskkill /T`.
Output caps without deadlock: read both pipes while the child runs, keep the first N bytes, keep draining the rest. A full pipe blocks the child, so `wait()` on a pipe nobody reads never returns.

Scrubbed environment: an allowlist (PATH, HOME, temp dirs, SYSTEMROOT on Windows), never a denylist. Python's `-I` ignores PYTHON* variables and the user site; an empty Node env also drops NODE_OPTIONS, which could otherwise inject `--require`.

Temp dir and result: `mkdtemp`, the child's cwd set to it, removed in `finally` even after a timeout. The result is a typed record, and a crash in the child is a result, not an exception in the parent.

What it does NOT isolate: reads of ~/.aws or .env, outbound network, memory and fork bombs (no cgroups), kernel exploits. gVisor adds a userspace kernel that intercepts syscalls; a microVM such as Firecracker adds its own guest kernel behind hardware virtualization; both still need egress through an allowlisting proxy and no credentials inside.
production: Anthropic's secure-deployment guide ranks the boundaries: OS sandbox runtimes (bubblewrap, Seatbelt) and containers share the host kernel; gVisor costs about nothing on CPU-bound work but can be 10 to 200x slower on heavy file I/O; Firecracker microVMs boot in under 125 ms with under 5 MiB overhead, per the guide.

Credentials never enter the sandbox: a proxy outside it holds them, enforces a domain allowlist and logs each request. Node `fetch` ignores HTTP_PROXY by default, so enforce egress at the network layer, not with an environment variable.

Warm starts come from snapshots, and Firecracker's docs warn that restoring one snapshot many times duplicates RNG state and tokens: regenerate per-sandbox secrets after restore and never bake a credential in.

Buy first: Modal Sandboxes run on gVisor by default and E2B on Firecracker-based VMs. At 100x the work becomes scheduling, warm pools, an idle reaper and an orphan sweeper that reconciles cloud inventory against the run table.
Language permission models are seat belts: the Node docs say `--permission` gives no guarantee against malicious code, and Deno's own docs say `--allow-run` children inherit no restrictions.

mcq.q: Your runner uses `subprocess.run(cmd, timeout=5)`. The generated code starts a server in a background process and then hangs. What happens at 5 seconds?
o: Python kills the whole process tree, because the timeout applies to every descendant
Nothing yet, because the timeout counts CPU seconds and the hung child is idle
The child is killed and the background server is reaped with it by the operating system
The direct child is killed; the background process lives on unless you killed its group
The call returns normally with exit code 124, the same convention as the timeout command
mcq.why: The timeout is wall clock and kills only the direct child. Start the child in its own session or process group and kill the group, or orphans outlive every run.

mcq.q: Which change actually stops agent-generated code from reading your cloud credentials?
o: Running it in a microVM or gVisor sandbox with no credentials mounted and egress through a proxy
Passing an allowlisted environment so that no API keys are inherited from the parent
Running it with `python -I` so that the child ignores environment variables
Running it in a fresh temp directory that is deleted after the run
Starting it with Node's `--permission` flag and no file read grants
mcq.why: A scrubbed environment removes keys from the env, but the child can still open ~/.aws/credentials as your user. Only a separate kernel boundary with nothing mounted, and egress controlled, removes access; Node calls its own permission model a seat belt.

mcq.q: Generated code prints a gigabyte to stdout. Your runner calls `proc.wait()` and only then reads the pipe. What happens?
o: It works, but the parent holds a gigabyte in memory
The child blocks on a full pipe, wait never returns, and only a timeout ends it
The operating system drops output beyond 64 KB and the child carries on
Python raises an error once the pipe goes past its buffer size
The child is killed by SIGPIPE as soon as the buffer fills
mcq.why: A pipe buffer is small; once it is full the child's write blocks until someone reads. Read both pipes while waiting (threads or `communicate`), keep the first N bytes, discard the rest.

open.q: The agent wrote a script and wants to run it. Build the runner in the next 20 minutes, then tell me what it doesn't protect us from.
open.probe: Whether you get the process mechanics right (tree kill, pipes, env) and are honest that a subprocess is not a sandbox.
a: Contract first: run(code, timeout, max_output) returns exit code, stdout, stderr, timed out, truncated and duration; a crash is a result.
Mechanics: temp dir as cwd, allowlisted env, own process group, both pipes drained with a cap, wall-clock timeout then kill the group, dir removed in finally.
Tests: an exit code, a crash, an infinite loop, a sleeping process, a megabyte of output, a secret in the parent env, the temp dir gone.
Limits, said plainly: same user, filesystem, network and kernel; no memory or pids limits; a Windows tree needs a Job Object.

Production: gVisor or a microVM per run, egress through an allowlisting proxy that injects short-lived tokens, CPU, memory and pids limits, snapshots for warm starts, and E2B or Modal bought before any fleet is built.

say: I'd build it as a subprocess with a temp dir, an allowlisted env, a wall-clock timeout that kills the whole group, and capped output. Then I'd say straight away that this isn't isolation.
The child still runs as me, so it can read my files and call out to the network. For real agent code I'd want gVisor or a microVM, nothing secret inside, and egress through a proxy.
I haven't built a sandbox fleet, so I'd buy one first, E2B or Modal, and learn where it hurts. That's the honest version.
avoid: Calling a scrubbed environment or a restricted `exec` a sandbox.
Implying you have run Firecracker, gVisor, Modal or E2B in production.

code.title: Child process runner: wall clock, group kill, drained capped pipes, allowlisted env, temp dir
code.src:
# Exercise: run untrusted generated Python in a child process: wall-clock timeout, output caps, scrubbed env, temp dir removed, structured result. Not a security boundary.
# Run its test: python interviews/coframe_builds/builds2-sandbox_test.py
import os
import shutil
import signal
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass

# What this does NOT isolate: the child runs as your user, with your filesystem (it can read ~/.aws),
# your network (it can exfiltrate), and your kernel. Real isolation is a layer below: gVisor or a microVM,
# no network except through an allowlisting proxy, no credentials inside.


@dataclass
class Result:
    exit_code: int | None      # None when we killed it
    stdout: str
    stderr: str
    timed_out: bool
    truncated: bool
    seconds: float


def _drain(pipe, cap: int, buf: bytearray, flags: dict) -> None:
    # Keep reading after the cap so the child never blocks on a full pipe; drop the excess.
    while chunk := pipe.read1(65536):
        room = cap - len(buf)
        if room > 0:
            buf += chunk[:room]
        if len(chunk) > room:
            flags["truncated"] = True
    pipe.close()


def _env(workdir: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    # Allowlist, not denylist: nothing from the parent unless named here. No API keys, no tokens.
    env = {"PATH": os.path.dirname(sys.executable), "HOME": workdir, "TMPDIR": workdir, "TEMP": workdir, "TMP": workdir}
    if os.name == "nt" and "SYSTEMROOT" in os.environ:
        env["SYSTEMROOT"] = os.environ["SYSTEMROOT"]   # Windows Python cannot start without it
    return env


def _kill(proc: subprocess.Popen) -> None:
    if os.name == "nt":
        proc.kill()      # direct child only; a tree needs taskkill /T /F or a Job Object
    else:
        os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL)   # the whole group: grandchildren too


def run_untrusted(code: str, timeout_s: float = 5.0, max_output: int = 64_000) -> Result:
    workdir = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="sbx-")
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with open(os.path.join(workdir, "main.py"), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(code)
        proc = subprocess.Popen(
            [sys.executable, "-I", "-B", "main.py"],    # -I: ignore PYTHON* env and user site; -B: no .pyc
            cwd=workdir, env=_env(workdir),
            stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
            start_new_session=os.name != "nt",          # own process group, so we can kill the tree
        )
        out, err, flags = bytearray(), bytearray(), {"truncated": False}
        readers = [threading.Thread(target=_drain, args=(p, max_output, b, flags), daemon=True)
                   for p, b in ((proc.stdout, out), (proc.stderr, err))]
        for t in readers:
            t.start()
        timed_out = False
        try:
            proc.wait(timeout=timeout_s)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            timed_out = True
            _kill(proc)
            proc.wait()
        for t in readers:
            t.join(timeout=1)    # a surviving grandchild can hold the pipe open; do not hang on it
        return Result(
            None if timed_out else proc.returncode,
            out.decode("utf-8", "replace"), err.decode("utf-8", "replace"),
            timed_out, flags["truncated"], round(time.monotonic() - start, 3),
        )
    finally:
        shutil.rmtree(workdir, ignore_errors=True)

# Test for builds2-sandbox.py: plain asserts, real child processes.
# Run: python interviews/coframe_builds/builds2-sandbox_test.py
import importlib.util
import os
import pathlib
import sys

_p = pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name("builds2-sandbox.py")
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("builds2_sandbox", _p)
m = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec)
sys.modules["builds2_sandbox"] = m
_spec.loader.exec_module(m)

# Normal run: stdout, stderr and the exit code come back structured.
r = m.run_untrusted("import sys\nprint('hi')\nprint('warn', file=sys.stderr)\nsys.exit(3)")
assert (r.exit_code, r.stdout.strip(), r.stderr.strip(), r.timed_out, r.truncated) == (3, "hi", "warn", False, False), r

# A crash is a result, not an exception in the parent.
r = m.run_untrusted("raise ValueError('boom')")
assert r.exit_code == 1 and "ValueError: boom" in r.stderr

# Wall-clock timeout: an infinite loop is killed and reported.
r = m.run_untrusted("while True:\n    pass", timeout_s=0.5)
assert r.timed_out and r.exit_code is None and r.seconds < 5, r

# A sleeping process is caught by wall clock, which a CPU limit would miss.
r = m.run_untrusted("import time\ntime.sleep(30)", timeout_s=0.5)
assert r.timed_out and r.seconds < 5

# Output cap: a megabyte of output is cut to the cap, flagged, and the child is not blocked.
r = m.run_untrusted("print('x' * 1_000_000)", max_output=1000)
assert len(r.stdout) == 1000 and r.truncated and r.exit_code == 0 and not r.timed_out

# Scrubbed environment: a secret in the parent is not visible to the child.
os.environ["FAKE_API_KEY"] = "sk-test-not-real"
r = m.run_untrusted("import os\nprint(os.environ.get('FAKE_API_KEY'))\nprint(sorted(os.environ))")
assert r.stdout.splitlines()[0] == "None", r.stdout
assert "FAKE_API_KEY" not in r.stdout

# Temp working directory: the child runs inside it, and it is gone afterwards.
r = m.run_untrusted("import os\nopen('scratch.txt', 'w').write('x')\nprint(os.getcwd())")
cwd = r.stdout.strip()
assert os.path.basename(cwd).startswith("sbx-") and not os.path.exists(cwd), cwd

print("builds2-sandbox: ok")

topics.title: Reading a trace the way an agent would
topics.brief: Given a flat list of span events from many runs, rebuild each run's tree and answer what someone debugging it asks: how long, how much, what it was waiting on, and what failed. The nuance: wall time is not the sum of durations (calls overlap), cost is summed over leaves only (parents may carry roll-ups), and a failure a retry recovered is not why the run failed.
points: Clarify first: does a parent carry a roll-up of its children's cost, can spans arrive twice or out of order, do timestamps share one clock, and who reads the summary (a person or the fixing agent, which decides how compact it must be).

Tree: group by run id, index children by parent id, keep the first copy of a duplicate. A span whose parent never arrived (dropped by sampling, or still in flight) becomes an orphan root and is flagged, not dropped.
Totals: wall time is the latest end minus the earliest start; cost over llm and tool spans only, tokens over llm spans. Summing every level double counts any parent that carries a total.

Critical path: start at the root's end, take the child that finished last (that is what the parent waited for), jump to that child's start, repeat, then recurse into each chosen child. A parallel call that finished early is off the path, so speeding it up saves nothing.

Failing tool calls: kind tool with status error, sorted by time, each marked recovered when a later sibling of the same name succeeded. The unrecovered one is the cause; recovered ones are noise or a cost problem.
The summary is a prompt: one line of totals, the critical path, one line per failure with its error and offset. That is what a trace-query tool hands an agent, instead of the whole trace.
production: Emit spans in the OpenTelemetry GenAI shape (invoke_agent above chat and execute_tool spans, with model, tool name and token counts) over OTLP so the backend can change. The spec is still in Development status, so expect attribute names to move.
Langfuse accepts OTLP at /api/public/otel and wants run-level attributes such as session and user id on every span, propagated with OpenTelemetry Baggage.
Keep every failed or expensive run and sample the rest (tail-based sampling), which is one reason orphan spans exist and the code must tolerate them; redact secrets and PII before export.

For agents reading their own traces: expose a query tool (a summary by run id, drill-down by span), give the fixing agent the failing span, its inputs and outputs and the diff it applied, cap the repair loop, and send the fix through the normal CI path.

At 100x: this in-memory pass becomes a columnar store such as ClickHouse with per-run aggregates computed at ingest. Anthropic reports multi-agent runs use about 15 times the tokens of a chat, so cost per run becomes an alert, not a report.

mcq.q: A run's root lasts 10 seconds. Its children: plan 0 to 1 s, lint 1 to 2 s, fetch 1 to 5 s, write 5 to 9 s, tests 9 to 10 s. Which change shortens the run?
o: Making lint twice as fast, because it is the first tool call after planning
Making plan twice as fast, but only if lint gets faster at the same time
Running tests in parallel with lint, because both of them are tool calls
Speeding up any of them equally, because wall time is the sum of durations
Making fetch or write faster, because they lie on the critical path and lint does not
mcq.why: Lint overlaps fetch and finishes first, so the parent never waits on it. Only spans on the critical path (plan, fetch, write, tests) move the end time.

mcq.q: Each run's root span carries the total cost of the run, and every llm span carries its own cost. Your report sums cost over all spans. What do you see?
o: The right total, because the root is only one span among many
A total that is too low, because the root replaces its children
About twice the real cost, because the roll-up is counted again
The right total, but only for runs that made no tool calls
A total that changes with the order the spans arrived in
mcq.why: A roll-up repeats its children's numbers. Sum one level only, the leaves (llm and tool spans), and keep roll-ups for display.

mcq.q: A run failed. The trace shows fetch_page failed at 1 s and succeeded at 3 s, and run_tests failed at 9 s. What should the summary handed to the fixing agent lead with?
o: fetch_page, because it failed first and probably caused everything after it
Both failures equally, ordered by the cost of each call
The whole trace, so the agent can decide for itself what matters
run_tests, because fetch_page was recovered by a retry and run_tests was not
The critical path alone, because failures already show in the statuses
mcq.why: A recovered failure did not end the run; the unrecovered one did. Marking recovery explicitly sends the agent to the test failure instead of a transient timeout, and a whole trace wastes its context.

open.q: Here's a JSON dump of spans from our agent runs. Build something that tells the agent why its run failed, and walk me through it.
open.probe: Tree building on messy data, the critical path idea, and designing output for a model to read.
a: Clarify: roll-up costs, duplicates, the clock source, and who reads the output.
Build the tree per run: duplicates kept once, orphans flagged as roots.
Totals: wall time from the earliest start to the latest end; cost and tokens over leaves only.
Critical path by walking back from the root's end through the last-finishing child; failures marked recovered or not.
A compact summary: totals, the path, the unrecovered failure with its error; then expose it as a trace-query tool with drill-down instead of pasting the trace.
Scale: OTLP in, tail sampling that keeps every failed run, aggregates at ingest in a columnar store.

say: I'd treat the output as a prompt, because the reader is an agent. So one line of totals, the critical path, and the failure that wasn't recovered, with its error.
The traps are double counting a parent's roll-up and adding up durations when calls overlap, so those are the two things I'd test first.

Our failure scanner at alfred_ works a bit like this: deterministic signals first, then an LLM classifies what's left. Cheap code narrows it down before a model reads anything, and I'd build this the same way.
avoid: Summing span durations to get wall time.
Pasting the whole trace into the fixing agent's context.

# Test for builds2-traces.py: plain asserts on a hand-built trace.
# Run: python interviews/coframe_builds/builds2-traces_test.py
import importlib.util
import pathlib
import sys

_p = pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name("builds2-traces.py")
_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("builds2_traces", _p)
m = importlib.util.module_from_spec(_spec)
sys.modules["builds2_traces"] = m
_spec.loader.exec_module(m)


def sp(run, sid, parent, name, kind, start, end, tokens=0, cost=0.0, status="ok", **kw):
    return {"run_id": run, "span_id": sid, "parent_id": parent, "name": name, "kind": kind,
            "start": start, "end": end, "tokens": tokens, "cost": cost, "status": status, **kw}


SPANS = [
    # r1: plan, a failing fetch retried, a lint in parallel, write, then tests fail. Root carries a roll-up cost.
    sp("r1", "a", None, "variant_run", "agent", 0, 10, cost=0.036, status="error"),
    sp("r1", "b", "a", "plan", "llm", 0, 1, 1200, 0.006),
    sp("r1", "c", "a", "fetch_page", "tool", 1, 3, status="error", error="timeout after 2s"),
    sp("r1", "d", "a", "lint", "tool", 1, 2),
    sp("r1", "e", "a", "fetch_page", "tool", 3, 5),
    sp("r1", "f", "a", "write_variant", "llm", 5, 9, 3000, 0.030),
    sp("r1", "g", "a", "run_tests", "tool", 9, 10, status="error", error="2 failed: test_cta_visible"),
    sp("r1", "b", "a", "plan", "llm", 0, 1, 1200, 0.006),            # duplicate delivery
    # r2: a sub-agent with two parallel searches. Wall time 4, the sum of leaf durations is 6.
    sp("r2", "s0", None, "research", "agent", 0, 4),
    sp("r2", "s1", "s0", "subagent", "agent", 0, 4),
    sp("r2", "s2", "s1", "plan", "llm", 0, 1, 500, 0.002),
    sp("r2", "s3", "s1", "search_a", "tool", 1, 3, cost=0.001),
    sp("r2", "s4", "s1", "search_b", "tool", 1, 4, cost=0.001),
    # r3: a span whose parent never arrived.
    sp("r3", "x0", None, "run", "agent", 0, 2),
    sp("r3", "x1", "ghost", "late_tool", "tool", 1, 2),
]

runs = m.build(SPANS)
r1 = m.analyse("r1", runs["r1"])
assert r1["spans"] == 7                                  # duplicate dropped
assert r1["wall"] == 10
assert abs(r1["cost"] - 0.036) < 1e-9                    # leaves only, the root roll-up is not added again
assert r1["tokens"] == 4200
assert [s["span_id"] for s in r1["path"]] == ["b", "c", "e", "f", "g"]   # lint ran in parallel, off the path
assert [(f["span"]["span_id"], f["recovered"]) for f in r1["failures"]] == [("c", True), ("g", False)]
assert r1["status"] == "error"

r2 = m.analyse("r2", runs["r2"])
assert r2["wall"] == 4 and r2["status"] == "ok"
assert [s["name"] for s in r2["path"]] == ["plan", "search_b"]
assert abs(r2["cost"] - 0.004) < 1e-9 and r2["tokens"] == 500

r3 = m.analyse("r3", runs["r3"])
assert r3["orphans"] == ["x1"] and r3["path"] == []

text = m.report(SPANS)
print(text)
assert "run r1: error | wall 10.0s | cost $0.0360 | tokens 4,200 | 7 spans" in text
assert "critical path: plan (llm 1.0s) > fetch_page (tool 2.0s) > fetch_page (tool 2.0s) > write_variant (llm 4.0s) > run_tests (tool 1.0s)" in text
assert "failed tool: run_tests at +9.0s: 2 failed: test_cta_visible (NOT recovered)" in text
assert "failed tool: fetch_page at +1.0s: timeout after 2s (recovered by retry)" in text
assert "warning: 1 span(s) with a missing parent: x1" in text
print("builds2-traces: ok")

topics.title: Durable execution for agent runs
topics.brief: A long agent run will be killed mid-way by a deploy, an out-of-memory kill or a reclaimed machine, so progress is recorded step by step and the run resumes from the last completed step. The nuance people miss: every engine gives you at-least-once steps, so a crash between doing a side effect and recording it repeats that step, and only an idempotency key makes the repeat harmless.
points: Step: the unit of recovery. Every LLM call you paid for and every tool call that touches the world is a recorded step; code between steps may re-run.

Replay against history (Temporal): on recovery the workflow code re-runs from the top and recorded activity results are read back, so workflow code must be deterministic: no `Date.now()`, no random, no unrecorded network calls.
Memoization (Inngest, Restate, DBOS): each `step.run` or `ctx.run` result is saved and never re-executed; DBOS writes checkpoints to your own Postgres, one write per step plus two per workflow.

Two kinds of stop: crash recovery is handled by replay; an intentional pause (human approval, waiting for CI) should hold no worker: Temporal signals and timers, Inngest `step.waitForEvent`, Restate awakeables.

In-flight tool call: if the worker died after the tool ran but before the result was saved, the step runs again. Pass an idempotency key such as `run_id:step_name` downstream, or check first ('does a PR for this branch already exist?').

Agent state is bigger than workflow state: persist the message list (or a compacted summary plus notes) at each step boundary, and keep transcripts and screenshots in object storage with only a reference in history.
production: Temporal warns at 10,240 events in one history and terminates a workflow past 51,200 events (Temporal docs); long agent loops call Continue-As-New every N turns and carry state forward.
Temporal has a first-party OpenAI Agents SDK integration: the agent loop runs in the workflow, model calls and I/O tools run as activities.

Anthropic used rainbow deployments so in-flight agents finish on the old code while new runs start on the new code; with replay engines the equivalent is worker versioning, since changing workflow code under a live history breaks determinism.

A Postgres queue claims one job with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, sets a lease, and a reaper requeues rows whose lease expired: fine for a first version, though you end up rebuilding retries, backoff and dead letters yourself as the product grows.

mcq.q: A Temporal workflow function calls `Date.now()` to decide whether to retry a tool. What goes wrong after a worker crash?
o: Nothing, because Temporal stores the return value of every function in the workflow
The replayed code can take a different branch than the history recorded, and the run fails with a non-determinism error
The timestamp is cached by the worker, so the retry decision is skipped on replay
The workflow restarts from the first step and pays again for every LLM call
The following activity runs twice because its idempotency key changed
mcq.why: Temporal replays workflow code against recorded history. A clock read is not recorded, so replay can diverge from what happened; time must come from the workflow API or an activity.

mcq.q: A worker dies after `open_pr` returned but before its result was checkpointed. Which statement holds for every mainstream durable engine?
o: The engine sees the partial step and skips it, because the call already returned
The engine rolls back the PR creation, because the step never committed
The step is marked failed and the run stops until an operator restarts it
The step runs again on resume, so the PR call needs an idempotency key or a pre-check
Only Temporal repeats it; memoizing engines such as DBOS never repeat a step
mcq.why: Steps are at-least-once everywhere: the result was never recorded, so the engine cannot know the call happened. The downstream call must be idempotent.

mcq.q: Four engineers, already on Postgres, agent runs of 5 to 20 minutes. Which first choice fits best?
o: DBOS or a Postgres-backed queue, since checkpoints live in the database you already run
A self-hosted Temporal cluster with a worker fleet, for the strongest durability
Plain serverless functions with no state, retried from the top on failure
Kafka, using consumer offsets as the checkpoint for each agent step
An in-memory step cache in each worker, flushed on graceful shutdown
mcq.why: Short runs and a small team favour the lowest operational cost. Temporal earns its weight on very long, fan-out heavy runs; in-memory and offset tricks lose state on a crash.

open.q: A coding agent has been running for 40 minutes and its worker is killed mid tool call. Walk me through what happens next and what the user sees.
open.probe: Whether you know the step boundary, at-least-once delivery, and where agent state lives.
a: The run is a workflow: each LLM call and tool call is a recorded step, and the message list is persisted at every step boundary.
The lease or heartbeat expires, another worker picks the run up, and replay or memoization skips everything already recorded.
The in-flight tool call runs again, so side-effecting tools carry an idempotency key or check before acting.
The worker reattaches to the sandbox if it is alive, or restores it from a snapshot, and continues the same conversation.
The user sees a 'resumed' event in the trace, not a restart. Caveat: the window between doing and recording narrows but never closes.

say: At alfred_ durable work is Postgres jobs. Lean Python workers claim one with SKIP LOCKED, a job whose worker dies becomes claimable again, and a scheduled sweep catches anything missed.
Side-effecting tools there take idempotency keys, so a retry does not do it twice. That's the part I'd keep in any engine.
I haven't run Temporal in production. For a small team on Postgres I'd start with DBOS or our own queue, and move to Temporal when runs get long, fan out a lot and need signals.
What I'd say about all of them is that they narrow the crash window. They don't close it.
avoid: Saying an engine gives exactly-once side effects. It gives at-least-once steps; exactly-once comes from your idempotency key.
Claiming Temporal or Inngest experience. Say what you read and how you would evaluate it.

topics.title: Isolated execution for agent code
topics.brief: Agents run code they wrote, from prompts that may carry injected instructions, so treat the agent as hostile: pick an isolation boundary, then the network and secrets model. The nuance: a microVM is not automatically safer than gVisor, and the blast radius is set more by what credentials and network the sandbox can reach than by the boundary itself.
points: Container: namespaces and cgroups on a shared host kernel; cheap, but a kernel bug can escape, so harden it: drop capabilities, seccomp, read-only root, non-root user, memory and pids limits.

gVisor: a userspace kernel intercepts syscalls; CPU-bound work runs near native speed, heavy file I/O can be 10 to 200 times slower, and some syscalls and `/proc` files are missing, so some software breaks.
Firecracker microVM: its own guest kernel behind hardware virtualization, boots in under 125 ms with under 5 MiB overhead; security then rests on the hypervisor and its device emulation.

V8 isolate (Cloudflare Workers style): many tenants in one process with very fast starts, but only JavaScript or WebAssembly and no real shell, so it fits edge logic, not an agent that runs `npm test`.

Egress and secrets: no network except one channel to a proxy outside the boundary that allowlists domains, injects short-lived scoped credentials and logs every request; credentials never enter the sandbox.
Snapshots: warm snapshot restores give the sub-second starts; restoring one snapshot many times duplicates RNG state, tokens and ids, so regenerate per-clone secrets and never bake a credential in.
production: Ramp rebuilds a filesystem snapshot every 30 minutes (clone, install, build); each session restores it and syncs only the newest commits, so it starts in seconds with the whole stack inside: Postgres, Redis, services and a browser.

Modal Sandboxes run on gVisor by default with a VM runtime option, a default lifetime of 5 minutes and up to 24 hours; Modal reports 1 million concurrent sandboxes created in under 60 seconds (vendor-reported).
E2B runs Firecracker-based VMs with templates and pause and resume that keeps filesystem and memory.
Claude Code on the web keeps git credentials outside the sandbox; a proxy validates each git operation and attaches a scoped token.
Enforce egress at the network layer, not with `HTTP_PROXY`: Node `fetch` ignores it by default (Node 24 and later can opt in with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`).

mcq.q: An agent needs to run `docker build` and mount a FUSE filesystem inside its sandbox. Which boundary fits?
o: gVisor, because it implements every Linux syscall in userspace
A V8 isolate, because it starts in milliseconds
A hardened container with all capabilities dropped
A bubblewrap OS sandbox on the host kernel
A microVM, because it has its own kernel and runs full Linux
mcq.why: Docker-in-sandbox and FUSE need a real kernel. gVisor leaves some syscalls unimplemented (Modal adds a VM runtime for exactly this), and a hardened container forbids what these need.

mcq.q: You fan out 100 sandboxes from one warm Firecracker snapshot taken after the agent logged in to a package registry. What is the real problem?
o: Restores will be slow because memory pages are copied eagerly
Network connections carry over, so all 100 share one socket
All 100 share the same token and RNG state, so secrets and random ids repeat across clones
Firecracker refuses to restore any snapshot more than once
The snapshot holds only the disk, so the login is lost
mcq.why: A snapshot holds memory, so the token and the generator state are cloned 100 times. Firecracker calls repeated restores insecure; regenerate secrets after restore and never bake credentials in.

mcq.q: You allowlist egress by setting `HTTP_PROXY` inside the sandbox. Why is that not enough?
o: Proxies cannot handle HTTPS, so all TLS traffic is blocked
Some clients ignore it, Node `fetch` included, so a tool can go straight out unless the network blocks it
The variable is visible to the agent, which leaks the proxy's password
The variable only applies to the root user inside containers
Allowlists must be enforced through DNS, never through a proxy
mcq.why: An environment variable is a request, not a control. Put the sandbox on no network with one channel to the proxy, so ignoring the variable gets nowhere.

open.q: We let an agent run arbitrary code from a customer's repo. What would you put around it, and what would you not pay for?
open.probe: Threat model first, then boundary, egress, credentials and limits, and a build-or-buy rule.
a: Threat model: untrusted repo content and prompt injection, so assume the agent is hostile and break the lethal trifecta: private data, untrusted content, a way out.
One sandbox per run, never reused across tenants: gVisor where it is fast and cheap enough, a microVM where I need Docker or FUSE or the code is riskiest.
No network except an allowlisting proxy outside the boundary that injects short-lived scoped tokens and logs every request; no `.env` or cloud credentials mounted, even read-only.
Hard CPU, memory, pids, disk and wall-clock limits plus an idle reaper; snapshots for warm starts with per-clone secrets regenerated.
Buy a managed sandbox first; run our own Firecracker fleet only when cost or compliance forces it.

say: I haven't built a sandboxed code execution fleet, so I'll tell you how I'd reason about it.
The pattern I do know from alfred_ is credentials: our voice worker gets a short-lived scoped token that can never send. I'd do the same here, with the token held by a proxy outside the sandbox.
For the boundary I'd start managed: gVisor-style for most runs, a microVM for anything that needs real Linux. Honestly the boundary matters less than what the sandbox can reach.
avoid: Saying a VM is always safer than gVisor. The hypervisor and device emulation are attack surface too.
Implying you have run E2B, Modal or Firecracker in production.

topics.title: Remote browsers for agents
topics.brief: Agents need a real browser to see a customer's page as a visitor does, to check that a variant renders, and to run end-to-end tests. The nuance: a browser session is stateful, costly and flaky, so the design is mostly pooling, timeouts, cleanup and waiting on conditions, not the automation library.
points: CDP: the Chrome DevTools Protocol is the common wire; Playwright can `connect_over_cdp` to a browser running anywhere, so self-hosted and managed fleets look the same to the agent.
Session pool: cap sessions per tenant, set a timeout on every navigation, close sessions in `finally`; a leaked session is billed and counts against concurrency.
State: a session holds cookies and storage, so after a crash route the run back to the same browser or recreate it from a saved context.
Flakiness: wait on a condition (an element, network idle), never a fixed sleep; anti-bot checks and proxies are the operational pain.
Separation and SSRF: keep the browser apart from the code sandbox so a hostile page cannot reach the agent's secrets, and block internal IP ranges so a page cannot pivot into your network.
production: Coframe's own Browserbase case study: they moved to managed browsers to run many workers at once and drop Playwright scripting and proxy management that did not work reliably in Docker.
Coframe forked Kernel's browser images, neko (a virtual browser in Docker with a WebRTC live view) and an agent-browser CDP CLI in 2026; forks are a weak signal, so ask whether they self-host or buy.
Record each session (screenshots, video, HAR) and attach its URL to the trace, so a person or an agent can see what the browser saw.
Ramp keeps Chromium inside each coding sandbox so the agent can run the app and look at it.

mcq.q: Your agents' browser checks pass locally and fail about one run in ten on the remote fleet. What do you check first?
o: The CDP version, since remote browsers speak an older protocol
Whether Playwright supports remote browsers at all
The model's temperature, since agents pick different selectors
Fixed sleeps where the code should wait on an element or network condition
The screenshot resolution, since remote screens are smaller
mcq.why: Remote browsers add latency and variance, so timing assumptions that held locally break. Waiting on a condition removes the race.

mcq.q: Your browser fleet sits at its concurrency cap, but few agent runs are active. Most likely cause?
o: Sessions never closed after an exception, still holding slots
The fleet scales down whenever CPU use is low
CDP allows only one page per browser at a time
Agents reuse one session across several tenants
Screenshots queue behind each other inside the pool
mcq.why: Leaked sessions are the classic cost and capacity bug. Close in `finally` and run a reaper that reconciles live sessions against active runs.

mcq.q: Why keep the remote browser outside the agent's code sandbox?
o: Because CDP cannot run inside a container
Because browsers need a GPU that sandboxes lack
So the browser can share the agent's cookies faster
Because Playwright requires a separate machine
So a hostile page cannot reach the sandbox's files or credentials
mcq.why: The page is untrusted content. Separating it from the code sandbox keeps a compromised page away from anything worth stealing.

open.q: How do you run a thousand browser sessions for agents without paying for idle ones or leaking them?
open.probe: Pooling, lifecycle, failure handling and cost, not Playwright syntax.
a: A pool with per-tenant caps and admission: a run leases a session, and the lease has a timeout.
Close in `finally`, plus a reaper that reconciles the provider's live sessions against active runs and kills orphans.
On a crash, recreate from a saved context (cookies, storage) instead of keeping sessions alive in case.
Wait on conditions, record screenshots and HAR into the trace, block internal IP ranges.
Buy first, as Coframe did with Browserbase; self-host only if cost or control demands it.

say: I haven't built remote browser infrastructure, so this is how I'd approach it.

Most of the cost is leaks and idle sessions. I'd treat a session as a lease with a timeout, and run a reaper that reconciles against live runs. It's the same shape as our Postgres queue, where a job whose worker dies becomes claimable again.
And I'd ask you whether you self-host today. I saw the Kernel and neko forks.
avoid: Claiming Browserbase or Playwright fleet experience.

topics.title: Orchestration and context management
topics.brief: Pick the least autonomy that solves the problem: a fixed chain or a router before a free agent, and one agent before many. The nuance: multi-agent is a token-spend lever, not free quality; it pays when work parallelises and one context would overflow, and it costs many times the tokens.
points: Patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer; a true agent is for open-ended work where the number of steps cannot be predicted.

Subagents: a lead plans and spawns workers with clean contexts that return condensed results, often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens; use them for independent, verbose work (search, test runs, browsing), not work that shares fine-grained state.
Compaction: summarise near the limit and restart the window; clearing old raw tool results is the lightest version.
Notes outside the window: the agent writes a plan or to-do file and re-reads it, and keeps identifiers (paths, URLs, queries) instead of contents, loading them with tools on demand.
Memory as data: short-term is the run's message list; long-term is keyed by tenant and site (what was tried, what won), readable, deletable, and tenant-scoped on every read.
Tool plumbing: validate arguments against a schema, return errors as tool results so the model can recover, cap output size, and budget turns, tokens and wall time per run.
production: Anthropic's research system beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% on an internal eval, at about 15 times the tokens of chat; token use explained about 80% of the variance on browsing tasks.
Its lead agent saves the plan to external memory because context can be truncated, and subagents write outputs to files instead of relaying everything through the conversation.
Its lead runs subagents synchronously, which becomes the bottleneck; a durable workflow fan-out and join is the platform fix.
Claude Code's compaction keeps the five most recently accessed files alongside the summary.

mcq.q: When does splitting work across subagents beat one agent with more tools?
o: Whenever the task has more than five tools, since one agent cannot hold them
When subtasks share fine-grained state that must stay consistent
When subtasks are independent and verbose, so isolated contexts protect the lead and run in parallel
When the goal is lower token cost, since smaller contexts are cheaper
When the model is weak, since several weak agents average out errors
mcq.why: Subagents buy context isolation and parallelism at a large token cost. Shared state across subagents is where they go wrong.

mcq.q: A long run starts making mistakes after many tool calls with large outputs. What is the lightest fix to try first?
o: Switch to a model with a larger context window
Clear old raw tool results from the context, keeping a short note of each
Restart the run from the first step with a new prompt
Move every tool call into its own subagent
Raise the temperature so the model explores differently
mcq.why: Stale tool output crowds the window and dilutes attention. Clearing it is the lightest form of compaction; bigger windows still degrade.

mcq.q: Why does a production agent return tool errors to the model as tool results instead of raising?
o: Raising would leak the stack trace into the trace store
Providers reject requests that contain exceptions
It keeps the token count lower than a retry would
The model can read the error and correct its next call, instead of the run dying
It lets the gateway retry the call on a different model
mcq.why: Minor tool failures cascade in agents. Returning the error lets the model recover, while budgets still stop a loop that never does.

open.q: When would you use subagents instead of one agent with more tools, and what does it cost you?
open.probe: Least autonomy, token cost, context isolation, and where state lives.
a: Start with the least autonomy: a chain or a router if the steps are known.
Subagents when subtasks are independent and verbose, so each gets a clean context and returns a condensed result.
The cost is tokens: Anthropic reports about 15 times chat for its multi-agent system, so it has to buy real quality.
Not when they share fine-grained state; then one agent with good tools and notes outside the window.
Run the fan-out as durable steps so one dead subagent does not kill the run.

say: I think the default should be the least autonomy that works.
At alfred_ the first pass is a fast model that answers simple turns or escalates to a heavier agent. That's routing, and it's cheaper than a big agent on every turn.
And state the model shouldn't own stays outside it: emails, threads and events are typed entities with ids, and the model sees opaque handles that code maps back to real ids.
So my test for subagents is: are the pieces independent and noisy? Then split. If they share state, don't.
avoid: Saying multi-agent is always better. Name the token cost.

topics.title: Tracing, and agents reading their traces
topics.brief: An agent run is a tree: the run, its turns, then model calls and tool calls under them, and you need to see it, search it, replay it and hand it to an agent so it can debug itself. The nuance: identical prompts produce different runs, so you debug from full traces rather than by reproducing, and an agent should query a trace, not swallow it whole.
points: OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions: an `invoke_agent` or workflow span with `chat` and `execute_tool` spans beneath; attributes such as `gen_ai.operation.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.agent.id`, tool name and call id, and token counts. The spec is in Development status, so names may shift.

Per span: model and parameters, tokens and cost, latency and time to first token, tool arguments, a truncated output plus a pointer to the full blob, retry count, run, tenant and sandbox ids, agent code SHA and prompt version.
Sampling: keep every failed or expensive run and sample the rest (tail-based); redact secrets and PII before export.
Replay, two meanings: viewing a timeline, or re-executing from step N with recorded tool outputs stubbed to test a fix against a real failure; durable step records already hold the inputs.

Agents reading traces: a trace-query tool with a summary view and drill-down by span; the failing span's inputs, output, error and the applied diff; a loop limit; and the fix sent back through the normal CI path.
production: Langfuse accepts OTLP at `/api/public/otel` and wants user and session ids on every span, propagated with OpenTelemetry Baggage and a `BaggageSpanProcessor`.
Emitting through OTLP keeps the backend swappable: Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust, Phoenix, Datadog, or ClickHouse with your own UI.
Anthropic traced decision patterns and interaction structure, not conversation content, to find root causes such as bad search queries and poor source choices.
Self-hosted against SaaS is a data-residency and cost decision, because traces contain customer page content and prompts.

mcq.q: A coding agent is stuck and you want it to fix itself from its own trace. What should it get?
o: A query tool over the trace, plus the failing span's inputs, output, error and the diff it applied
The full raw trace pasted into its context so nothing is missed
Only the final error message, to keep its context small
A screenshot of the trace viewer, read by a vision model
Write access to the trace store so it can correct bad spans
mcq.why: A whole trace floods the context, the last error alone hides the cause. A query tool and the failing span give it evidence it can drill into.

mcq.q: You can afford to keep 10% of traces. Which sampling keeps the most debugging value?
o: Head-based random 10%, decided when each run starts
Keep the first 10% of runs each hour
Keep only runs from the largest tenants
Keep only the root span of every run
Keep every failed or expensive run and sample the healthy rest
mcq.why: Tail-based sampling decides after the run, so the rare failures you need are always kept. Head sampling throws most of them away.

mcq.q: The GenAI conventions are still in Development. Why emit through OTLP rather than a vendor SDK anyway?
o: OTLP guarantees the attribute names are frozen
Vendor SDKs cannot record token counts
OTLP keeps the backend swappable; you accept that names may change and map them
OTLP traces are encrypted end to end by default
Vendors require OTLP for any LLM tracing
mcq.why: The protocol is stable even where the GenAI names are not. A rename is a mapping change; a vendor lock-in is a migration.

open.q: A run took 30 minutes and produced a wrong variant. How do you find out why, and could the agent find out itself?
open.probe: What is in a trace, how you navigate it, replay, and a bounded self-repair loop.
a: Open the run's trace tree and walk back from the wrong output to the first tool result or model call that went wrong.
Check the versions on the span: prompt, model, agent SHA; a fallback model answering is a common culprit.
Re-execute from that step with recorded tool outputs stubbed, change one thing, and compare.
For self-repair, give the agent a trace-query tool and the failing span, not the whole trace, with a loop limit.
Turn the failure into a regression case so it stays fixed.

say: The habit I'd bring is that a model's claim isn't evidence. At alfred_ action claims are checked in code against the turn's tool-execution ledger, so the record decides what actually happened.
We also have a production failure scanner: deterministic signals first, an LLM classifies, and real agent bugs get promoted above a confidence bar.
For an agent reading its own trace, I'd give it a query tool and the one failing span, with a cap on attempts. Dumping the whole trace into context burns it.
avoid: Quoting OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute names as settled. Say the spec is still moving.

topics.title: Evals as a deploy gate
topics.brief: A prompt, model or tool change is a code change and needs a regression gate, but outputs are non-deterministic and partly graded by judges, so the gate has to be statistical. The nuance for Coframe: offline evals only predict the live test, so the live result is the real eval and it flows back into the offline set.
points: Layers: cheap deterministic checks on every PR (it compiles, tests pass, the variant renders without console errors, length and brand rules), judge scores nightly or on a label, and a small human-graded set to calibrate the judge.
Paired and repeated: run old and new on the same cases with several samples each, and gate on a confidence interval for the delta, not one number.
Judge calibration: grade a sample by hand and measure agreement, use a different prompt or model family, blind the judge to which version is which, and judge both orders to control position bias.
Flaky fails: if a PR fails by one case, run the same eval on main; if main fails too it is noise, if main passes it is a regression.
Closing the loop: offline evals gate shipping to a test, the live test is the ground truth, and winners and losers become new offline cases.
production: Promptfoo is an MIT-licensed CLI that exits nonzero on failure, so it can fail a pipeline; Braintrust's GitHub Action posts a score summary on the PR and can block the merge.

Anthropic's research eval started with about 20 representative queries because early changes had large effects, then a rubric judge scoring 0.0 to 1.0, plus people catching hallucinations on unusual queries.

Coframe's winner-prediction post compares screenshot pairs in both orders with a majority vote of about 9 samples, and reports a large drop on its own production pairs against a public benchmark: held-out production data is the honest test.

mcq.q: Your eval gate fails a prompt PR by a single case out of 200. What do you do first?
o: Merge it, since one case is inside any reasonable margin
Run the same eval on main: if main also fails it is noise, if not it is a regression
Delete the failing case, since it is clearly flaky
Rerun the PR's eval until it passes
Raise the judge's temperature to smooth the score
mcq.why: Main is the control for noise. Rerunning until green or deleting cases trains the gate to pass anything.

mcq.q: Which check belongs on every PR rather than on a nightly run?
o: A rubric judge scoring brand voice across the full dataset
A human review of a random sample of outputs
A live A/B test of the new prompt on real traffic
Checks that the generated code builds, tests pass and the variant renders without errors
A pairwise judge comparison over several samples per case
mcq.why: Deterministic checks are cheap and unambiguous, so they run every time. Judges and people cost money and time, so they run on a slower cadence.

mcq.q: You compare prompt A and prompt B with an LLM judge that sees both outputs side by side. What must you control?
o: Position, by judging both orders, and blinding the judge to which version is which
Temperature only, since the judge is otherwise unbiased
Output length, by truncating both to the same size
The judge's model, which must match the generator
Nothing, since side by side cancels out bias
mcq.why: Judges favour a position and can favour their own family. Coframe's own winner-prediction work counterbalances order for this reason.

open.q: How do you stop a prompt change from silently making our generated variants worse?
open.probe: Layers, statistics, judge calibration, and the link to live results.
a: Treat it as a code change with a gate over a fixed set of cases from real pages and real failures.
Fast deterministic checks on every PR; judge scores on a slower cadence, both orders, blinded, calibrated against people.
Paired runs with several samples per case; gate on the interval for the delta, and check a one-case fail against main.
Offline only predicts: the live test is the eval, so guardrails watch rollout and results return to the dataset.

say: At alfred_ what signed off the multi-turn rewrite was a harness of a little over a hundred cases, each from a real production failure, running the real agent against a frozen copy of that user's email and calendar. Tool calls per task went from about 2.5 to 2.2.
Now it's a replay bench over real production turns, graded by a person.
Honestly, it's a sign-off step, not an automated gate on every PR yet. For you I'd put the cheap checks on every PR and keep the judge on a slower cadence, because it costs money.
avoid: Saying alfred_ has an automated eval gate on every PR. It is a sign-off before a ship.

topics.title: LLM gateway, tenancy and quotas
topics.brief: One internal service in front of every model provider holds retries, fallbacks, rate limits, caching, keys and cost, and it is where tenant fairness is enforced. The nuance: agent loops are where a bug becomes a bill, so budgets per run and per tenant matter more than clever routing, and every limit is enforced twice, at admission and at the resource.
points: Reliability: retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `retry-after` on a 429, cool down a failing deployment, fall back across models; a timed-out call may still have been billed.
Fallbacks change behaviour: record which model answered on the trace, and never fall back silently during an eval.
Rate limits at three levels: the provider's tokens per minute, per-tenant fairness, and a per-run budget; a token bucket is the primitive.

Caching: exact-match response caching is safe only for identical prompts at temperature 0; provider prompt caching of a long stable prefix (system prompt, tools, repo context) is the real saving, so put stable content first.

Tenancy: tenant id on every row (Postgres row-level security), per-tenant queues drained fairly so one customer's 500 runs do not starve the rest, quotas on sandboxes, browsers, tokens and wall time, a kill switch and per-tenant pause.
Cost: record input, output and cached tokens per call with tenant, run and feature tags, price them from a versioned table, and stop a run at its hard budget.
production: LiteLLM's router offers shuffle, latency, usage, least-busy and cost-based routing, cooldown after `allowed_fails`, fallback chains, and shared state in Redis across instances.
Buy to start (LiteLLM, Portkey, Cloudflare AI Gateway, OpenRouter) and build only the tenant budgets and trace tagging you cannot get.
When fanning out agents with `asyncio.gather`, pass `return_exceptions=True`: without it the first failure raises out while the other tasks keep running unobserved.
Ramp found human review becomes the bottleneck as agent parallelism rises, so open agent PRs per repo are a quota too.

mcq.q: Provider A returns 429s at peak and every agent retries at once. What happens, and what is the fix?
o: The provider queues the retries and serves them in order, so nothing needs fixing
Retries are free because 429 responses are never billed, so raise the retry count
The gateway should move every tenant to provider B permanently and drop provider A
Agents should cache the 429 and return it to the user as the final answer
Retries land when capacity is lowest and deepen the outage; back off with jitter and admit at the gateway
mcq.why: Synchronised retries are a self-inflicted load spike. Jitter spreads them, retry-after paces them, and admission at the gateway keeps them out of the agents.

mcq.q: Where does caching save the most for a coding agent loop?
o: An exact-match response cache keyed on the whole prompt, at any temperature
Caching tool outputs across tenants so similar repos share results
Provider prompt caching of the stable prefix: system prompt, tools, repo context
A semantic cache that returns answers to similar past questions
Caching the model's final diff and replaying it for retries
mcq.why: Each agent turn resends a long identical prefix, which prompt caching discounts. Exact-match caching rarely hits on agent turns, and cross-tenant caching leaks data.

mcq.q: One customer launches 2,000 runs at once. Which design keeps other customers served?
o: One global FIFO queue, so runs are served in arrival order
Per-tenant queues with a concurrency cap, drained fairly, and quotas checked again at the gateway
Autoscale sandboxes without limit, so nobody waits
Reject every run above the cap with no queue and no status
Move every tenant to a cheaper model until load drops
mcq.why: Fair queues stop the noisy neighbour at admission, and the gateway check protects shared capacity if admission is wrong. The burst waits only for its own tenant.

open.q: Provider rate limits hit at peak. Walk me through the gateway's behaviour, and how you keep one customer from taking all the capacity.
open.probe: Retry discipline, admission, fairness and budgets.
a: Honour retry-after, back off exponentially with jitter, cool down the deployment, then fall back to another provider and record which model answered.
Retries count against a total time budget per run, since a timed-out call may still be billed.
Admission at the gateway: a token bucket for the provider's tokens per minute, then per-tenant shares so a burst queues for that tenant only.
Hard budgets per run and per tenant stop a looping agent; usage is shown to the tenant; an alert fires on queue age.

say: I haven't run a shared gateway for many tenants, so here's how I'd build it.
The first thing I'd fix is the retry storm. Retries come exactly when there's least capacity, so jittered backoff and admission at the gateway, not in each agent.
Then budgets. An agent loop is where a bug turns into a bill, so every run gets a hard token and time cap, and every tenant gets a share.
avoid: Quoting exact discounts for provider prompt caching. Check the provider's docs first.

topics.title: CI/CD for agents that open PRs
topics.brief: The control plane lives outside the sandbox and the agent's brain runs in a durable workflow, while its hands (shell, tests, browser) run in the sandbox; the agent pushes a branch and normal CI takes over. The nuance: the agent never merges its own PR to a protected branch, and review capacity, not compute, becomes the bottleneck.
points: Brain and hands: the loop and LLM calls run as cheap workflow steps; code execution and the browser run in a sandbox joined by an API, so a dead sandbox does not lose the run.

Compute homes: serverless suits short bursty steps and edge logic but has time limits and no real disk; long-lived workers suit long steps and warm caches; engines that call your HTTP endpoints give serverless economics per step.
Scoped credentials: a GitHub App installation token limited to one repo and `agent/*` branches, no workflow-file edits, held by a git proxy outside the sandbox.
Same CI as people, plus agent checks: a diff size limit, no CI config or lockfile changes unless asked, secret scanning.
Self-repair with a cap: the agent reads CI logs and its trace, tries a fix up to about three times, then hands over to a person with the evidence.
Ship safely: a preview URL per PR, experiment-scoped or flagged changes so a bad one is turned off by config, and prompt, model and agent SHA stamped on every PR.
production: Ramp's background agent: a control plane takes the trigger (Slack, a ticket, the web), restores a sandbox from a recent snapshot, the agent iterates on failures, pushes a branch and opens a PR; Ramp reports it now accounts for over half of merged PRs.
Claude Code on the web pushes through a proxy that validates git operations and attaches a scoped token, so the token never sits in the sandbox.
An idempotency key on the branch name stops a retried step from opening a duplicate PR.

mcq.q: How should a coding agent get push access to GitHub?
o: A personal access token in the sandbox's environment, rotated daily
A deploy key baked into the warm snapshot for fast starts
The user's own OAuth token, so commits carry their name
A git proxy outside the sandbox holds a repo-scoped App token and validates each push
An org-wide admin token, restricted by an instruction in the prompt
mcq.why: Anything inside the sandbox can be exfiltrated by an injected agent. The proxy holds the credential, checks branch and file rules, and logs the operation.

mcq.q: An agent keeps failing CI and pushing new fixes. What bounds it?
o: A cap of a few fix attempts, then a handover to a person with the trace and logs
Let it loop until CI passes, since each attempt is cheap
Let it edit the CI config so the failing check is skipped
Merge after three attempts if the diff is small
Restart it from scratch with a new prompt each time
mcq.why: Self-repair loops can circle or game the check. A cap plus a handover with evidence keeps cost bounded and the decision with a person.

mcq.q: Why run the agent loop in a workflow and the code in a sandbox, rather than everything in the sandbox?
o: Sandboxes cannot make outbound calls to model providers
Workflow engines run LLM calls faster than sandboxes do
It removes the need for idempotency keys on tool calls
Sandboxes are billed per request rather than per second
The sandbox can die or pause without losing the run, and the loop runs on cheap stateless workers
mcq.why: Splitting brain from hands makes the expensive, fragile unit disposable. The run's state lives in the workflow, so a sandbox is restored, not mourned.

open.q: How do you let an agent fix its own failing CI without it going in circles or making unsafe changes?
open.probe: Credentials, policy, a bounded loop, and a person at the merge.
a: Same CI as people plus agent rules: diff size, no CI config or lockfile edits, secret scanning.
The agent reads CI logs and its trace; at most about three attempts, then a handover with the evidence.
A scoped token through a git proxy, `agent/*` branches only; it never merges to a protected branch.
Small PRs with a trace link, test evidence and a preview URL, because review capacity is the real bottleneck.

say: The closest thing I've built is the confirm flow at alfred_. Side-effecting tools first return a preview, and only an explicit confirm executes. There are code floors no prompt can override.
An agent opening a PR is the preview. The merge is the confirm, and a person or a policy gate owns it.
I'd cap the self-fix loop at a few attempts and make the PR easy to review, because reviewers run out before compute does.
avoid: Proposing auto-merge for agent PRs without a policy tier and a rollback path.

modules.title: Coframe-shaped design
modules.blurb: Run a 45-minute design on Coframe's own problems: the variant pipeline, edge delivery, assignment, the bandit, guardrails and a fleet of coding agents, naming the hard part and what breaks at 100x.

topics.title: The variant pipeline, in the 45-minute shape
topics.brief: Run a design answer as requirements, the hard part, the boxes, two deep dives, then what breaks at 100x. For Coframe the pipeline is generate, validate in a real browser, approve, deploy, monitor and learn, and the hard part is not generation: it is shipping changes onto someone else's revenue page without breaking it, then learning from thin traffic.
points: Requirements first: is a variant copy, a component or arbitrary code; does it go in at the edge or in the browser; how much traffic per page; how fast do conversions arrive; how much risk of a broken page is acceptable.

Boxes: ingest (remote browsers capture DOM, styles, a screenshot), ideation agent (page, goal metric, site memory), implementation agent (sandbox plus browser), QA gate, human approval, edge serving, measurement, optimiser, learning loop.
Validate in a real browser: screenshot, console errors, accessibility and layout shift; failures go back to the agent with the evidence and a retry cap.
Copy against code: copy-only variants are cheap, safe and measurable; code variants multiply risk and need sandboxed rendering and a rollback path.
Durable and traced: the whole run is a durable workflow with a trace, and approval is a pause that holds no worker.
production: Coframe's product analyses the site, generates ideas and variants, a person approves in-app, then it deploys, optimises, personalises by segment and tracks results; its site mentions approval gates before deployment and automatic fallback systems.
Coframe uses Browserbase workers to extract site code and styles in parallel.
Coframe targets sites with 200,000 or more monthly visitors (lower for high-ticket), because bandits and tests need traffic.
Pavlo's take-homes all end with 'Productionization': how would you make it a scalable system. Have that answer ready for anything you draw.

mcq.q: In a 45-minute design of Coframe's variant pipeline, what is the hard part to name early?
o: Getting the model to write a good headline, since generation is the product
Choosing between Python and TypeScript for the agent runtime
Shipping generated changes onto a live customer page without breaking it, then learning from thin traffic
Storing variants, since thousands of rows will need sharding
Rendering screenshots fast enough for the ideation agent
mcq.why: Generation is the easy, visible part. The risk sits on someone else's revenue page and in measuring with little traffic, so that is where the deep dives go.

mcq.q: Which kind of variant should a first version favour, and why?
o: Copy-only changes: cheap, safe to render, easy to roll back and measure
Full-page code rewrites, since they move conversion the most
Component swaps, since they need no browser check
Visual redesigns, since judges score them most reliably
A variant per visitor, since traffic then splits evenly
mcq.why: Risk grows with how much of the page a variant can change. Copy is the cheapest thing that still moves the metric.

mcq.q: Where does the human approval step belong in the run?
o: Before ideation, so people choose hypotheses before anything is generated
After deployment, as a review of what already went live
Inside the agent loop, as a tool the agent calls each turn
As a durable pause after the QA gate, holding no worker while it waits
Nowhere: the QA gate's judge replaces it at scale
mcq.why: People should review what passed the automatic checks, before it reaches the edge, and a wait of hours must not hold a worker.

open.q: Design an agent that generates and ships website variants, and the infrastructure to test them.
open.probe: Whether you clarify, find the hard part, and keep the risk at the delivery edge.
a: Clarify: copy or code, edge or browser injection, traffic per page, conversion lag, acceptable risk.
Name the hard part: safe delivery onto someone else's page, and learning from little traffic.
Boxes: ingest with remote browsers, ideation with site memory, implementation in a sandbox, a browser QA gate, approval, edge serving, events, optimiser.
Deep dive one: the QA gate and automatic rollback. Deep dive two: assignment and the bandit.
At 100x: browser and model capacity, review throughput, event volume; buy browsers and sandboxes first.

say: I'd start by asking what a variant is, copy or code, because that sets the risk for everything after it.
The hard part isn't writing the headline. It's putting a change on someone else's checkout page and being sure it can't break it.
So the shape I'd draw is: generate, check it in a real browser, a person approves, ship at the edge, watch the guardrails, and feed what won back into memory.
avoid: Spending the first ten minutes on the model prompt. Coframe's risk is delivery and measurement.

topics.title: Edge delivery without flicker or breakage
topics.brief: Flicker happens when the original renders and a script swaps in the variant afterwards; every fix trades first paint against reach. The nuance: Coframe's own snippet hides the body for up to one second and fails open, which is right for showing the page, while the gate that lets a generated change reach a customer's page should fail closed.
points: Client-side swap with anti-flicker: works on any site, but hiding the body delays first paint and LCP by up to the timeout.
Edge decision: middleware assigns the variant and rewrites to a variant route before any HTML is sent, so the control never shows and no client script runs; it needs control of the serving path.
Fail open against fail closed: if the SDK is slow or errors, show the original page (Coframe: a 1 s timeout and `onerror` both reveal it); if a variant fails a check, it does not ship.
CSP: a strict `script-src` blocks injected inline scripts and styles unless they carry the page's nonce; Coframe offers a CSP nonce option.

SPA routes and hydration: a client-side navigation does not reload the page, so variants must reapply on route change; mutating DOM before React hydrates it can cause a hydration mismatch, and React may re-render that part and wipe the change.
CDN caching: never cache one visitor's variant for everyone; key the cache on the variant, or serve each variant from its own cacheable path.
production: Coframe's snippet: a synchronous inline script in `<head>` (not a tag manager, because anti-flicker is on), body opacity set to 0 through a CSS variable, `setTimeout(show, 1000)`, then the SDK loads async from its edge; `script.onerror` also reveals the page.
Escape hatches: `?cf_disable` in the URL, a feature-flag emergency shutdown, tracking-only mode, and anti-flicker modes that hide the body, only marked elements, or all but marked elements.
Vercel's A/B write-up assigns in Edge Middleware, stores the assignment in a cookie and rewrites to the variant route, so there is no layout shift and no client script.
Log the exposure when the visitor actually sees the changed element, or the analysis is diluted by visitors who never reached it.

mcq.q: Coframe's SDK fails to load on a slow mobile network. What should the visitor see?
o: A blank page until the SDK loads, so the control never shows
The original page after the timeout, because display fails open
An error banner asking the visitor to reload
The last variant cached from the visitor's previous session
A server-rendered fallback variant chosen at the edge
mcq.why: A third-party script must never cost a customer the page. The 1 s timeout and `onerror` both reveal the original.

mcq.q: An agent-generated variant fails the browser check on mobile Safari. What should the deploy gate do?
o: Ship it to desktop only, since Safari is a minority
Ship it at a lower traffic share and let the bandit judge it
Ship it and rely on the one-second anti-flicker timeout
Retry the check until it passes, then ship it
Block it from shipping, because generated changes fail closed
mcq.why: Showing the page fails open; letting a change through fails closed. A broken variant is a defect, not an experiment arm.

mcq.q: A variant applies on the landing page of a Next.js site, then disappears after a client-side navigation. Most likely cause?
o: The route changed without a page load, so the variant was never reapplied to the new view
The CDN served a cached control page for the new route
The visitor's cookie expired between the two pages
CSP blocked the script on the second page only
The bandit reassigned the visitor on the new route
mcq.why: In a single-page app the snippet ran once at load. Route changes need a listener (history changes or a DOM observer) to reapply variants.

mcq.q: Your edge rewrite works, but some visitors get another visitor's variant. Most likely cause?
o: The hash function collides for similar visitor ids
The rewrite added a redirect that dropped the cookie
The CDN cached a variant response without keying on the variant or cookie
Edge workers share memory across requests by design
The browser shared the assignment cookie across sites
mcq.why: The cache is where edge personalisation leaks. Vary on the variant, or give each variant its own cacheable path.

open.q: Our script hides the body for up to a second. Is that acceptable? What are the alternatives and their costs?
open.probe: Flicker against performance, fail-open behaviour, and what changes when you control the edge.
a: It is a deliberate trade: no flash of the original, at the cost of first paint and LCP up to the timeout, and it fails open.
Shrink the cost: hide only the elements being changed instead of the whole body.
Where serving is under our control, decide at the edge and rewrite before HTML is sent: no flicker, no client script, but the cache must key on the variant.
Cover the long tail: CSP nonce, reapply on SPA route changes, no mutation before hydration, a kill switch.

say: I think a one-second ceiling that fails open is a reasonable default for a script on someone else's page. The page always shows.
I'd push toward hiding only the elements being changed, and toward the edge wherever you control serving.

It's a bit like my voice agent. A lean agent answers on the call while the main agent works in parallel, so the caller never waits on the slow path. Same idea here: the visitor never waits on the SDK.
avoid: Saying the edge removes all risk. The CDN cache and hydration are where it breaks next.

topics.title: Assignment and sticky bucketing
topics.brief: Hash the experiment id, a salt and the visitor id into [0, 1) and compare against cumulative weights: stateless, stable, and independent across experiments. The nuance: when a bandit changes the weights, a pure hash moves existing visitors between variants, so the first assignment has to be persisted.
points: Hash: `sha256(exp + ':' + salt + ':' + visitor)` mapped to [0, 1); same visitor, same variant, no lookup table; changing the salt reshuffles everyone on purpose.
Experiment id in the key: without it the same visitors land in the first half of every test, which correlates experiments.
Sticky: keep the visitor id in a first-party cookie, and re-derive it from a login id when the cookie is lost.
Bandit trap: new weights shift the bucket boundaries; persist the first assignment (cookie or server record) and apply new weights only to new visitors, or edit a fixed bucket-to-variant map.
Sample ratio mismatch: a 50/50 test showing 52/48 at large n means broken assignment, logging, redirects or bots; a chi-square test alerting at p < 0.001, plus A/A tests.
production: Groups of 5,200 and 4,800 on a 50/50 test give a chi-square p-value of about 6.3e-05: investigate before reading any result.
Over 20,000 ids, a sha256 bucket gave a control share of 0.499 on a 50/50 split.
Coframe's status object exposes `userToken`, `sessionId` and `variantsAndElements`, which is where a sticky assignment shows when you debug.
Microsoft Research's SRM write-up lists the usual causes: assignment bugs, logging loss, redirects and bot filtering.

mcq.q: You run Thompson sampling and recompute weights hourly. Assignment is a pure hash against the current weights. What goes wrong?
o: Nothing, because the hash of a visitor id never changes
New visitors all land in the first variant until the next hour
The hash collides more often as weights become uneven
Returning visitors move between variants as boundaries shift, corrupting both experience and data
The bandit stops learning because assignments are cached
mcq.why: The hash is stable but the cut points move. Persist the first assignment, or edit at the bucket level, so only new visitors see new weights.

mcq.q: A 50/50 test shows 50,800 against 49,200 visitors. What is the right reading?
o: Normal noise at this size, so proceed with the analysis
A sample ratio mismatch: check assignment, logging, redirects and bots before trusting any result
The larger arm is winning, since more visitors stayed in it
Rebalance by dropping visitors from the larger arm
Lower the significance threshold to compensate
mcq.why: At 100,000 visitors an 800 gap gives a χ² near 25.6, a p-value far below 0.001. Something is losing or adding visitors to one arm.

mcq.q: Why include the experiment id in the hash input?
o: So the same visitor gets the same variant in every experiment
So the hash is harder to reverse, for privacy
So changing weights does not move existing visitors
So the cookie can be shared across domains
So assignment in one experiment is independent of every other
mcq.why: Without it, a visitor's bucket is the same in every test, so the same people always share arms and experiments contaminate each other.

open.q: How do you know your hash-based assignment is not biased, and how do you keep it sticky when the bandit changes weights?
open.probe: Hashing correctly, persistence under moving weights, and SRM and A/A as the proof.
a: A deterministic hash of experiment, salt and visitor id into [0, 1), against cumulative weights.
The experiment id in the key keeps tests independent; the salt reshuffles on purpose.
Persist the first assignment, because moving weights move boundaries; new weights apply to new visitors.
Prove it: an SRM chi-square alarm at p < 0.001 on every test, and A/A tests before trusting the pipeline.

say: I'd hash experiment, salt and visitor id, and compare against the weights. No table, and the same person always gets the same thing.
The catch with a bandit is that the weights move, so I'd store the first assignment and only give new weights to new visitors.
And I'd never trust it without an SRM check. A 52/48 split on a 50/50 test means something's broken before it means anything else.
avoid: Saying a hash guarantees balanced traffic. It balances ids, not bots, redirects or logging loss.
