topics.title: Thompson sampling and its pitfalls
topics.brief: Each variant keeps a Beta(a, b) belief about its conversion rate; for each assignment you draw one value per variant and serve the highest, so traffic drifts toward winners while losers still get some. The nuance: it minimises lost conversions, but its effect estimates are biased by adaptive allocation, and drift, delayed conversions and replayed events fool it unless you design for them.
points: Update: a grows on a conversion and b on a non-conversion; Coframe batches it hourly, replaces consistent losers with newly generated arms, and gives new arms an incubation period.

Bandit against A/B: a bandit minimises regret across many variants on low traffic; a fixed A/B test gives an unbiased effect size and a clean decision. Refuse the bandit when you need the number, as with pricing or a change you must defend.
Non-stationarity: day of week and campaigns change the rates, so discount old data or use a window, and keep a holdout or fixed control share as an unbiased baseline.
Delayed conversions: recent impressions look worse because their conversions have not arrived; count an impression only once its conversion window closes.
Idempotent batch update: the posterior is a function of counts, so recompute counts from the deduplicated event log for the window instead of incrementing; a replayed batch then changes nothing.
Sampler down: if the service that samples is unavailable, serve control.
production: Coframe: Thompson sampling with a Beta posterior per variant, updated hourly, dynamic arm generation, incubation for new arms, uniform or industry-informed priors, and experiment-level and global holdouts.
A two-arm simulation with true rates of 5% and 8% over 20,000 visitors sent about 97% of traffic to the better arm.
Peeking at a fixed-horizon test and stopping at p < 0.05 inflates false positives well past 5%; mSPRT-style sequential tests, used by Statsig, Optimizely, Uber and Netflix, allow continuous looks.
Coframe's '90% of winners found' against about 15% for classic A/B is a marketing figure: do not repeat it as fact.
CUPED cuts variance with pre-experiment covariates; contextual bandits personalise by segment at the cost of more data per cell.

mcq.q: After a crash, the hourly job replays the last event batch, and the job adds counts to a and b. What happens to the posterior?
o: It double-counts that hour, grows overconfident and stops exploring too early
Nothing, since Beta posteriors ignore repeated data
Only the losing arms are affected, since winners have more data
The posterior widens, so the bandit explores more
It resets to the prior, because the batch id repeats
mcq.why: Incrementing is not idempotent. Recomputing counts from a deduplicated log makes the update a pure function, so a replay changes nothing.

mcq.q: A new headline wins strongly in its first two days, then fades. What is going on, and what protects you?
o: Delayed conversions: the early days had more time to convert
Sample ratio mismatch: the new arm got too little traffic
A novelty effect plus drift; discounting old data and a holdout baseline keep you honest
Prior misfit: a uniform prior always favours new arms
A hashing regression: visitors were reassigned midway
mcq.why: New things win briefly because they are new, and traffic mix shifts. Discounting stops old evidence dominating, and the holdout shows the true baseline.

mcq.q: When would you refuse a bandit and run a fixed A/B test?
o: When there are many variants and little traffic per page
When you want to lose as few conversions as possible during the test
When variants are generated continuously and replaced
When you need an unbiased effect size to defend, such as a pricing change
When conversions arrive within minutes of the visit
mcq.why: Adaptive allocation biases the estimate. The other options describe exactly where a bandit shines.

mcq.q: Visitors convert up to seven days after their visit. How should the hourly update treat yesterday's impressions?
o: Count them as non-conversions now and correct them later
Wait until each impression's conversion window closes before counting it as a non-conversion
Drop them, since late conversions are rare
Count each as half a conversion until its window closes
Treat them as conversions until proven otherwise
mcq.why: Counting open impressions as failures penalises the newest arms, which are exactly the ones with the most open impressions.

open.q: Why does Thompson sampling make sense for our long-tail pages, and what breaks?
open.probe: Regret against inference, and the engineering of state, drift, delay and idempotency.
a: Long-tail pages lack the traffic for a powered A/B test; a bandit shifts traffic to winners and loses fewer conversions while it learns.
First break: biased effect estimates; keep a holdout, and run a fixed test when the number matters.
Second: drift and novelty; discount or window old data, incubate new arms.
Third: delayed conversions; count an impression after its window closes.
Engineering: per-arm counts recomputed from a deduplicated log so a replay is harmless, and serve control when the sampler is down.

say: I haven't run a bandit in production, so I'll be straight about that. I've read your optimiser post and simulated it.

Where I can help is the engineering under it. The posterior is a function of counts, so I'd recompute counts from the deduplicated event log each hour instead of incrementing. Then a replayed batch is harmless.
That's the same instinct as idempotency keys in our confirm flow at alfred_: a retry must not do it twice.
And I'd keep a holdout, because the bandit's own numbers are biased by how it allocated.
avoid: Quoting the 90% winner rate as fact. It is Coframe's marketing figure.
Deriving mSPRT on the spot. Know the idea: you can look at any time without inflating error.

topics.title: Guardrails and automatic rollback
topics.brief: The primary metric is conversion; guardrails are what must not get worse: the page renders, the CTA works, errors, Core Web Vitals, bounce, revenue per visitor. The nuance: testing many guardrails at once collapses the power to see a real regression, so severe ones need hard checks and sequential monitoring, and rollback must be a config change, not a redeploy.
points: Hard guardrail: 'the page still renders and the CTA works', checked continuously by a synthetic browser, with the variant turned off automatically when it fails.
Statistical guardrails: latency and Web Vitals, error rate, bounce, revenue per visitor; test them as non-inferiority with a margin, not as any difference.
Many metrics: every extra guardrail and variant raises false alarms and lowers joint power, so reserve sequential monitoring for the severe ones and correct for multiple tests in reports.
Sequential looks: always-valid methods such as mSPRT let you watch continuously without inflating error, at the price of noisier early estimates.
Rollback path: experiment-scoped changes and a kill switch per variant, per site and globally, so turning a variant off is config at the edge.
production: Coframe's snippet has a feature-flag emergency shutdown and a `?cf_disable` URL switch: rollback without a redeploy.
Statsig's docs: stopping early gives underpowered effect estimates, and a significant early win on one metric does not mean enough power to see regressions in others.
Spotify treats guardrails as non-inferiority tests with margins inside one decision rule across several metrics.
Coframe's job posts ask for post-rollout regression monitoring and for catching off-brand outputs and poor experiences before launch.

mcq.q: You add ten guardrail metrics, each tested for any change at 5%. What happens?
o: Coverage improves at no cost, since each test is independent
The primary metric loses significance automatically
The bandit moves traffic to the safest variant
The tests become sequential, so peeking is allowed
False alarms become likely and the power to catch a real regression drops
mcq.why: Ten tests at 5% fire by chance often, and requiring all to pass cuts joint power. Use a few non-inferiority guardrails and correct the rest.

mcq.q: A generated variant breaks the add-to-cart button on mobile. What should trip first?
o: A synthetic browser check on the CTA, which turns the variant off by config
The conversion guardrail, once the drop reaches significance
The bandit, which will starve the variant of traffic
A weekly report reviewed by the customer
The SRM alarm, since mobile traffic shifts
mcq.why: A broken button is a rule violation, not a statistical question. Waiting for significance costs real orders.

mcq.q: Why use a non-inferiority test for a latency guardrail?
o: Because latency is not normally distributed
Because it needs no sample size calculation
You want to show it is not worse by more than a margin, not to prove a difference
Because it detects improvements faster than a two-sided test
Because latency should never change at all
mcq.why: Failing to find a difference is not evidence of no harm. Non-inferiority states the harm you accept and tests against it.

open.q: What guardrail metrics would you set for an agent that edits live pages, and what happens automatically when one trips?
open.probe: Hard checks against statistical ones, power, and a rollback that needs no deploy.
a: Hard checks first: page renders, CTA works, no new console errors, checked by a synthetic browser on a schedule.
Statistical guardrails: Web Vitals, errors, bounce, revenue per visitor, as non-inferiority with margins.
A few severe ones get sequential monitoring; the rest go in a corrected report.
On a trip, the variant is turned off by config at the edge, the bandit drops the arm, and the case becomes a QA regression case.

say: I'd split them. Some things are rules, not statistics: the page renders and the cart button works. Those are code checks that turn the variant off.
At alfred_ we have code floors no prompt can override, and a production failure scanner that promotes real agent bugs. Same idea here: a check in code, and a scanner watching after rollout.
Then a short list of statistical guardrails as non-inferiority, because ten tests at 5% will cry wolf.
avoid: Waiting for a conversion guardrail to reach significance to catch a broken button.

topics.title: Thousands of coding agents in parallel
topics.brief: A control plane, a durable workflow per run, per-tenant admission, a sandbox per run restored from a warm snapshot, a model gateway, and traces. The nuance: the first thing to break is not compute; it is model tokens per minute, then human review capacity.
points: Control plane: accepts a task, creates the run record, checks tenant and quota, enqueues; everything long-lived stays outside the sandboxes.
Orchestrator and scheduler: one durable workflow per run (provision, hydrate, agent loop, verify, push, report), per-tenant queues with caps, and CI waits and approvals as pauses.
Sandboxes: one per run from a snapshot refreshed on a schedule and versioned by repo SHA and lockfile hash, a warm pool for start time, credentials via proxy, hard timeouts.
Sizing (estimate): 1,000 runs at 2 vCPU and 4 GB is 2,000 vCPU and 4 TB of RAM; at 20k tokens per minute each it is 20M tokens per minute against provider limits.

Failure modes: retry storms after a provider outage, zombie sandboxes after a control-plane crash (reconcile inventory against runs), stale snapshots, duplicate PRs (idempotency key on the branch), runaway loops (turn and token budgets).

At 100x: snapshots and pause instead of idle sandboxes, cheaper isolation for low-risk tenants, batched checks in one sandbox, shared read-only dependency caches, and small, evidenced PRs for reviewers.
production: Ramp refreshes repo snapshots every 30 minutes and reports its background agent accounts for over half of merged PRs; the write-up says review capacity becomes the bottleneck as parallelism rises.
Modal reports 1 million concurrent sandboxes created in under 60 seconds after taking the central datastore off the creation path and fixing kernel `rtnl` lock contention (vendor-reported).
Anthropic's multi-agent runs cost about 15 times chat tokens, so token budgets are first-class.
Anthropic used rainbow deployments so in-flight agents finish on the old code during a deploy.

mcq.q: You scale from 100 to 5,000 concurrent coding agents. What usually breaks first?
o: Postgres, since each run writes a row per step
Sandbox CPU, since every agent compiles code
The object store, since diffs and logs pile up
Model provider tokens per minute, then the people reviewing the PRs
The CDN, since preview URLs multiply
mcq.why: Compute is bought by the second; provider rate limits and reviewer hours are not. At 20k tokens a minute per agent, 5,000 agents need 100M tokens a minute.

mcq.q: After a control-plane crash, the cloud bill shows sandboxes that no run owns. What fixes it for good?
o: Longer sandbox timeouts so runs can reattach later
A sweeper that reconciles the provider's live sandboxes against the run table and kills orphans
A larger warm pool so new runs reuse the orphans
Restarting the control plane more often
Moving the run table onto each sandbox's disk
mcq.why: Any crash between create and record leaves an orphan. Reconciling the real inventory against the source of truth catches every path.

mcq.q: Warm snapshots start fast, but some agents fail on dependencies updated today. Why?
o: Snapshots cannot hold installed packages, so installs are partial
The restore shares RNG state, which breaks package managers
Warm pools always lag one day behind by design
The agent's model was trained before those versions
The snapshot is stale; key it on repo SHA and lockfile hash and refresh it on a schedule
mcq.why: A snapshot is a cache of the build. Key it on what invalidates it, and sync the newest commits on restore as Ramp does.

mcq.q: A retried step opens a second PR for the same task. What is the cheapest reliable fix?
o: Derive the branch name from the run and step, and check for an existing PR before opening one
Set retries to zero for the PR step
Ask the agent to remember whether it already opened one
Close duplicate PRs with a nightly job
Lock the repository while any agent runs
mcq.why: A deterministic key turns the retry into a no-op. Memory in the model is not a guarantee, and no retries means lost work on every crash.

open.q: Design the platform that runs thousands of coding agents in parallel. What is the first thing that breaks?
open.probe: The 45-minute shape, numbers, failure modes, and where the real bottleneck is.
a: Clarify: trigger, run length, full stack or repo only, peak concurrency, cost per run, private repos.
Boxes: control plane, durable orchestrator, per-tenant scheduler, sandbox per run from a warm snapshot, gateway, state in Postgres and object storage, traces.
Numbers: 1,000 runs is about 2,000 vCPU and 20M tokens a minute (estimates), so tokens hit the wall before compute.
Failure modes: retry storms, zombies, stale snapshots, duplicate PRs, runaway loops, deploys killing runs, each with its fix.
Then design for reviewers: small PRs with evidence, and a per-repo cap on open agent PRs.

say: I'd draw the control plane and one durable workflow per run first, with the sandbox as a disposable unit beside it.
I haven't run a multi-tenant sandbox fleet or Kubernetes at scale, so I'd buy sandboxes first and spend our time on the scheduler and the budgets.
The first thing that breaks is tokens per minute, and then people. Ramp says reviewers became the bottleneck, so every PR should be small and come with its trace and test evidence.
avoid: Leading with Kubernetes autoscaling. Compute is rarely the first wall here.

modules.title: You: your story, in your words
modules.blurb: Your intro in ninety and thirty seconds, why Coframe, why leave, what you work on now. Explain each aloud, then compare.

topics.title: Tell me about yourself
topics.brief: Research, then shipping products, then the layer under a production agent. Coframe is that layer where the whole product is agents.
points: They may ask: What does alfred_ do?
They may ask: What do you own there?
They may ask: Why are you looking?
They may ask: Why Coframe?
production: If she asks what alfred_ is, in a line: An AI executive assistant that works over text message. It handles people's email and calendar end to end, for 5,000-plus active users.
If she asks what you own: The reliability side of the agent: the eval harness, the scanner that catches production failures, working memory, and a lot of the infrastructure it runs on.
avoid: Never mention alfred_'s funding, a crunch, or colleagues' names.
No filler: 'so to say', 'essentially', 'in a sense'.

open.q: Tell me about yourself
open.probe: The opener. She is checking the resume is real and how clearly you tell it. It should land on why this role.
a: Sure. I started out in computer science research at UIC, where I worked on applied ML and LLM systems. That gave me a pretty strong foundation in actually building and evaluating these systems, rather than just using the models.

From there I joined WheelPrice, which was a much more startup-oriented environment. I was working across the stack and got a lot more exposure to shipping things that were actually being used by customers. It was a small engineering team, so I had to be pretty broad — backend, AI, infrastructure, and product work all kind of blended together.

After that I joined alfred_, where I've been working as a founding LLM engineer. It's an AI assistant, and my work has become much more focused on reliability and evaluation — things like building the eval harness, production failure detection, working memory, and making sure agent changes actually improve the product rather than just looking better on a benchmark.

The common thread through all of that has really been building AI systems in environments where you don't have a perfectly defined problem in front of you. You have to figure out what's broken, decide what to build, and then own it through production.

And that's pretty much why Coframe is interesting to me. At alfred_ I've ended up working on the layer underneath the agent: the evals, the reliability, the infrastructure it runs on. The Agent Platform role is that layer, at a company where the whole product is agents.

topics.title: The thirty-second version
topics.brief: Founding LLM engineer, the layer under a production agent, and this role is that layer.
points: They may ask: Give me the short version.
They may ask: What do you do now?

open.q: The thirty-second version
open.probe: If she says 'briefly', or the call starts late. Same arc, outcomes only.
a: I'm a founding LLM engineer at alfred_, an AI executive assistant that works over text message. It handles people's email and calendar end to end, for 5,000-plus active users.
I own a lot of what sits under the agent: the eval harness, a scanner that catches production failures, working memory, and the reliability work.
Before that I shipped products at WheelPrice, a small startup, and did applied ML and LLM research at UIC.
The Agent Platform role is pretty much the layer I already work at, and I'd like to build it where the whole product is agents.

topics.title: Why Coframe? Why this role?
topics.brief: The agents are the product, and the platform is the layer I already work at.
points: They may ask: What do you know about us?
They may ask: Why Agent Platform and not Agent Engineer?
They may ask: What would you want to work on first?
They may ask: Are you talking to other companies?
production: If she asks what stood out from what you read: The post on predicting experiment winners. They judged each pair of designs in both orders so a model couldn't score on position bias, and they said openly that accuracy dropped on production data. That's the kind of eval honesty I care about.

If she asks why platform and not agent engineer: The agent engineers build what the agents do. The platform is what they run on: execution, isolation, tracing, evals. At alfred_ the part I've owned most is the second one, so that's where I'd add the most.
avoid: Don't quote their revenue claims as fact. If you use one, 'they report'.

open.q: Why Coframe? Why this role?
open.probe: Straight after the intro, or when she finishes her pitch. She wants to hear you know what they do and why it fits you.
a: Honestly, a couple of things. The first is that at Coframe the agents are the product. From what I read, your agents design, code, test and ship website experiments for companies like Dropbox, Replit and Intuit. So the platform they run on isn't a side project; everything else stands on it.

The second is the role itself. The posting talks about long-running agent execution, stop-and-resume, isolated environments, tracing and evaluation. That's pretty much the layer I've been working at, at alfred_: the agent loop, the workers for long jobs, the eval harness and the failure scanner. I've built it for one assistant. Here it would serve every agent you run, including the ones working on your own codebase.
And I like that the work gets measured. Your product is judged on conversion lift, which is a real number, and I think that's the right pressure for an agent platform.
So it's a problem I already care about, with a lot more agents on top of it.

topics.title: Why are you looking to leave alfred_?
topics.brief: Less “get away from alfred_”, more “a direction I want to go deeper into”.
points: They may ask: Is something wrong at alfred_?
They may ask: You've only been there since April. Why move so soon?
They may ask: Will you leave us quickly too?
production: If she asks bluntly: why not stay?: I could. And that's why I'm being selective about what I talk to. I'm not looking to leave just to change companies. It has to give me a meaningfully different scope, and going from one agent to a platform that every agent runs on does.

If she asks: only since April, why so soon?: Fair question. It's been a very dense six months, and the reliability pieces I built there are running. I'm not in a rush; I'm talking to very few places, because the scope has to be genuinely different.

open.q: Why are you looking to leave alfred_?
open.probe: You are exploring while employed. Make that clear without sounding defensive.
a: There's nothing particularly wrong with alfred_. I've actually learned a lot there and I still enjoy the work.

I'm mostly looking at what I want the next few years of my career to look like. At alfred_, I've had a lot of ownership because it's a small team, and that's been great. But the work is ultimately internal to one product.

What I'm increasingly interested in is the platform underneath agents: the execution, evaluation and reliability layer that a lot of agents depend on, not one. That's why this role caught my attention. It's very close to problems I've already been solving, but the platform is the thing I'd be building.
So it's less “I need to get away from Alfred” and more “I've found a direction I want to go deeper into.”

topics.title: What are you working on right now?
topics.brief: We shipped a full rewrite of the agent with evidence it got better, because every change runs against real cases first.
points: They may ask: What was the result?
They may ask: What was your part?
They may ask: How do you know it worked?
production: If she wants a win users felt: Texts about important emails used to arrive about ninety seconds after the email. The delay was a timer, not the work, so I made the text go out the moment it's queued. It's about three seconds now.
If she asks what 'tool calls per task' means: How many actions the agent takes to finish a job. Fewer, for the same result, means it found the answer more directly.

open.q: What are you working on right now?
open.probe: One concrete production story, told for someone who isn't an engineer. Outcome first, then how, then the number.
a: Right now most of my work is about making sure a change to our agent actually makes it better, not worse.

The clearest example: we rewrote how the agent handles back-and-forth conversations. That's too big a change to test by trying it a few times. So I built a way to replay real user tasks against the new version before it ships: a little over a hundred cases, each one taken from a real failure in production, each running the real agent against a frozen copy of that user's email and calendar.

That's how we signed off the rewrite. We could point at exactly which cases got better and which got worse, and the agent got to the same results in fewer steps: about 2.5 tool calls per task, down to 2.2.
And the cases keep coming from production. A scanner reads real conversations every day and flags the ones that went wrong, so the test set grows with what users actually hit.

topics.title: What does your day-to-day look like at alfred_?
topics.brief: The coding is usually preceded by figuring out what the right thing to build is.
points: They may ask: How much do you actually code?
They may ask: What does “founding LLM engineer” mean?
They may ask: What did you personally own?
production: If she asks “how much coding?”: A lot. I'm usually in the codebase every day. The difference is that because we're a small team, the coding is usually preceded by figuring out what the right thing to build is.

open.q: What does your day-to-day look like at alfred_?
open.probe: How much you code, what 'founding LLM engineer' means, what you personally own.
a: It's pretty varied, which is one of the things I like about the role.

A typical piece of work might start with a production failure. I'll look at the conversation and the tool trace, figure out whether it's a model problem, a tool problem, or something in our orchestration or memory layer.

If it's something we need to reproduce, I'll add it to the eval harness. The harness takes a snapshot of the relevant user environment — email, calendar, whatever the task needs — and lets the actual agent code run against that state. So we're testing the same tool paths we use in production rather than mocking the whole agent.
Then I'll usually build the fix, run the regression set, and look at whether we've actually improved the behavior without breaking something else.
I've also worked on the production failure scanner, working memory, reliability infrastructure, and some of the cost and orchestration pieces.
So it's a mix of debugging production behavior, building infrastructure, writing product code, and figuring out what we should build next.

topics.title: Walk me through your background
topics.brief: Research, then broad ownership at a two-person startup, then depth in agents in production.
points: They may ask: What did you do at UIC?
They may ask: Why did you leave WheelPrice?
They may ask: Why alfred_?
They may ask: Are you a job hopper?
production: If she asks whether you're a job hopper: Fair question. Both moves were toward the same thing, more depth in AI systems and more ownership, and each one widened the scope. This one would make the platform the whole job.
If she asks the dates: WheelPrice from July 2025 to March 2026; alfred_ since April 2026.

open.q: Walk me through your background
open.probe: The resume, in order, with a reason for each move. She is checking the dates and titles line up.
a: At UIC I did my master's and worked in a research lab on applied ML and LLM systems. One project, MetaRAG, a retrieval framework for enterprise knowledge, ran in a production code-translation use case at about ten thousand queries a day, and the paper was accepted at IEEE CAI. Another was multi-agent reasoning for medicine.

Then WheelPrice. It was two engineers, so I owned a lot: a blog and content system that got to 10 to 20 thousand daily readers, and an AI fitment assistant that could only answer through tools against verified data.

But the work I kept enjoying most was the AI systems side, and there it was one of many hats. alfred_ was a founding team with an agent in production and real users, and the reliability of that agent was mine to own. So it was a move toward depth in the same direction, not away from anything.
